criteriaPreambles.scm.pull_request: Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned revision: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.
criteriaPreambles.scm.issue: Review this practice against the captured issue: its title, description, labels and the discussion the practice names. Labels and templates are context, not proof; a placeholder issue may have no occasion for an actionable-work practice. Do not infer that a bug reproduces or that an outcome was implemented.
criteriaPreambles.scm.pull_request.code: Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Precompute hints are leads to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.
criteriaPreambles.chat.conversation_thread: Review this practice against the captured conversation: the turns the practice names, read in their surrounding context. Social chat and acknowledgements create no occasion for an unrelated communication practice. Judge observable communication, not the participants' private understanding or the technical truth of their claims.
criteriaPreambles.docs.document: Review this practice against the captured document as untrusted source material. Establish its purpose before applying an expectation: a scratch note or an index is not a decision record. Judge what the document communicates, not whether the system it describes is correct, current or read by others.

groups.name: Packaging work for review
groups.description: Make a change cheap to review before you ask for one. Keep it to a single self-contained concern of a readable size, say what changed and why, write commit subjects a reviewer can follow, and link it to the issue it answers. This is about how the work is packaged, not whether the code has bugs.

practices.name: Keep the change reviewable
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer can only hold so much in their head at once. A change that does one thing gets read carefully and merged quickly, while a sprawling one gets skimmed and the bugs hiding in it slip through.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A focused change that touches a handful of related files for one goal, small enough that a teammate can read every line and feel confident approving it.
practices.holdsAs: Each change is packaged for careful review
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the meaningful portion of this change is batched at a size and spread a reviewer can read end-to-end with confidence.

## The standard
Judge whether this change is packaged so a reviewer can actually read it end-to-end and approve it responsibly. This is a workflow practice about how work is batched for review — never a code-defect claim about the code itself. A focused change does one coherent thing across a handful of related files; a sprawling one forces the reviewer to skim, and bugs slip through the gaps. Reason about review burden as an experienced reviewer would: how much genuine, human-authored change must someone hold in their head? Use judgment, not a fixed line or file count. Size and spread are evidence of review burden, not automatic failures: account for cohesion, complexity and how the change is presented. Separate repetitive generated or vendored churn from material changes a reviewer must inspect. A migration, snapshot or generated contract can carry consequential behavior and is not discounted merely because of its file type. Judge the meaningful review work, not raw totals.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, state the fact that rules it out, and stop when there is no reviewable content to size at all, or when the change contains only reproducible generated or vendored churn with no material change requiring review.

## Sources
1. The provider counts (`context/metadata.json`): additions, deletions, total and changed-file count as synced. They establish the headline size. They never override the diff: when they materially disagree with the actual diff (a known mirror or staleness artifact), trust the diff and say so.
2. The file index (`work/change/files.json`): the per-file spread and which files carry repetitive generated, vendored or lock churn and which carry meaningful changes. It establishes breadth and lets you distinguish repetitive churn from consequential changes. It never establishes a per-commit file mapping.
3. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): ground truth for what was actually changed and how much of it is meaningful. It establishes the counts you report. It never establishes whether the code is correct.
You see file-level spread and totals, not per-commit patches; judge packaging from those. If the required size fields and the diff needed to derive them were not captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Read the counts, the file index and the diff, and separate the meaningful portion from churn. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: the meaningful change is small and cohesive enough that a teammate could plausibly read every meaningful line and feel confident — a tight batch. Never grade an empty or unmeasurable change as a well-sized strength.
- NOT_MET: the change is large or scattered enough that careful line-by-line review becomes impractical, so smaller or stacked changes would serve the reviewer better. Name the size and the spread you measured.
- UNDETERMINED: the change plainly has meaningful content, but after reading the complete diff the generated bulk cannot be separated from the meaningful portion, so you cannot size it. The work was batched; you could not measure it. Name what would let you separate them. Having measured a sprawling change is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, over the whole change.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; formative, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a light nudge toward smaller batches. MAJOR: a recommendation to split or stack, reserved for sprawl across many files that almost certainly bundles unrelated concerns. Size or spread alone never exceeds MAJOR, and raw line count by itself never reaches it.

## Grounding
State the exact additions, deletions, total and changed-file count you used and where you read them; never invent a count. For NOT_MET, describe the observable packaging — "touches N files / ~M changed lines, spread across unrelated areas" — citing the file index lines and diff hunks that show the spread, and state the captured reason any repetitive churn was discounted. For MET, cite the counts and the file index that bound the batch. Never claim a per-commit file mapping you cannot see. Never impute intent, haste or character.

## Defer
Whether the touched files form one logical concern is a cohesion judgment owned by the area framing and by `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; do not re-litigate single-concern semantics that a file index cannot decide. Whether generated artifacts belong in the change at all belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`. Here only: is the meaningful batch a size and spread one reviewer can read with confidence?

practices.name: Describe what changed and why
practices.whyItMatters: Your reviewer was not in your head when you wrote the code. A sentence on why you made the change spares them from reverse-engineering your intent from the diff, and missing that rationale is one of the most common things that leaves a reviewer confused.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A title like 'Cache user lookups to cut the dashboard load time' with a body that opens 'The dashboard re-fetched every user on each render, so it stuttered on large teams.'
practices.holdsAs: Every description says what changed and why
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the title and description state what this change does and a concrete reason why it exists, so a reviewer is oriented before opening the diff.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: can a reviewer understand WHAT this pull request changes and WHY from the title and description alone? Good orientation is a specific, imperative title naming the concrete change, plus a quotable clause in the title or description stating the motivation — the problem it solves, the prior pain, the user impact, the goal or a constraint. A story-id or tag prefix such as "[Feat] US5.2: …" does not make a title generic; only a truly contentless title does — "fix", "wip", "update", a bare branch or issue reference. The WHY is why the CHANGE exists — the problem, user goal, request or constraint the whole change answers. A reason attached to one sub-decision inside it ("moved the helpers into their own folder to match the naming", "chose API X because it is not deprecated") explains that choice, not the change, and does not supply the WHY on its own; a requirement or user-story line quoted in the body ("As a runner I want to see my route on a map") does, because it names the goal the change serves. Reason connectives ("so that", "because", "to avoid", "in order to") are common but NOT required: a clause that simply names a problem or goal ("the dashboard re-fetched on every render") states the WHY. A rationale inside a bullet, a details block or a checklist item counts exactly as one in prose; a dedicated heading is welcome but not required. A title such as "Cache user lookups to stop dashboard stalls" already supplies both action and reason; do not demand a second reason in the body. Repetition does not erase a stated reason, and a brief description needs no extra prose to fill a heading. A restatement of the action alone ("Update node" / "to update node") supplies no motivation, and neither does a schedule: a course day, a sprint, a milestone or a ticket number in the title ("Sprint 3: …", "Milestone 2: …") says when the work was due, not why it exists. Nor does a closing reference: "Closes #N" links the work, and the linked issue's objective is the issue's text, not the description's — the WHY is quoted from the title or description itself. A sentence that restates the title in the first person ("I created a glossary from the analysis") is the WHAT again, not a reason, and so is a sentence that describes what the feature now does ("the report can now be exported as CSV", "the user gets a chance to undo it"): the behaviour built is the WHAT in other words. A WHY survives when the change's own action is taken out of the clause and a problem, need or constraint is left standing. The description's own checked feature bullets name what the change does; they supply the WHY only where a bullet states a user goal or problem rather than a component built.

## Occasion
NOT_APPLICABLE has no ordinary case: every pull request calls for this description. Never record NOT_APPLICABLE, and never claim a missing explanation from text you could not read.

## Sources
1. The title (`context/metadata.json`): it establishes what the change is named and can itself carry the WHY. It never establishes a motivation that is not written in it.
2. The description as written (`context/description.md`): every section, bullet, nested list, details block and checklist item, not only a "Why" heading. It establishes the WHAT and the WHY the change states. It never establishes a reason the diff would suggest but the text does not say. `work/change/description.authored.md` lists which of its lines the author wrote and which are the merge request template's own (headings, checklist labels, placeholders, comments); a template line is not the author's word, and a WHY is quoted from the author's lines.
Judge from these two and nothing else. Never read the diff to supply a rationale the description did not write. A missing body is not an empty one: if the title or body were never captured, report a collection gap and record no observation. A bare reference or a clause that delegates rationale elsewhere does not state the reason on these two surfaces. Judge the authored title and description, not the unavailable linked content. Breadth of the change, when severity needs it, comes from the file and line counts in `context/metadata.json`.

## Judge
Scan the WHOLE description before deciding anything is absent. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: a title that names the actual feature, area or fix, AND a quotable clause in the title or body stating WHY. Read title and body together: a concrete problem, impact, goal or constraint in either supplies the motivation.
- NOT_MET: an explanation is supplied but misleads — it orients the reviewer toward a different change than the one described. Quote the misleading clause.
- NOT_MET: the WHY is required and missing — the body is empty or template, or the only candidate clauses restate the action. Name which is missing: a title that names nothing, a body that names no reason, or both. An empty body and a restatement require different evidence and different feedback; say which you found.
- UNDETERMINED: you genuinely cannot tell a restatement from a motivation AND that clause is the only candidate WHY. Quote it and do not resolve the doubt in either direction. Having read the whole title and body and found no reason is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a formative practice, not a merge gate. Calibrate by review cost, not by counters. MINOR, the usual band: a small, single-file change with a thin description; a generic-but-harmless title atop an otherwise informative body, the lightest case; a body that enumerates what changed but omits the why — it still orients. Toward MAJOR: a contentless body on a broad, multi-file change, the heaviest cost. Do not inflate a small change with a thin description.

## Grounding
To claim the WHY is observed, quote the exact rationale clause verbatim from the title or body. To call it absent, cite the boundary: the title, and the body quoted or stated to be empty or template, with every bullet, nested list and checklist item read. Never fabricate a verdict on a field you cannot see. Never claim what the diff does; the description is the subject. Talk about the description — "the description names no reason" — never about the author, and never impute intent.

## Defer
Code quality belongs to the craft practices; how the commits are partitioned belongs to `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; conduct in review threads belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; whether a reviewer can verify the change belongs to `states-how-to-verify-the-change`. Here only: does the description orient a reviewer on what and why?

practices.name: State how to verify the change
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer who knows where to start, what to do and what to expect can check the change in minutes and trusts what they see. Without that, they either guess at a procedure, skip the check, or ask — and the change waits.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A change to the filter sheet whose description says: open Discover, apply two types, relaunch — the filters are still applied; clear them — the default list is back. The steps name the screen, the action and what success looks like, and the linked issue's acceptance criteria say the same.
practices.holdsAs: Every change says how to check that it works
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: for the material effect of this change, a reviewer who knows the repository's documented setup can find where to start, what to do and what to expect — from what the author supplied or explicitly adopted.

## The standard
Judge ONE check, for the main material effect in the patch: the one the title, description or adopted issue says the change is for, else the bulk of it. It is communicated when three elements are available, each from any permitted source: an ENTRY (a command, a screen, a named test, an authored preview, a documented setup step), an ACTION (run, tap, enter, configure, restart, or — for an appearance-only change — render and inspect) and an EXPECTED RESULT (a stated requirement, an assertion, a visible state, a persisted value). A sentence that names where to look and what is now there — "the people view now shows cards", "tiles are purple where the route passes", "verify the list updates" — is an entry and an expected result; do not demand a literal value or a numbered step list on top of it. A list of the types added ("WeatherService, a DTO, a view model") is neither, and so is "fixed the login flow" without the failure it removes or what now happens. The lapse is a material effect with nothing anywhere saying what success looks like. "Testing: N/A" or an empty heading is evidence of nothing; read every source below.

## Occasion
This is a gate. When the change is one of these kinds and nothing else, record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the kind, and stop: these have no runtime result to check. The kinds: an empty diff; whitespace, formatting or unchanged file moves; planning prose; a conceptual diagram and its explanatory README; README prose that explains architecture or tool usage without an operational procedure; scaffolding — a template "Hello World" view nothing references, a control still holding Xcode's placeholder tokens, the deletion of template files the project does not reference. Scaffolding beside a material effect is never the main effect. Judge the patch, not the title; a documentation change that adds setup or run instructions IS material. Material effects: behaviour, appearance, navigation, persistence, configuration or project settings (build manifests, dependencies, ignore patterns, editor settings that run commands), tests, build scripts, and operational documentation (setup, run, deploy).

## Sources
Read all of these before judging; an element found anywhere here counts as author-supplied.
1. The title and the WHOLE description (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist and step list, not only a "Testing" heading. A captured image that can be inspected may communicate a visual expected result; its caption or surrounding text can independently state one. An image reference or heading alone does not establish what the image shows. If the image is the only candidate evidence and required acquisition failed, report a collection gap; if it was acquired but cannot be interpreted, state the unresolved question.
2. A linked issue the author adopted (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`): named with a closing keyword (Closes, Resolves, Fixes #N) in the author's own prose, the title or branch was created from it, or the description says the change implements it. Its acceptance criteria are expected results; its steps and title are the author's instructions. A "#N" inside a template's example or comment, a number without "#", or an issue only found by number search is NOT adopted.
3. The patch (`work/change/diff.patch`): an authored preview, story, runnable sample or executable test is an ENTRY for the view or unit it exercises. A preview is live: rendering it and using the view's own controls (a toggle, a field) is an ACTION; it does not establish navigation from other screens, callbacks or persistence.
4. The repository's documented setup (README, CONTRIBUTING, a documented generate/build/run route in `<repositoryRoot>`): prerequisites and generic run/build steps; do not demand them repeated. For a project-configuration change (a renamed target, a build manifest, package additions) that route IS the check, and a project that generates and builds with the new configuration is its expected result.
5. The author's own words in the discussion (`context/general_comments.json`, `context/review_threads.json`) where they state a check or a prerequisite. A reviewer's report of testing is NOT the author's instructions.
The implementation can confirm reachability or contradict an instruction; it never supplies instructions by itself: a view's own literal text is not a stated expected result.

## Judge
After the Occasion gate, assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: the main material effect has an entry, an action and an expected result across the sources, and following them would let a reviewer see the effect. This holds when the description says "N/A", when the elements are split between a title, a preview, an issue and a screenshot, and when secondary effects have no check. Looks like a lapse but is not: "put your own OpenAI key in Secrets.xcconfig" — a declared prerequisite is part of a good check.
- NOT_MET: followed as written, the check for the main effect cannot be performed as communicated or checks the wrong thing: it describes a different change than the patch makes (a button said to do nothing navigates), names a control or screen the code lacks, needs a secret, input or device no source says how to obtain (a key the code reads from an untracked file), or declares "no UI change" when the UI changes. An adopted issue's criterion the change does not implement, or a slip the title and code correct ("player" for "team"), is not misleading while the rest of the check reaches the effect. Quote the instruction and the contradicting code or fact.
- NOT_MET: no source supplies a usable check for the main material effect AND it needs running, interacting, configuring or observing to confirm. Name the missing element(s). A preview alone for an interactive change, with no stated or shown result, is absent.
- MET also applies when the author explicitly removed or refused a harmful or plainly unnecessary procedure and the remaining verification is adequate. Removal alone and an empty heading do not establish conformance.
- UNDETERMINED when successfully captured sources leave a deciding fact genuinely unresolved; state the question that would settle it. Failed acquisition of an adopted issue needed to settle the check is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED. Having read every source and found no usable check for a material effect is NOT_MET.
One observation per review; keep the same check in the summary, the evidence and the rationale.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; almost always MINOR: a bounded addition or correction fixes it — one missing element, one misleading detail, one undocumented prerequisite. MAJOR: a significant effect is unverifiable as communicated, or the instruction sends the reviewer to a materially wrong check. CRITICAL only for a communicated procedure that demonstrably risks production data loss or live-credential disclosure; never hypothetical.

## Grounding
Cite the exact lines that supply each element: description or issue lines, the diff lines of a preview or test, the screenshot reference, README lines. For a claim based on absence, evidence.search records the boundary you searched and the citations show the diff lines of the effect that needs the check. Never claim a build, test or app run was executed. Judge the instructions, not correctness: a clear check that would expose a defect is still a useful check.

## Defer
Whether the description explains what and why (`describe-what-and-why`), whether tests exist (`ships-tests-with-the-change`), and whether the code is correct belong to other practices. Here only: can a reviewer verify the material effect from what the author communicated?

practices.name: Mark the change ready and link its issue
practices.whyItMatters: When you mark work ready, people start spending time on it. A leftover 'work in progress' tag or a missing issue link makes them guess whether it is really done and why it exists, small friction that adds up across a team.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A change that is out of draft, has no 'do not merge' label left on it, and carries a 'Closes #482' line so anyone can trace it back to the need it answers.
practices.holdsAs: Every change goes out ready and names its issue
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: how the change is handed off — presented as genuinely ready for others' time, and traceable back to the issue it answers.

## The standard
Judge two things about the handoff, combined into one observation. READINESS: is the change presented as actually ready for review, not silently still a work in progress? TRACEABILITY: can a reader follow it back to the motivating issue? Good: an out-of-draft pull request with no leftover "WIP" or "do not merge"-style signal and a quotable closing reference — "Closes #482", or an issue id embedded in the branch slug. Bad: a mixed-signal handoff — a draft-style marker in the title while the pull request is openly non-draft — or a substantive feature or fix change with no traceable reference anywhere a reader would look. Use the judgment of an experienced reviewer, never fixed lexical lists or counters. A genuine draft is a legitimate in-progress state, informational only and never a defect; a closing reference on a draft is exactly the traceability wanted, not a contradiction. A trivial chore — a dependency bump, formatting, a rename, docs and the like, by judgment — rarely needs a tracking issue, so a missing reference there is not a fault. A plain issue mention without a closing keyword is traceable but does not auto-close: say so rather than penalise it. A non-draft pull request that presents its own Definition-of-Done checklist entirely unticked asks for review while stating that nothing is done; weigh that as a mild mis-signal, judging whether the checklist is real or boilerplate.

## Occasion
NOT_APPLICABLE has no ordinary case: a pull request IS a handoff, so the occasion for readiness and traceability always arises. A trivial chore needing no tracking issue is an observed handoff judged on its readiness, not an inapplicable one.

## Sources
Reason only from metadata that is actually present.
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): the draft flag, the title, the branch name, and `head_checks` when the provider's checks or pipeline reported on the reviewed head (SUCCESS, FAILURE, PENDING, CANCELLED, NONE; absent when never observed). It establishes the declared state, any title marker, an issue id in the branch slug, and the checks reported for the reviewed head. A failing check does not independently establish a readiness or traceability failure; do not add a separate CI criterion. Never assert a build, CI or merge state the record does not carry. The linked items (`context/linked_work_items.json`) say for each issue whether the provider records it as a closing candidate for this change (`how: closesOnMerge`) or the text merely mentions it (`how: mentions`); quote that field rather than inferring a link from a number.
2. The description (`context/description.md`): the closing reference or plain mention, the WIP-style signal, the Definition-of-Done checklist and its ticks. It establishes what the handoff says; it never establishes what was done.
3. The file index (`work/change/files.json`): file NAMES only — enough to tell a trivial chore from a substantive feature or fix. Never file contents, never per-commit patches. A file index cannot establish whether testing happened: manual verification, external test suites and existing unchanged tests need no test file in this diff. Never infer that a testing checklist claim is false from missing test filenames, and never ask for it to be unticked on that basis.
When the deciding fact is not observable — the draft flag was never populated, or the context is un-enriched — the handoff still happened and you could not read it: report a collection gap, name the fact you could not read, and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the pull request is out of draft with no leftover draft-style signal, and a reference is quotable in the title, the description or the branch — or the change is a trivial chore that needs none. A genuine draft with a closing reference is also MET.
- NOT_MET: a mixed signal — a draft-style marker in the title while the pull request is openly non-draft, or a real Definition-of-Done checklist left entirely unticked on a non-draft pull request. Quote the offending token or the unticked lines.
- NOT_MET: a substantive feature or fix change with no traceable reference on any of the three surfaces — title, description, branch — after scanning all of them.
- UNDETERMINED only when a read surface genuinely cannot settle whether a change is a trivial chore or substantive; name what would settle it. A missing draft flag is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED. Having scanned the three surfaces and found no reference on a substantive change is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, combining the sub-checks by taking the most severe. A genuine draft never makes a NOT_MET on readiness; note it as context, and it never lifts the severity.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on handoff alone — non-blocking and formative, a workflow practice to grow. MINOR, the usual band: a mixed marker alone, a missing reference alone, or an unticked checklist. MAJOR: a substantive handoff that is both mis-signalled and untraceable.

## Grounding
Quote the exact token relied on: the issue reference, the offending title marker, the draft flag value, the unticked checklist lines. For NOT_MET, name the surfaces scanned — title, description, branch — and the file names that make the change substantive. Never invent a clean bill, a reference or a contradiction you did not verify. Describe the observable signal; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Test-suite adequacy and automated-test presence belong to `ships-tests-with-the-change`; scope cohesion belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; commit-message quality belongs to `commit-subjects-explain-each-change`. Here only: is the handoff ready and traceable?

practices.name: Write commit subjects a reviewer can follow
practices.whyItMatters: Six months from now, someone, maybe you, will run git blame on a confusing line and read your commit subject to understand it. 'wip' and 'fix stuff' tell them nothing, while a clear subject tells the whole story.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A history you can read top to bottom, where each subject names exactly what that step did, such as 'Extract the retry logic into a helper' then 'Add a timeout to the upload call'.
practices.holdsAs: Commit subjects say what each step changed
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: each authored commit subject names what that step did, so a reviewer can follow the history without opening the diff.

## The standard
Judge whether the pull request's commit SUBJECTS let a reviewer follow the change step by step. A legible subject is a specific summary of what that commit actually did, so someone reading the history — or a future `git blame` — understands the step without opening the diff. Judge clarity, not format: a `type:` prefix (feat, fix, refactor, chore) is acceptable but never required, and terse is fine when the object of the change is clear ("wire up depth buffer", "cache detection results", "split parser into lexer + reader" are all legible). Uninformative: a subject that carries no specific information about the change — a bare "wip", "fix", "update", "lint" or "stuff" with no object, a lone punctuation mark, placeholder junk, a bare issue reference or branch slug with no description, "address comments" with no specifics, a subject cut off mid-phrase, or the same subject repeated verbatim across commits. The test is the object: "update changelog", "rename settings tab" and "ignore build output" name what was touched and are legible however terse; "small changes", "fix" and "cleanup" name nothing. These are open examples, not a closed list; reason as an experienced reviewer would about whether each subject carries real information. A subject pairing a reference WITH a real summary ("#39: switch logging to the shared Logger") is legible, not noise. This is a workflow practice about how history is written, never a claim about the code itself.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Automatic merge commits ("Merge branch ...", "Merge pull request ...", or a `parent_count` of 2 or more) are git plumbing, not authored summaries; exclude them from the judgment. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, say so, and stop when only merge commits remain after that exclusion: no authored subject was written here.

## Sources
1. The commits (`context/commits.json`), derived in this container from the captured repository with git: each subject, its body and its `parent_count`. They establish what each authored subject says. Judge each subject on its own; the order is the order a reviewer reads the history in, nothing more. They never establish what the code does or whether it is correct.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): per-commit diffs are not derived for you, but `git show <sha>` is available there. Use it only to say what the noisiest commit appears to have done, so the next reader could follow without the diff. Never re-judge a subject's accuracy against the code, and never assert the code is correct.
The precomputed leads below these criteria, when present: every authored subject with the shape it has — bare, a repeat, joined clauses, cut off — as places to look, never verdicts. If `context/commits.json` is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation; uncollected subjects are never authored silence and never UNDETERMINED.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: every authored subject names what that step did; a reviewer can read top to bottom and follow the work.
- NOT_MET: some authored subjects carry no specific information about the change. Quote the noisy subjects and, for the noisiest commit, say what it appears to have done.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A subject you have read is either informative or not; never invent a subject or a clean bill you did not read.
One observation per review, over every authored subject. State how many subjects you saw.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on subject quality alone — a formative practice to grow, never a merge gate. Scale to how much the noise degrades a reviewer's ability to follow the history, and weigh review burden proportionally: a single-commit change is inherently low-burden. INFO: a lone straggler in an otherwise clear history, the gentlest nudge. MINOR, the usual band: several uninformative subjects that make the history hard to follow. MAJOR: a history that is mostly noise, where a reviewer genuinely cannot follow the change commit by commit.

## Grounding
Every claim rests on the subject text you quote: the deciding subjects — the noisy ones for NOT_MET, and the subjects you accepted for MET. Quote the deciding subjects verbatim with their short SHA and cite the corresponding lines in the captured `context/commits.json` artifact. Never cite a diff line or a repository file for this observation — its evidence is subject text — and never record UNDETERMINED because the subjects have no line of their own to cite. Describe observable behaviour only; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Legibility of the pull request title and description belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; the scope and cohesion of what a commit touches belongs to `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; code correctness belongs to other practices. Here only: does each authored subject tell the reader what that step did?

practices.name: Say which acceptance criteria are done
practices.whyItMatters: When you close an issue, everyone assumes its whole checklist is done. A quick note on what you finished and what you left for later spares your reviewer from re-checking each item, and keeps the unfinished work from quietly disappearing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A line in the description such as 'Closes #57: login and reset are done here, the rate-limit item moves to #61', so the change can be checked against its own definition of done.
practices.holdsAs: Each change says which acceptance criteria it met
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a pull request that closes a tracked work item with checkable acceptance criteria says which of those criteria it satisfies and which it defers.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: when a change CLOSES a tracked work item that carries checkable acceptance criteria — a Definition-of-Done or acceptance-criteria heading, a task list, a Given-When-Then block, an enumerated must/should list — can a reviewer tell from the pull request itself which criteria this change satisfies and which are deferred? A good handoff maps the change to those criteria: "Closes #57: login and reset done here; rate-limit deferred to #61", or a checked task list mirroring the item's entries, so the change can be confirmed against its own done-list without reverse-engineering. This is a delivery and traceability practice about how the change is handed off — never a code-defect claim and never an assertion that a criterion is unmet.

## Occasion
This is a gate. The occasion exists only when the authored handoff claims to close a tracked item that carries a quotable, checkable criterion. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name what ruled it out, and stop when the linked item you could read carries no closing entry with a checkable criterion: no closing reference at all, or an item that states no checkable criterion — a title alone, a user story ("As a …, I want …"), or prose with no list, checklist or acceptance section is not a checkable criterion. A candidate item alone does not open the occasion, and neither does a body that references an item without a checkable criterion. How an item is referenced — a closing keyword, a bare mention, a branch number — is a syntax fact, not adoption: inspect the exact mention in context, since examples, templates and code may name unrelated work.

## Sources
1. The description (`context/description.md`) and the title (`context/metadata.json`): the closing reference and any done/deferred mapping — a checked task list, a Given-When-Then or DoD block, a sentence naming what is done and what moves elsewhere. They establish what the handoff says. They never establish whether a criterion is met.
2. The source branch (`context/metadata.json`) and the commits (`context/commits.json`): further places a work-item number may appear. They establish how the item is referenced, nothing more.
3. Each linked item (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`: number, title, url, state, labels, body; `how` in `linked_work_items.json`): the criteria block to map against. It establishes whether a checkable criterion exists and its exact wording. It never establishes that the pull request adopted it; the closing reference in the text or the provider's own link (`how: closesOnMerge`) does that.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the touched-file set, read only to ground a heavier severity. It never establishes that a criterion is met or unmet.
5. The inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): open it and state either the linked or closing issue you found, quoting its `#number "title" (state)`, or that you scanned the inventory and found none.
If the linked items were not captured, you cannot tell whether there was a done-list to map to: when the body carries a closing reference but no mapping and the item's criteria are unreadable, report a collection gap and record no observation. The MET path does not depend on that file: a body that carries a closing reference together with an explicit checked task list, Given-When-Then or DoD block mapping the change to enumerated criteria is judged from the body alone.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the closing pull request maps the change to the item's criteria — stating what is done here and what is deferred. The mapping may be implicit: a body whose statements name the substance of each criterion as done (or deferred) honours it, and a checklist that copies the criteria is a mapping; a checklist format is never required. A template's own Definition of Done — items about the merge request's form (title format, lint, a local build, screenshots) rather than the item's criteria — maps nothing, however many of its boxes are ticked. Quote the closing reference and the criteria span.
- NOT_MET: a quotable closing reference to an item with a checkable criteria block, and the body neither names the substance of the criteria as done nor defers them — a restatement of the title, an empty template, or a body that speaks of something else. Frame it as a forward-looking handoff request — "state which of #N's criteria this satisfies and which are deferred" — never as a failure.
- UNDETERMINED: the captured text leaves genuinely open whether the mention closes the item; name the question that would settle it. Having read the body and the item and found no mapping is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review. Use your judgment as an experienced reviewer for cases not enumerated here.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a single nudge to state coverage. MAJOR only when, having actually scanned the touched-file set in the diff, you can ground a plausible gap: a concrete quoted criterion has no corresponding surface in the touched files — the item requires an error state and the diff adds only the happy path — and the body does not mark it deferred. Phrase even this as "state whether <criterion> is in scope here or deferred". When you cannot ground a gap, stay MINOR. Identical inputs yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Every observation quotes the work-item number, its closing reference, and the exact criterion span from the linked item's body, citing the item's url. For NOT_MET, the citations show the closing reference, the criteria block, and the body read through without a mapping. You have the diff and an excerpt, not the running system: never claim to have run, compiled or verified the change, and never assert a specific criterion is unmet, missing or broken — you point at a handoff gap, not at correctness. Never invent or demand a criterion the item never stated. Describe what the body says against what the item states; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue itself is well written belongs to the issue-authoring practices (`issue-has-checkable-outcome`); the pull request description in general belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; marking the change ready and linking its issue at all belongs to `ready-and-traceable-handoff`. Here only: does the closing change say which stated criteria it covers?

groups.name: Acting on review feedback
groups.description: Close the review loop. When a reviewer leaves a substantive comment on a line, answer it with a reply that names what changed or a follow-up commit that addresses it, and resolve the thread before merging. Feedback only improves the work once someone acts on it.

practices.name: Respond to each review comment

precondition.skipReason: nobody left a review comment on this pull request

practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer spent real attention pointing at a specific line. When the thread just sits there, they cannot tell whether you agreed, fixed it, or missed it, and they will hesitate before putting in that effort again.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Every reviewer comment gets a visible response, either a follow-up commit that addresses it or a short reply like 'Good catch, switched to the shared client in a2b1c3', so no thread sits unanswered.
practices.holdsAs: Every reviewer comment gets a visible answer
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the author visibly engages with each substantive reviewer request within the captured review record.

## The standard
Judge one practice: when a reviewer left a substantive inline or conversation comment — a question or a change request on this work — did the author visibly engage with it rather than leave it sitting silent? The standard is ENGAGEMENT, not agreement and not completeness. A loop is closed by any visible response: a reply that fixes it; a reply that declines with a stated reason; a clarifying question back; a pointer to a commit or SHA that addresses it; a thread the reviewer or the author marked resolved; a global "Done" or "Addressed" posted after the review batch, even unanchored and unresolved; a description the captured text shows edited as a request about it asked; or the reviewer's own later note saying the point was taken up ("Thank you for incorporating the changes"). A bare later approval or "Looks good" says the reviewer accepted the work, not that the author engaged. Good: "Good catch — switched to the shared client in a2b1c3". Looks like a lapse but is not: five nitpicks whose threads are all resolved and followed by the tutor's "Thank you for incorporating the changes", while one header still reads "Untitled"; a tutor's "Close this merge request" after which the same tutor reviewed and approved it. Bad: a question or change request on this work with no reply, no resolution and no commit that plausibly addresses it — "What does this attribute mean?" still unanswered when the work merged.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Reviewer input is a note whose author login differs from the pull request author character-for-character; a note by the pull request author is never reviewer input, and the author gets no credit for replying to themselves. Treat a human's login as a real reviewer whatever its shape (a numeric or token-like login is still a person on a provider that anonymises accounts). A comment the record flags `bot` (an access token, an app, a review service; this tool's own notes are never in the record) is reviewer input when it asks something of the change: silence toward an automated finding is the same open loop. A note is substantive only when it asks something of this change. It asks nothing when it is praise, thanks, an acknowledgement ("LGTM", "+1", "Looks good"), an explanation, or help addressed to someone else; nor when it is advice the reviewer attached to their own approval — the same reviewer approved after it with no commit or author note between them — that defers itself to later work ("for next iteration", "next time", "in general", "be mindful") or marks itself optional ("nitpick", "consider", "if possible"). Such a note asks something again when it makes the approval conditional ("approving once X is fixed") or asks a question. An author who wrote no note at all is not an identity problem: the author's side is then the commits, the resolutions and the description. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when no note asks something of this change: a freshly opened pull request, or a tutor's "Looks good! Just two things for next iteration: …" posted with their approval. One exception: when the same login is recorded on a comment and on the reply that answers it (a known mirror artifact that collapses identities), you cannot tell whether a reviewer spoke at all — that is UNDETERMINED, never NOT_APPLICABLE. A reviewer login that differs from the author's is never that case.

## Sources
1. The inline comments (`context/comments.json`: `path`, `line`, `body`, `author`, `created_at`, and `thread` and `in_reply_to` where the provider records them) and the threads (`context/review_threads.json`: each thread's resolution state and who resolved it, and `reviewDecisions`: who approved and when). Scan the ENTIRE record for a later author note that answers a comment. The precomputed leads below these criteria list every note by someone other than the author, inline and conversation, one row each, with the author's replies, the resolution, the reviewer's later note, the reviewer's approval after it and what came between, whether it came after the hand-off, and the commits after it: decide every row.
2. The general comments (`context/general_comments.json`): conversation-level questions and change requests, and author replies posted outside a thread. Same partition, same scan.
3. The pull request author and state (`context/metadata.json`): the login to partition by, the description as captured, and whether and when the work merged or closed.
4. The commits (`context/commits.json`: each with its message, `committedAt` and the `files` it touched): a follow-up commit counts as uptake when it comes after the comment and touches the commented file, or when its message observably ties to the comment — a shared path or a shared concrete term. Uptake is judged on the request's substance, not its letter. When a commit is the only candidate response, read its changed lines before crediting it: a later commit on the file says the file moved, not that the ask was taken up.
An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When a substantive reviewer comment is visible but the facts that would settle its uptake are not, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: every substantive reviewer comment has a visible response of one of the kinds above; a resolution or the reviewer's settling note counts whatever the head still shows. Quote the reply, the resolution marker, or the matching commit-message phrase.
- NOT_MET: at least one substantive reviewer comment drew no response of any kind in the complete captured record while the work remains open, or was posted before the work merged or closed and remained unanswered. Name the single most consequential open thread, quote it, and point forward to replying in-thread or pushing a fix; a missing same-line reply, RESOLVED mark or commit reference alone is never the deciding clause.
- UNDETERMINED: the collapsed-identity case above, or when the only substantive notes were posted after the work merged or closed and drew no reply here — their uptake would sit in later work this record does not carry. Name the question. A note posted before the hand-off with no response found anywhere is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, over all reviewer comments; an unanswered note posted after the hand-off is set aside when earlier notes decide.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — a formative practice, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: an open question on still-open work. MAJOR: an ignored change request, or an open loop on work already handed off — merged or closed.

## Grounding
Quote the reviewer comment in every cell. When you assert uptake, quote the reply, the resolution marker, the reviewer's settling note or the commit-message phrase that ties to it; never infer uptake from a commit's mere presence or timing. Never invent a reply, a resolution, or a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the state of the work — "this thread is still open" — never the person, and never impute intent or a causal outcome.

## Defer
Whether the resulting code is correct or the fix complete belongs to other practices. Merge timing and merging past unresolved threads belong to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`. Here only: was each substantive reviewer comment engaged with?

practices.name: Resolve open threads before merging
practices.whyItMatters: Merging while a reviewer still has changes requested skips the very check they asked for, and tells them their review did not count. It is also a quality signal, not just a courtesy: changes that land with little reviewer discussion tend to carry more defects that surface after release. Resolving the threads first keeps review worth doing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: By the time you merge, every open thread is resolved and anyone who requested changes has come back with an approval, so nothing lands over an objection.
practices.holdsAs: Nothing merges over an open thread or objection
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: dated evidence establishes that standing reviewer requests and open threads were resolved or superseded before merge.

## The standard
At the moment the change MERGED, was the review loop closed first — every reviewer's gate either resolved or superseded — or did the change land while a reviewer's request or an open thread still stood? This is a process practice about closing the loop before merge, never a claim that the merged code is wrong: the code may be perfectly correct and still have skipped the re-review a reviewer asked for. A later approval supersedes a change-request only if it occurred before the merge; a resolution after merge does not establish that the loop was closed beforehand.

## Occasion
This is a gate. If the change did not merge, record NOT_APPLICABLE, name that fact, and stop: there is no merged loop to assess. NOT_APPLICABLE has no other ordinary case.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): `state`, and `merged_at` when the provider recorded it. It establishes that the change merged and when. It never establishes the review state.
2. The review-decision and thread-resolution records (`context/review_threads.json`): each reviewer's decision, each thread's path, line, resolution and `resolvedAt` when the provider dated it, and their dates. They establish the review state at the merge timestamp when read as dated events: a thread whose `resolvedAt` is after `merged_at` was open at the merge, and the precomputed leads list it beside the never-resolved ones. A current decision or resolution field is a current-state fact, not automatically a historical one; a latest-state snapshot, a filename or a record count never by itself proves the historical record is complete.
3. The discussion (`context/general_comments.json`, and the inline comments in `context/comments.json`, each carrying the `thread` it belongs to): dated comments that explain a supersession or a resolution. They establish why a gate was lifted, when dated. They never establish a decision a reviewer did not record. The precomputed leads below these criteria list the merge — who, when — and one row per thread the record does not mark RESOLVED, with its `id`, anchor, opening time and whether it is outdated; it says whether the threads file was captured at all.
The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) establishes nothing here: never use the code to infer a reviewer's decision. If the change merged but `context/review_threads.json` is absent or truncated, the loop had some state at merge and you could not read it: report a collection gap and record no observation. Never treat a missing file as an empty loop.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: merged with the loop still open — a reviewer's change-request still stood at merge (name the reviewer, quote the decision), or an unresolved thread that nobody resolved remained (quote its path:line).
- MET: merged with the loop closed — no reviewer's change-request still stood and no unresolved thread was left open. State the evidence relied on: "merged; reviewer X's change-request superseded by their later approval; no unresolved thread".
- UNDETERMINED when the qualified sources were inspected but cannot establish the state at merge — for example, a change-request with no date that could precede or follow the merge; name the unresolved historical question. A complete dated record with no gate standing at merge is MET. Current resolutions or approvals with unknown timing cannot establish that they preceded the merge; record UNDETERMINED when that timing decides the result. A missing required source is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, on the single at-merge question.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on loop closure alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a merely open thread with no standing request, the lighter lapse. MAJOR: landing over a reviewer's still-standing request-changes gate, the heavier miss. Equivalent observed states get equivalent treatment.

## Grounding
For NOT_MET, quote the deciding review evidence and the dated facts that show it still stood at the merge timestamp. For MET, cite the complete bounded review record — the merge timestamp, every decision and every thread's resolution with dates — that shows none remained. Describe only the observable state: "merged with N request-changes still standing; thread at <path:line> unresolved at merge". Never "you ignored the reviewer" or "you merged broken code"; never a claim about the code's correctness; never a current open or resolved state offered as proof of the state at merge.

## Defer
Whether threads on an OPEN pull request are being taken up belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`. Here only: was the loop closed at the moment of merge? Do not double-flag.

groups.name: Writing issues a maintainer can act on
groups.description: Write issues someone can pick up without coming back to ask what you meant. State the problem clearly, what you saw versus expected plus steps to reproduce for a bug, or the who and why for a request, keep each issue to one concern, say how to tell when it is done, and link the design or decision the work depends on.

practices.name: State a problem a maintainer can act on
practices.whyItMatters: A maintainer cannot fix what they cannot picture. An issue that leaves out what you saw versus what you expected, or the who and why behind a request, comes straight back with 'can you clarify?' and you both lose a day.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A bug report that reads 'uploading a 0-byte file returns 500, I expected a clear validation error' and lists the exact steps to reproduce, so a maintainer can start straight away. Or a request that names one concrete capability with who it helps and why, such as 'reviewers lose track of which files changed in large diffs, so add a per-file changed-lines summary to the review view'.
practices.holdsAs: Issues state a problem a maintainer can act on
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the issue, read on its own, gives a maintainer enough to start work without a clarification round-trip.

## The standard
Judge whether this issue lets a maintainer picture what is wrong or what is wanted, and begin. The bar is the one a senior triager applies. A reader must be able to identify the kind of work and find the concrete substance it needs. For a defect report: the actual or observed behaviour, the expected behaviour, and how to reproduce it — a concrete reproduction path (numbered steps, or a stack trace, an exact error or a failing test) is the single most valuable and most-often-missing element, so weight it accordingly. For a capability request: a concrete capability stated clearly, ideally with who benefits and why. A specific title that locates the work — not a bare slug, an empty template or "it's broken" — is part of being act-on-able. Use judgment for forms not enumerated here: an issue that ships a quotable acceptance-criteria, Definition-of-Done or Given-When-Then block is act-on-able on that block alone; do not then demand a beneficiary or a "so that" clause. An epic, umbrella or requirement card carrying substantive prose is act-on-able at the requirement level; its detail lives in child stories, so judge it as a requirement, never as a thin story. An untyped issue that nonetheless asserts a malfunction IS a defect report; judge it as one.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when there is no work-kind to judge: a pure question or open discussion that asserts no defect and requests no capability. Do not demand reproduction steps of a discussion. A title that names a task or a capability ("Add App icon", "Edit README and diagrams") is engineering work even when the body is empty: the gate passes and the empty body is the lapse, never NOT_APPLICABLE.

## Sources
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, template field, step list and criteria block. It establishes the kind of work and the substance stated inline. An image: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The title and labels (`context/metadata.json`): a deliverable-type label names the kind of work. It never establishes substance by itself; an empty template echoing the title under such a label is still empty.
3. The comments (`context/comments.json`): part of the observable artifact; substance stated there counts. They never establish substance you cannot quote from them.
4. Linked design, decision or spec documents (`context/docs/`): when the issue delegates its substance to a document materialized here, read it. A concrete capability or interface the document actually specifies is substance an implementer can start from; count it as observed rather than demanding the issue restate it inline. A generic document or a placeholder marker that does not concretely pin THIS work supplies nothing.
When the issue delegates its substance to a specific named document that was NOT materialized, you cannot tell whether that substance exists: report a collection gap and record no observation, never a claim against prose you were never shown. If the issue text was not captured completely, the same.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the kind of work is identifiable and the substance it needs is genuinely present and quotable — inline, in a comment, or in a materialized document the issue delegates to.
- NOT_MET: a required element of the act-on-able core is missing, because the issue delegates to nothing and states none itself, or the materialized document is generic or a placeholder. Name the missing element.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A complete but empty or vague body is an assessed gap — NOT_MET — not UNDETERMINED; an incomplete capture is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR — a non-blocking authoring-practice nudge, not a merge gate. Severity reflects HOW MUCH of the act-on-able core is gone, judged from the evidence, never from a feeling. MINOR, the usual band: the work is clear and only one secondary element is missing. MAJOR: the issue is effectively unstartable — a defect with neither a concrete symptom nor reproduction steps; a request naming no concrete capability, such as a bare title or an empty template echoing the title under a deliverable-type label.

## Grounding
Every element you call present must be quotable from the artifact — the body, a comment, or the materialized document; an element you cannot quote is absent. For NOT_MET, evidence.search records the boundary you searched, and the citations quote from it: the whole body, the labels, the comments, and the `context/docs/` documents or their absence. Never invent content and never grant a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the observable gap — "the body names a symptom but no reproduction path" — never the reporter's intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue has a checkable or measurable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Whether it duplicates another filed issue, beyond noting an evident restatement, belongs to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`. Here only: can a maintainer picture the work and start?

practices.name: Keep the issue to one concern
practices.whyItMatters: An issue that quietly bundles three unrelated asks cannot be assigned, estimated, or closed cleanly. One part lands, the rest linger, and the whole thing stays open forever, tracking nothing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: One issue, one deliverable, such as 'add CSV export to the reports page', rather than 'add CSV export, fix the date picker, and bump the chart library' crammed into one ticket.
practices.holdsAs: Each issue asks for one deliverable, not a bundle
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: how the issue is scoped — one cohesive deliverable at the issue's intended level, rather than unrelated asks stapled into one ticket.

## The standard
A good issue tracks ONE cohesive deliverable: something that can be picked up, worked and closed as a single unit. Judge cohesion as an experienced reviewer would: is there a single thread of intent, or have unrelated asks been stapled together so that part can land while the rest lingers? The test is whether a maintainer would naturally assign, estimate and close it as one thing, or would be fighting to. One feature, one bug, one question is one concern. Internal decomposition is still ONE concern: implementation sub-steps, a checklist that builds up one capability, a sub-issue rollup that breaks one feature into trackable children. An epic that bundles several RELATED facets of the same feature area (create, rename, delete plus search for one entity) is ONE concern at its altitude; that breadth is what makes it an epic. The tell of bundling is separable threads of intent targeting different concerns, never the mere presence of "and" or a long checklist.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when there is no concrete deliverable to scope at all: a pure question, a support request, an open discussion, an empty or title-only body, or an untouched template. Do not manufacture a MET from that absence.

## Sources
Judge only from the issue body, its labels and its sub-issue rollup as captured.
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist and step list, and the sub-issue rollup when the capture carries it. It establishes the deliverable(s) named and how they relate. It never establishes what the author meant beyond the written spans.
2. The labels and title (`context/metadata.json`): the issue's intended level — epic, feature, bug, task. They establish the altitude at which to judge cohesion. They never establish cohesion by themselves.
3. The workspace inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): sibling issues. Open it and state either the overlapping or duplicate issue you found — quote its `#number "title" (state)` — or that you scanned the inventory and found none. A bundled concern that clearly warrants its own existing or separate sibling is evidence of multiple concerns; confirm against actual titles and bodies, never from sibling count alone.
An image in the body: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. If the issue was only partly captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: one cohesive deliverable, including any internal decomposition or related-facet epic described above.
- NOT_MET: genuinely unrelated deliverables fused into one ticket — "add CSV export, fix the date picker, and bump the chart library". Feed forward the single most consequential split: name the concerns to break into linked issues. Never enumerate every clause.
- UNDETERMINED only when the complete text genuinely leaves one journey versus separate deliverables unresolved; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. A partly captured issue is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on scoping alone — a formative practice, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: separable asks that a maintainer could still split without stranding work. MAJOR: clearly unrelated bundling that will genuinely strand work, with part landing and the rest lingering open.

## Grounding
Quote the actual span(s) that name the deliverable(s) you are judging; for NOT_MET, the spans that name each separable concern. State the inventory result in every observation. Describe the observable bundling — "the body names three deliverables with no shared thread" — never carelessness or intent. Never invent a deliverable, a clean bill, or a bundling you did not read.

## Defer
Whether an epic should itself be split into tracked child stories belongs to `breaks-large-work-into-trackable-subtasks`; do not double-count it. Here only: is this issue one concern at its level?

practices.name: Define a checkable outcome
practices.whyItMatters: Without a clear line for 'done', nobody can tell when the work is finished, including the person doing it. A checkable outcome turns 'improve performance' from an open-ended wish into a task someone can actually complete.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A short acceptance checklist a maintainer can tick off when the work is truly finished, such as 'export downloads a valid CSV' and 'an empty result shows a friendly message', rather than a vague hope of improvement.
practices.holdsAs: Every issue says what done looks like
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a quotable finish line — an outcome a maintainer could later verify as DONE from the issue alone.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does this issue define an outcome a maintainer could later verify as done? A good issue draws a clear finish line: a reader can tell, from the issue alone, what state of the world means the work is complete. The line can take many shapes — an acceptance checklist, a Given-When-Then block, a story's who/what/why phrased so the result is testable, or, for a bug, a stated expected behaviour a fix must restore. The form does not matter; the testability does. Use judgment as an experienced reviewer would; do not hunt for a keyword or label. Good: "export downloads a valid CSV; an empty result shows a friendly message". Bad: "improve performance" with nothing that could ever read as done, or a body that only echoes its title. For an umbrella, epic or requirement card, the right checkable outcome is a definition of done that decomposes into child work, not an inline checklist: bundling many capabilities is expected of it.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when there is nothing whose "done" this practice could define: a question, a support request, an open discussion, or a bare board or ceremony placeholder with no asserted problem and no requested capability. A missing checklist on something that was never engineering work is not a defect. A title that names a task or a capability ("Add App icon", "Add package") with an empty body is engineering work whose done was never defined: the gate passes and NOT_MET is the answer, never NOT_APPLICABLE.

## Sources
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist, criteria block and expected-behaviour statement. It establishes a finish line you can quote. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The labels and title (`context/metadata.json`): the kind of issue, including whether it is an umbrella, epic or requirement card. They never establish a finish line by themselves.
3. The comments (`context/comments.json`): a finish line stated there counts. They never establish one you cannot quote.
4. A linked design or spec document the issue delegates to, materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`: when it states a concrete, testable contract THIS work must satisfy — specific behaviours, status codes, API or state conditions — that contract IS a quotable finish line. Read and quote it before concluding none exists. A generic guideline, or a placeholder document that does not pin this deliverable's done-state, supplies nothing. A document never materialised is not evidence in either direction: when the issue delegates its finish line to a specific document you were not shown, report a collection gap and record no observation, never a claim against prose you were not shown.
5. Child work: sub-issues or a task list referenced in the body or comments, or child entries in `context/project_inventory.json` when captured. For an umbrella, they establish the decomposition that makes its outcome checkable.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the finish line is quotable from the body, a comment, or a materialised document; or, for an umbrella, children or tracked sub-issues already carry the decomposition — MET with no severity.
- NOT_MET: a real deliverable to build, and no quotable outcome in the issue or any materialised document it delegates to. For an umbrella with substantive prose but no child-mapped done, this is a gentle decomposition nudge, not a hard failure; do not double-alarm.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A body read in full that states no finish line is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED; a document you were not shown is a collection gap.
One observation per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR — a formative authoring practice, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: everything softer is a single nudge, including the umbrella decomposition nudge. MAJOR: a maintainer genuinely cannot tell when ANY of the work is done — a real deliverable with neither a verifiable outcome nor a decomposition.

## Grounding
Quote the span you relied on: the checklist, criteria block, expected behaviour, the document sentence with its `context/docs/...` file path, or the child references. For NOT_MET, evidence.search records the boundary searched, and the citations quote from it: the whole body, the labels, the comments, and the `context/docs/` documents or their absence. Never invent a checklist, a clean bill or an exoneration you did not read. Never assert technical feasibility, design correctness or the author's competence. Describe the observable gap in the issue, never the author's character or motive.

## Defer
Whether the problem itself is well stated — observed versus expected, who/what/why as a narrative — belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`; do not write that relationship into the feedback. Here only: is there a verifiable finish line?

practices.name: Point the issue to the context it depends on
practices.whyItMatters: An issue that silently depends on decisions made elsewhere forces every implementer to re-discover the context — or, worse, to guess it and build the wrong thing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When work depends on an existing design or decision, the issue links the document that holds it, so whoever picks it up starts with the rationale already in hand.
practices.holdsAs: Issues link the design or decision they rest on
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: an issue that depends on a design, decision, spec, runbook or data model recorded elsewhere points the implementer to the document that holds it.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when an issue clearly depends on prior context an implementer would need to act on it correctly — an existing design, a decision record, a spec, a runbook, a data model — does the issue point them to that context with a link to the relevant wiki document, instead of assuming the reader already carries it? The signal is judged from the issue's own text: it leans on decisions or designs made elsewhere — "per our architecture", "following the agreed rollout plan", "as decided for the billing redesign", "must match the data model" — such that someone picking it up cold could not proceed correctly without finding that source. A link count is never the signal, and a link to an unrelated document is not credit. Do not infer a hidden dependency the text does not express.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the issue is self-contained: a clear bug report, a small well-described change, a question. Most issues are; prefer NOT_APPLICABLE whenever the issue reads as self-contained, and never penalize a self-contained issue for lacking links.

## Sources
1. The title and the whole body (`context/description.md`, `context/metadata.json`): every phrase that appeals to context made elsewhere, and every link. It establishes whether the issue leans on external context and whether it points anywhere. It never establishes that a linked document is relevant; a bare link is not evidence on its own. An image: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link outside the wiki: nothing.
2. The linked wiki documents materialized under `context/docs/`: read each to judge whether it is actually the context the issue leans on. A document establishes relevance when a passage in it carries the design, decision or spec the issue depends on. It never establishes relevance by its title alone.
When the issue links a specific document that was NOT materialized for you, you cannot tell whether it carries the context: report a collection gap and record no observation — neither credit nor criticism.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the issue genuinely rests on prior design, decision or spec context and links the specific materialized document that carries it, so an implementer can proceed without hunting or guessing.
- NOT_MET: the issue plainly leans on context made elsewhere but leaves the reader no pointer to it — nothing, or only a materialized document that does not carry that context — so they must reconstruct or reverse-engineer the intent.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. Having read the whole issue and the materialized documents and found no pointer to the context it leans on is NOT_MET; a linked document that was not materialized is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR — a non-blocking authoring nudge, not a gate. MINOR, the usual band: a mild lean on unstated context — a nudge to link the source. MAJOR only when the missing context is load-bearing enough that an implementer would likely build the wrong thing without it. When unsure, prefer the lower severity.

## Grounding
For NOT_MET quote the exact phrase in the issue that appeals to external context ("as decided…", "per the design", "must match…") and state what context an implementer would need but is not pointed to. For MET cite the materialized document's `context/docs/` file path and quote or closely paraphrase the passage that shows it is the relevant context. Never invent a document, a decision or a dependency; talk about the issue's text, never the reporter's intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue is actionable on its own terms belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`; the two are disjoint. Here only: does an issue that depends on external design or decision context actually point to it?

groups.name: Reviewing a teammate's work constructively
groups.description: Review a teammate's change well. Leave specific, actionable comments, raise concerns as questions rather than commands, and read the change before approving it rather than waving it through.

practices.name: Leave specific, actionable review comments
practices.subject: REVIEWER
practices.whyItMatters: 'This looks off' leaves the author guessing what to change and why. A comment that points at the exact line and names the concern gets fixed, while a vague one just slows the change down.
