practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A note anchored to the line that says 'this throws when items is empty, so guard the loop or return early on a null list', so the author knows exactly what to do next.
practices.holdsAs: Review comments name the line and the fix
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the substantive comments a reviewer wrote on this pull request each point at something concrete and tell the author what to do about it.

## The standard
Judge the craft of the comments a reviewer wrote — never whether the reviewer's claim about the code is correct, and never the author's code. A useful comment names a specific construct or anchors to a real line AND states an actionable substance: what is wrong, what to change, a concrete alternative, or a pointed question a maintainer can actually answer. A vague comment is a content-free gesture that leaves the author guessing: "this is messy", "fix this", "cleanup", a bare "?". Inline (diff-anchored) notes and conversation-tab notes meet the same standard. A blunt but specific comment is useful here; a polite but vague one is not. A reviewer comment is one whose author differs from the pull request author in the metadata.

## Occasion
This is a gate. The practice judges reviewer activity, not the changed code: "a big pull request got little review" is not an observation, and an unreviewed or draft pull request is never a substandard review. Build one list of every review note in your context, wherever it is carried — inline arrays, general or conversation notes, any discussion thread rendered in the artifact text. Set aside the notes that carry no reviewer-craft signal: the author's own self-notes; automation output (a comment the record flags `bot`: an access token, an app, a review service — the reviewer craft judged here is a person's); bare approvals or acknowledgements ("LGTM", "+1"); author-uptake or status replies that report what was done rather than ask for a change; off-topic chatter unconnected to anything this diff touches. When no substantive reviewer comment survives, the occasion never arose, whether or not `context/review_threads.json` records a bare approval — the common case for a freshly opened pull request: record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never absent. Do not abstain merely because a field name or flag is missing while a real reviewer comment is plainly visible: read it and judge it.

## Sources
1. The inline review threads (`context/review_threads.json`): each comment's author, body and path:line anchor, and the review decision. They establish the diff-anchored comments and their positions.
2. The conversation notes (`context/general_comments.json`): each note's author and body. A conversation note has no position; it establishes only author and body.
3. The pull request metadata (`context/metadata.json`): the pull request author, which separates reviewer comments from author notes.
4. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the hunk a comment anchors to. Read it to confirm the comment points at something real. It never establishes whether the comment's claim is correct; assess the comment, not the code.
If the artifact shows a review happened but the comment bodies were not materialized for you, reviewer craft exists that you could not read: report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
assess the standard against all relevant evidence over the substantive reviewer comments that remain.
- MET: every substantive comment is specific and actionable — the author can tell what to change.
- NOT_MET: vague comments leave the author guessing — from a stray straggler among useful notes to a review that is predominantly empty gestures. Quote each one.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A comment you can read is judged; one you cannot read is a collection gap.
One observation per review, over all the substantive reviewer comments together.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on comment quality alone — a workflow practice, not a merge gate. Scale to how much of the review is content-free. MINOR, the usual band: a stray vague straggler; a lone unhelpful comment is a light cost, never a serious one. MAJOR: a review that is predominantly empty gestures, leaving the author unable to act. Equivalent situations yield equivalent severity.

## Grounding
Quote verbatim every comment you call vague — with its path:line for an inline comment; by author and body for a conversation note, which has no position, so never invent a file:line for it. Quote at least one useful comment when one exists. Never call a comment vague without quoting it; never fabricate a comment to avoid looking idle. Talk about the comments; never grade the reviewer as a person or impute intent.

## Defer
Whether the author took the comments up or left threads open belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; tone and politeness belong to `reviews-respectfully-asks-rather-than-demands`. Here only: could the author act on what the reviewer wrote?

practices.name: Comment on the code, not the person
practices.subject: REVIEWER
practices.whyItMatters: The same point can be made as a question or as a put-down, and people remember which one you chose. A curious question gets acted on, while sarcasm and bare orders breed defensiveness and make the next review harder.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: 'What happens if this runs twice, could we hit a race here?' rather than 'this is obviously broken, did you even test it?', so disagreement lands on the code and never on the author.
practices.holdsAs: Comments land on the code, never on the author
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: how the REVIEWER's substantive comments are voiced — as questions, suggestions and reasoned disagreement aimed at the code, or as orders, sarcasm or contempt aimed at the person.

## The standard
Judge whether the reviewer's comments stay civil and collaborative: concerns raised as questions or suggestions, disagreement carrying a reason ("I'd prefer X because Y"), rather than bare orders, belittling, sarcasm, contempt, name-calling or hostility aimed at the author. This is about HOW feedback is voiced, never whether the technical point is correct. Directness, brevity and strong technical disagreement are not incivility: "This will NPE when items is empty" is blunt and civil. A command paired with a reason is fine. Do not flag a word like "just" or "obviously" when it reads neutrally; judge the whole phrasing in context as an experienced reviewer would. The subject is the reviewer, never the changed code: "a big pull request got little review" is not an observation.

## Occasion
This is a gate. A reviewer is anyone whose author differs from the pull request author; never grade the author's own words. Skip comments the record flags `bot` and bare approvals ("LGTM", "+1") — they carry no human reviewer tone. The flag is the provider's classification; never guess from the shape of a login: a numeric or token-like login without the flag is a real human reviewer, not automation. When no substantive reviewer comment survives this filter, whether or not a bare approval was recorded — the common case for a freshly opened, unreviewed pull request — the occasion never arose: record NOT_APPLICABLE, say so, and stop. Never absent; an unreviewed pull request is never a substandard review. This is the only NOT_APPLICABLE case.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): the author, to apply the filter, and the state. It establishes who is a reviewer. It never establishes tone.
2. Inline review comments (`context/review_threads.json`): each carries path, line, body and author. They establish what a reviewer said at a position in the code.
3. Conversation-tab comments (`context/general_comments.json`): author and body, no path or line. They establish what a reviewer said about the change as a whole.
Judge tone across both comment sources. An image in a comment: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. If the record shows a review happened but the comment bodies are not in your context, there was reviewer speech you could not read: report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: at least one substantive reviewer comment survives the filter and every one is civil and collaborative — a concern posed so the author can respond, disagreement kept on the code.
- NOT_MET: one or more comments carry a quotable incivility marker: a bare order with no reason and no softening ("Change this."), belittling that implies the author should not have needed telling, sarcasm or contempt, name-calling, hostility aimed at the person.
- UNDETERMINED when the complete captured context leaves the tone of a quoted comment genuinely ambiguous; name what would settle it. Comment bodies you could not acquire are a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, over every surviving reviewer comment.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on tone alone — a formative communication practice, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a single sharp-but-impersonal edge. MAJOR: a pattern across several comments, or contempt, name-calling or hostility aimed at the person. Identical comments yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote every marker you count verbatim, with its author; never fabricate a comment, a clean bill or an exoneration. Cite an inline comment only by the path and line it actually carries; cite a conversation-tab comment by author and quoted text and leave the location empty. Frame everything about the COMMENT — "this phrasing reads as a demand" — never about the reviewer as a person; no hunches, no psychoanalysing, no intent inferred beyond the words. For MET, cite the surviving comments you read.

## Defer
Whether a comment is specific, actionable or technically right belongs to `leaves-useful-specific-review-comments` and `reviews-substantively-with-understanding`; a vague-but-civil comment is still MET here. Here only: does the phrasing land on the code and not on the author?

practices.name: Explain consequential review judgments
practices.subject: REVIEWER
practices.whyItMatters: A short explanation makes the basis of an important approval or concern available to the author and other reviewers. A bare approval alone does not show what was checked; it also does not prove that the reviewer failed to read the change.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: For a consequential authorization change, a reviewer names the permission check they considered and explains why it addresses the concern, or asks a specific unresolved question. A routine change with no material concern may need only a brief approval.
practices.holdsAs: Reviews that call for reasoning get it in writing
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a review whose captured context called for written reasoning carries a substantive comment grounded in the change.

## The standard
Judge the written explanation accompanying a review, not whether the reviewer read or understood the change. A substantive comment makes the reviewer's reasoning inspectable: it names or quotes a concrete diff element — a path, a symbol or a term that actually appears in the diff or summary you can see — or asks a real clarifying question about the change. One such comment is enough; polish, tone and specificity are not graded here. A bare approval or acknowledgement ("LGTM", "+1", a lone thumbs-up) supplies no written reasoning, but it does not establish that the review was careless or superficial. Written reasoning is owed only when the captured context establishes an occasion for it: a request to explain a consequential trade-off, or a documented review requirement. Change size or risk alone does not make commentary mandatory. A reviewer is anyone whose login differs from the pull request author. Discount machine noise and empty ceremony: a comment or decision the record flags `bot` is not human review, and a content-free approval is not engagement. The flag is the provider's classification of the account; a login's shape decides nothing.

## Occasion
This is a gate. This practice judges REVIEWER activity, never the changed code; "a big PR got little review" is not an observation. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when no review has happened yet (no reviewer comment and no approval), when `context/review_threads.json` has no review decision and no substantive reviewer comment survives the author-exclusion filter, or when the context demonstrates no need for an explanation and none was supplied. An unreviewed or draft pull request is never a substandard review; do not manufacture praise or criticism from a bare approval.

## Sources
1. The review threads (`context/review_threads.json`): the review decisions and the inline diff comments, with their authors. They establish who reviewed, what was approved, and any inline reasoning. An empty inline thread never establishes missing reasoning across the other sources, nor an unperformed review.
2. The general comments (`context/general_comments.json`): the conversation and discussion notes. The substance of a review may live here rather than inline; read whatever review notes are materialized, under whatever heading, before concluding nothing substantive exists. They also establish a request for an explanation, when one was made.
3. The description and metadata (`context/description.md`, `context/metadata.json`): the author's login for the reviewer filter, and any documented review requirement or trade-off the change raises. They never establish that reasoning was written.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) and the checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether a comment's named path, symbol or term actually appears in the change, and the real size of the change once obviously generated or vendored bulk (lockfiles, generated clients, migrations, snapshots) is discounted — a "big" diff that is mostly generated is smaller than its line count. They never make commentary mandatory on their own.
Judge from the review notes and the change-size signals present in your context; do not claim per-comment or per-line facts you cannot see. Missing or incomplete required sources are a collection gap with no observation; never read a missing count as zero.

## Judge
assess the standard against all relevant evidence, after inspecting every declared source of review comments.
- MET: an applicable review includes a substantive comment grounded in the change, inline or in the discussion.
- NOT_MET: the captured context establishes that written reasoning was demonstrably required or requested, the review was approved without it, and every declared review-comment source holds nothing but bare approvals or acknowledgements.
- UNDETERMINED only when the captured requirement or explanation remains genuinely ambiguous after every available source is inspected; name the unresolved question. Having read every source and found no reasoning where none was demonstrably required is NOT_APPLICABLE, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review. Equivalent inputs yield equivalent calls.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR — a non-blocking practice. Severity reflects the concrete coordination or decision-recording consequence of the missing explanation, never an assumption about how carefully the reviewer read. MINOR, the usual band: the missing reasoning costs the team little to recover. MAJOR: the missing reasoning leaves a consequential decision with no inspectable basis for the author or other reviewers.

## Grounding
Cite the written comment for MET, and the diff element it names when it names one. For NOT_MET, cite the context that establishes why an explanation was needed, the approval that supplied none, and the boundary: every declared review-comment source inspected. Never invent a comment, a file, a size or a clean bill you did not verify. Neither a not-yet-reviewed change nor an approval without commentary establishes a superficial review; describe what was written, never how the reviewer read.

## Defer
Whether the comments were specific and well-worded belongs to `leaves-useful-specific-review-comments`; whether the author acted on them belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`. Do not double-flag them here. Here only: does the written explanation meet its demonstrated purpose?

groups.name: Testing your changes
groups.description: When a change adds or fixes behaviour, it comes with the tests that exercise it. And it never quietly deletes, skips, or weakens a test just to make the build pass.

practices.name: Include tests with the change
practices.whyItMatters: Code without a test is a promise nobody can check, and it is one careless refactor away from quietly breaking. Adding the test alongside the logic locks in the behaviour you just built, which matters most when you are fixing a bug.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: New logic arrives with a test beside it, and a bug fix comes with a test that fails on the old code and passes on the new, proving the behaviour is what you say it is.
practices.holdsAs: New logic and fixes arrive with a test beside them
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a test for the changed production behaviour arriving in the same change.

## The standard
Judge one workflow practice: when the change introduces non-trivial production behaviour, does a test for THAT behaviour arrive in the same diff? You are not hunting for missing edge cases, doing a lint sweep or re-judging the change's size; you are asking whether the new logic ships locked in by a test that could observe it. Production behaviour: a new function or endpoint, a new branch or computation, a changed validation or state transition. A covering test plausibly exercises that behaviour: it touches the same symbol, endpoint or path, or asserts the corrected result. A bug fix is strongest when it ships a test that would fail on the old code and pass on the new. Judge the PRESENCE and plausible linkage of a covering test, never its naming, readability or assertion style.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when there is no production surface to judge: the diff is empty, or — after setting aside generated, vendored, lock and migration files, which are neither production logic nor a test of it — it is test-only, docs-only, config-only, or a pure rename, format or type-only change with no quotable added behaviour. Layout is not behaviour: a view, control or style change with no branch, computation or state transition — a button whose action is empty, a title, a colour, a spacing — leaves nothing a test could observe, and is NOT_APPLICABLE. A test-only change does not establish the occasion.

## Sources
This is decided from the diff alone.
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): classify each changed file as production or test by its path and name, using judgment about test conventions across languages. The production hunks establish the behaviour added or changed; the test hunks establish whether a test names the same symbol, endpoint or path, or asserts the corrected result. Neither establishes that any test ran.
2. The commits (`context/commits.json`): subjects that say what the change does, such as naming a fix. They establish the shape of the change; they never establish a per-commit mapping, since per-commit patches are not in your context.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): existing tests near the changed code, for context on where a covering test would live. The absence of a repository-wide test inventory is never a reason to abstain: load-bearing, testable logic shipped into a repository with no test target at all is the lesson, and is judged, not abstained from.
If a required part of the production or test diff is truncated or unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the diff adds or changes real production behaviour and the same diff adds or updates a test that plausibly exercises it. Quote the production line and the test span that names the shared symbol or asserts the corrected result.
- NOT_MET: the diff adds testable production behaviour, and no test in the same diff exercises it — after scanning every test file in the diff. Never manufacture untested logic to force this cell.
- UNDETERMINED only when the complete captured evidence leaves the relationship between a test and the changed behaviour genuinely ambiguous; name what would settle it. Having scanned every test file in the diff and found none that covers a quotable behaviour is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED. A truncated diff is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential untested behaviour when there are several.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. Reason about consequence, never a line count. MINOR, the usual band: a single small, focused piece of untested logic that one test would pin. MAJOR: a defect fix shipping with nothing to lock the corrected behaviour in, or substantial or branching untested logic. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the exact added span relied on: the `[L<n>]` production line embodying the behaviour, and for MET the `[L<n>]` test span naming the shared symbol. NOT_MET requires the quoted untested production line AND a stated scan of the diff's test files confirming that none covers it — that scan is the boundary. Never invent a test, a file or a clean bill you did not read. Never claim a test ran or passed, and never claim a per-commit mapping you did not observe. Describe the observable delivery; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Change size belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; weakening an EXISTING suite belongs to `keeps-the-test-suite-honest`. Here only: did a test for the new behaviour ship with it?

practices.name: Keep the test suite honest
practices.whyItMatters: Deleting or skipping a failing test to get a passing build hides the breakage instead of fixing it, and removes the alarm that would have caught it next time. The suite only protects you while it tells the truth.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Existing checks retain their regression coverage. A check that no longer applies is removed with a reason tied to the changed behavior; a still-relevant failing check is fixed at the cause rather than disabled.
practices.holdsAs: Existing checks stay effective or their removal is justified
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: changed existing checks retain their regression coverage, or their removal is justified by the captured change.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: does the change preserve the existing checks, or does it weaken them without a justified reason? An honest suite keeps telling the truth: when a test starts failing, the fix addresses the underlying cause, and when a test genuinely must go, it goes with a stated, quotable reason. Unjustified weakening deletes, disables, skips, comments out or hollows out a test or its assertions without explaining why the check is gone. Do not infer the author's motive or whether the build passed. The test is one of judgment, not keywords: can the check still fail on the regression it guarded? A faithful migration that preserves assertion strength — a rename, a move, an API upgrade, splitting one test into several, or deleting a test whose subject under test is itself removed in this same diff — is not a suppression. This is a craft practice about how the change treats its safety net, not a line-by-line lint sweep and never a merge gate.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when there is no existing test the change could be lowering: the diff changes no existing hand-written test or assertion, or the patch is empty. Exclude generated or vendored test code, then inspect every remaining changed check regardless of how much generated output surrounds it. A feature with no test changes is NOT_APPLICABLE here, not an assessed observation. New tests alone create no existing check to compare. A changed existing check creates the occasion whether it is preserved or weakened.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, read exhaustively, with `work/change/files.json` to find the test files): every test hunk — an added skip or disable, a removed assertion or test block, commented-out executable test code, an assertion made trivially true, and any adjacent comment naming a tracker or a `reason=` / `@Disabled("…")` argument. It establishes what happened to each check and any reason written beside it. It never establishes that the suite ran.
2. The commits (`context/commits.json`) and the description (`context/description.md`): a line explaining a removal or skip. They establish a quotable reason tied to the change; they never establish a reason they do not state.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the unchanged surroundings of a touched test, to tell a hollowed assertion from a faithful move or split, and whether a deleted test's subject is gone. It never supplies a justification nobody wrote.
When the change touches a test surface but the patch is truncated so those hunks cannot be read, report a collection gap and record no observation; unread required evidence is not a judgment.

## Judge
The undesirable behaviour is unjustified weakening. Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: a real assertion becomes trivially true, an entire test block is dropped, executable test code is commented out, or a test is skipped or disabled — and no quotable reason is tied to it anywhere in the sources above. Quote the deciding line(s).
- MET: the change touches real test code and, after a complete bounded search of every test hunk, every check is at least as strong as before, or each removal or skip has a quotable reason supported by the captured change. An arbitrary explanation does not justify discarding a still-relevant check. A faithful migration is MET, not a suppression. Name the test file(s) you inspected.
- UNDETERMINED only when a read hunk genuinely cannot settle whether a check can still fail on what it guarded; name what would settle it. A missing or truncated patch is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review. Name the single most consequential suppressed test and show the shape of the fix: restore the check, or record a reason that explains why it is no longer appropriate.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on test suppression alone — formative, non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a single unexplained skip. MAJOR: a deleted test, a hollowed assertion, or several unexplained suppressions, since more of the suite's honesty is lost.

## Grounding
Every observation quotes the deciding test line(s) from the diff: the added skip or weakened assertion, or the removed line for a deletion. For MET, cite the test hunks inspected and any quoted reason; never record it for a diff that touches no test surface. Never claim to have run, compiled or executed the suite; you see only the patch. Never assert a suppression, or a justification, you cannot point to in the captured files — if you cannot quote it, it does not exist. Describe the observable behaviour of the diff; never impute intent or character, and never grade the author.

## Defer
Whether NEW tests were added for new logic belongs to `ships-tests-with-the-change`. Here only: does the change WEAKEN the existing safety net without saying why?

groups.name: Writing maintainable code
groups.description: Keep the changed code easy for the next person to read and change. Factor out duplication, keep units small and single-purpose, and leave no clutter behind, such as dead code, debug leftovers, or comments that just restate the line.

practices.name: Factor out duplication instead of copy-pasting
practices.whyItMatters: Copy-pasted logic means every future fix has to land in every copy, and the copy you forget keeps the old behaviour, which is exactly the bug. Pull the shared part into one place and you fix it once.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: By the time the same validation logic shows up a third time, you stop copying it and lift the shared concept into one named helper every caller uses, leaving a single source of truth instead of copies that drift apart. You hold off when blocks only look alike by coincidence, since forcing a shared abstraction on them is worse than the duplication.
practices.holdsAs: Repeated logic gets lifted into one named helper
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: added hand-written code expresses each maintained rule in one appropriate place, without unjustified copy-paste.

## The standard
Judge one closed corpus: the lines this pull request adds. A senior reviewer flags copy-paste: two or more added blocks near-identical in shape that differ only in a few literals, identifiers or types — the kind of repetition an Extract Function, a shared constant, a loop or a small lookup table would collapse into one source of truth (Fowler; Hunt & Thomas, DRY; Martin). The harm is drift: a fix has to land in every copy, and the copy that is forgotten becomes the bug. Judge the repeated unit of knowledge — the same computation or rule expressed twice — not text that merely looks alike. A coherent multi-line computation, validation, mapping or transform, or constant or config block can be a flaggable copy. A one-liner, a guard clause, a field assignment or a forced-similar idiom (equals/hashCode, builder chains, switch arms, DI or route registrations) is not — an idiom is a few lines the platform dictates; a repeated multi-line block can carry duplicated knowledge, including a view body or a fetch-decode-assign sequence. Length alone never establishes that two blocks express the same rule. Legitimately parallel repetition is not a defect: test cases, fixtures and table-driven or parametrized bodies are meant to look alike. Duplication can live within one function: sibling `if`, `case` or branch bodies that each repeat the same multi-line computation differing only in a constant are as flaggable as cross-function copies. Use judgment on whether two blocks are a genuine copy-paste or a coincidental shared idiom.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop only when the change offers no surface to judge: a documentation, diagram, image diff, or one whose added lines are entirely generated, vendored or test fixtures. Hand-written configuration that repeats a maintained rule is a surface to judge. A diff you read and found clean is not one of these; NOT_APPLICABLE says the work had no subject here, which is false of it.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the `[L<n>]` new-side spans of the added hunks. It establishes every candidate pair — a flaggable pair must sit inside these lines. It never establishes duplication against unchanged repository code, which is out of scope either way; pre-existing duplication you cannot see being introduced here is not judged.
2. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`): which paths are generated or vendored (`*.gen.*`, lockfiles, OpenAPI specs, route trees, migrations and the like) or test fixtures. It establishes the hand-authored remainder you assess. It never establishes a pair.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the surrounding lines of a hunk cut off mid-block. It establishes the full shape of an added block. It never establishes a pair against code the change did not add.
The precomputed leads below these criteria list every pair of added blocks whose lines share a shape once names and literals are set aside, with both spans, the run length and the names that differ: decide every pair, and quote both spans. If the diff was not captured completely, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Before choosing, scan every added hand-written block for structural sameness, including branch bodies, not just whole functions. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- NOT_MET: you can quote a near-identical added pair. Cite both occurrences and name the small delta between them.
- MET: you read every added hand-written hunk and no near-identical pair is in them. This is a proof over a closed corpus, not a failure to find: the copy-paste that could have arrived with this change did not.
- UNDETERMINED for a candidate pair you read and genuinely cannot call; quote it and name what would settle it. Do not resolve the doubt into MET, NOT_MET or NOT_APPLICABLE. Having read every added hunk and found no pair is MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, covering every flagged pair.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this signal alone — a formative practice, not a merge gate. Calibrate to consequence and spread. MINOR, the usual band: a duplicated pure-UI or markup block with no logic — a gentle "extract a component" nudge. Duplicated logic where a divergent copy is a real bug risk weighs more. MAJOR: a copy already spreading to several places, or several distinct duplicated blocks. Identical added code yields identical severity.

## Grounding
For NOT_MET quote both occurrences by path and `[L<n>]` span and name the delta; a duplication claim you cannot ground in two quoted added spans is not made. For MET record `evidence.search` over the diff, cite the repeated-looking blocks you actually checked, and state in the boundary that duplication against code outside the diff is out of scope either way. Describe only the observable copy-paste practice: never assert the code is buggy, will diverge or will break, and never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether one block is too long or does too many things belongs to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`; never flag a single block here. Here only: repetition across added blocks.

practices.name: Keep functions small and single-purpose
practices.whyItMatters: A function that does five things is hard to name, hard to test, and hard to change without breaking a part you forgot it touched. Small, focused functions are the ones you can actually hold in your head.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Instead of one long method that parses, validates, saves, and notifies, you have a few short functions, each doing one clearly named step you can read and test on its own.
practices.holdsAs: Functions stay short and do one named step each
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: added or substantially rewritten functions keep a coherent, scannable purpose without tangled concerns or obscuring nesting.

## The standard
Ask of the largest function the change introduces or substantially rewrites what a senior reviewer asks: can I hold its purpose in my head, name it in a phrase, and follow it at a glance? A focused function does one nameable job. The defect is a single body that visibly interleaves several SUBSTANTIAL, separable concerns — each a real multi-step block, genuinely interwoven, not a short serialize/encode/respond tail on a coherent pipeline — OR nests control flow so deep the core action is lost in indentation, OR runs so long its purpose stops being scannable. Not a defect: a linear pipeline of single-purpose stages (guard → build → encode → return; validate → operate → respond) is ONE purpose even when it ends by serializing a result; a thin body that delegates each step to a named helper in one call each (parse → fetch → render) is ONE orchestration, because the responsibilities live in the helpers — counting one-line delegated calls as separate concerns is the false positive to avoid. A defect: one body that parses input AND performs I/O AND applies business rules AND formats output, each written out and tangled together; a handler whose real action sits four conditionals deep. Reason like an expert about THIS code's shape. Apply no line count and no fixed concern count, and never quote a threshold to the developer. Use your judgment for cases these examples do not cover.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the concrete fact, and stop only when the change adds no function body that could carry the defect: a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff, a pure deletion or rename, or a diff dominated by generated or vendored files with essentially no hand-written body. That value says the work had no subject here, which is untrue of a change whose bodies you read and found focused.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and rewritten bodies with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers — a closed set you can enumerate. It establishes each body's length, nesting and the concerns written out in it. It never establishes that a function is correct, or how it is factored against collaborators you cannot see.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the pinned source of a body the diff truncates. Read it to finish reading that body. It never adds an unchanged caller, or a function merely renamed or called but not shown, to what you judge.
If a required body cannot be captured from either, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Read every added or substantially rewritten body through. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- NOT_MET: a quotable added body that carries the defect. Grade the single most consequential function; never sum across files, and never escalate because many separate small functions exist — many small focused units IS the baseline.
- MET: the change adds bodies, you read every one, and none sprawls, nests deeply or interleaves separable concerns. The sprawl that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with `evidence.search` over the diff, cite the largest body you read, and say in the boundary that you judged shape, not whether the functions are correct or well factored against collaborators you cannot see.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A body you can see is judged on its visible shape; a body you cannot see is a collection gap.
One observation per review.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on function shape alone — a craft practice about how work is shaped, never a correctness claim, non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a reader can still follow the body and a single extraction would help. MAJOR: a body that clearly does it all, or whose core action is genuinely obscured by nesting.

## Grounding
Every NOT_MET quotes the specific `[L<n>]` added span and names the responsibilities to split out or the nesting to flatten; a sprawl you cannot anchor to a quoted hunk is not emittable. Judge only function bodies visible in the diff or its pinned source; never reason about an unchanged caller, a function merely renamed or called but not shown, or code you did not read. Never claim to compile or run anything. Describe the observable shape; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Repeated or near-identical blocks belong to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; dead, commented-out or leftover scaffolding belongs to `leaves-the-code-clean-with-intent-revealing-comments`. Do not repeat another practice's complaint. Duplication or dead code alone does not establish tangled responsibilities, but neither removes the function-body occasion: assess the shape on its own evidence, with MET only after the full read. Here only: does each introduced body hold one nameable job a reader can follow?

practices.name: Leave the code clean and comment the why
practices.whyItMatters: Stray debug output, blocks of commented-out code, and comments that just echo the line all add noise the next reader has to wade through. Clean code with a comment that explains the why reads like someone meant it.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: No leftover print statements or commented-out branches, and where a line looks surprising, a short comment gives the reason, such as 'retry once: the upstream API drops the first call after an idle period', rather than restating what the line does.
practices.holdsAs: Code lands clean, with comments that explain why
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: added hand-written code has no established writing residue, and comments explain intent or constraints rather than restating code.

## The standard
Judge the added lines, every one, for code that ships clean and comments that earn their place. A senior reviewer scanning them should find no residue: no commented-out code, no leftover debug or trace output, no throwaway scaffolding shipped as if final. Any comment that IS present should explain the WHY — intent, a non-obvious constraint, a unit, a caveat, a reference — rather than restate the WHAT the next line already says. Blemishes, open and illustrative: an added line that is itself plausible source behind a comment marker (a commented-out assignment, call or control statement); a bare trace print or breakpoint; a "TEMP" or "remove before merge" stub; "// increment i" above `i++`; a comment that narrates the editing session rather than the code ("// FIX 1: added episodes and year", "// changed this to use X", "// moved from Foo"); a comment with no code under it, left where code was meant to follow; a scratch or empty file added to the tree (`File.txt` holding a copied line); a template placeholder left in a manifest the change edited (`# TODO: Adjust …`). A bare `print`, `NSLog`, `console.log`, `dump` or `debugPrint` can be a debug leftover when its surrounding purpose establishes that it is temporary tracing. The spelling alone does not establish that purpose. Clean, open and illustrative: a comment that gives a reason ("retry once: upstream drops the first call after idle"); output that is the file's deliberate purpose (a CLI's own stdout, a test's expected output); a logger call through a real logging facility; a sanctioned TODO referencing a tracked issue. Code-shaped text inside a comment is not sufficient evidence of debris: documentation examples, API usage, commands and explanations may legitimately quote executable syntax. Assess the surrounding purpose, and flag an inactive implementation only when the captured context establishes it is leftover rather than an intentional example.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when there were no hand-written added lines to read: an empty diff, or a diff that is all generated or vendored surface (lockfiles, `*.gen.*`, specs, build output, migrations). Exclude those files first; if no hand-written added surface remains, the work had no subject here. Source code is the subject: a change that adds no source-code line — a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff — has no subject here and is NOT_APPLICABLE. When the diff is truncated where the added lines live, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): only the lines marked ADDED (`[L<n>] +` in the annotated diff). Residue is visible in the line itself. Removed and unchanged lines are not graded; code the author commented out and DELETED is a cleanup, never a blemish.
2. The file list (`work/change/files.json`): which files are generated or vendored and so excluded.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the surrounding purpose of a file — whether its output is deliberate, whether a quoted snippet is an example. It never turns an unquotable line into a blemish.
An image or an external link: nothing.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: a quotable blemish on an added hand-written line. A diagnostic call is a blemish here only when the captured context establishes that it is leftover debugging output, rather than intended reporting; logger choice belongs to `logs-through-the-platform-logger`. One blemish is enough: a single restating comment, marker or leftover you can quote is this cell at its lightest severity, never rounded down to MET because it is alone.
- MET: you read all the added hand-written lines through and none carries a blemish. This is a covered search, not a lucky miss: the residue that could have shipped did not. Record it.
- UNDETERMINED only for a single candidate line you read and genuinely cannot call — a prose comment that may be restatement or explanation, or an inactive implementation that may be leftover or an example. Quote it and do not resolve the doubt in either direction.
One observation per review, over all added lines; a scatter of leftovers is one observation.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a proportionate, non-blocking nudge about clarity and maintenance burden. MINOR, the usual band: a lone stray comment or marker is the lightest touch; a scatter of leftovers is a modest cleanup. MAJOR only for a demonstrated, consequential source of confusion about the maintained implementation. Line count never raises severity: a long commented-out block is still one cleanliness nudge. Do not borrow error-handling or security consequences from other practices. Identical added lines yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the exact `[L<n>]` span and file path for every blemish; a blemish you cannot quote is not counted. For an inactive implementation, also quote the context that shows it is leftover. Never infer that a line is dead or debug-only unless its quoted text shows it. For MET, cite the search over the diff and state the boundary you did not cover: unchanged lines, files this diff does not touch, generated and vendored surface. Never claim a build or test ran. Describe what was left in the code; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Naming, function and file size belong to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`; scope to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; duplication to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; swallowed errors to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`. Dead branches in live code and runtime defects belong to other practices. Here only: residue on added lines, and WHAT-versus-WHY comments.

practices.name: Log through the platform logger, not print
practices.whyItMatters: Print-style diagnostics bypass the platform's logging facilities. The platform logger — `Logger` on Apple platforms, `Log`/Timber on Android, SLF4J on the JVM, `logging` in Python, a logger module in Node — lets application diagnostics be collected and filtered where the app runs.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Diagnostics in application code go through the platform's logger. `print`, `console.log`, `println` and `System.out` are left to output a program means to print — a command-line tool, a script, a build step, a test, a playground or a `#Preview` — or to a `DEBUG`-only block.
practices.holdsAs: Application code logs through the logger, never print
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: diagnostic messages the change adds go through the platform's logger, not through print-style output, in application code.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the application code this change adds: when it reports a diagnostic — a state, an error, a step reached — does it use the platform's logger or print-style output? Print-style output is the closed list `print(`, `debugPrint(`, `dump(` (Swift), `printf(` (Objective-C), `println(`/`print(` (Kotlin), `System.out.println`/`System.err.println`/`printStackTrace()` (JVM), `console.log/debug/info/warn/error` (TypeScript and JavaScript in application code), `print(` (Python). A logger is `Logger(subsystem:category:)`, the `os_log` functions or `NSLog`/`NSLogv`, which write to the Apple system log (Swift and Objective-C), Android's `android.util.Log` (`Log.v/d/i/w/e/wtf`, whatever its tag) or Timber, SLF4J/Log4j/`java.util.logging`, a `winston`/`pino`/framework logger, Python `logging`. Print-style output is not a lapse where it is the program's output: a command-line tool, a script, a build step, a test, a playground, a `#Preview`, or a `DEBUG`-only block (`#if DEBUG`) that removes itself from release. Judge added lines only; an existing print the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change adds no diagnostic line at all: no added print-style call and no added logger call in application code. A change that adds only logger calls is an occasion with a positive answer; a change whose only prints are the program's output (a CLI, a script) has no occasion. Added diagnostic lines are the occasion.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers and the file list (`work/change/files.json`): each added print-style or logger call, the file it lands in, and whether a `#if DEBUG` or a test target encloses it. It establishes what was added where. It never establishes what an unchanged file does.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether the project already has a logger (`Logger(` definitions, a logging dependency in the manifest) and whether the file is an application target or a tool. Read it to classify the file and to say whether the print was written beside an existing logger.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the print-style and logger calls it found per file, and whether the checkout defines a logger, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where the calls are added, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added diagnostic lines first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added diagnostic in application code goes through the platform logger, and any print-style call is the program's output or `DEBUG`-only. Quote a representative logger call.
- NOT_MET: an added print-style call reports a diagnostic in application code that ships — outside a CLI, script, test, preview or `DEBUG` block. Quote the line and the file.
- UNDETERMINED: whether a file is an application target or a tool cannot be told from the diff or the checkout; name the file.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential lapse when there are several; count the rest in the summary.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one or two prints in application code. MAJOR: an error path reported only by print, or a print that emits personal or secret data. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` call and its file; for NOT_MET say why the file is application code (its target, its `import SwiftUI`/`UIKit`, its path). Never claim a print is debugging output without the line; never claim a file is a tool without the fact that makes it one.

## Defer
An error swallowed rather than reported belongs to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; a secret in a message to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`; a leftover debugging line of another kind to `leaves-the-code-clean-with-intent-revealing-comments`. Here only: does the diagnostic go through the logger?

groups.name: Handling failure well
groups.description: Fail safely when things go wrong. Handle errors instead of swallowing them, check inputs and edge cases where data enters, and do not crash on a problem the code could recover from.

practices.name: Handle errors instead of swallowing them
practices.whyItMatters: An empty catch block turns a failure into a silent one: the code carries on as if nothing went wrong, and you find out only when something downstream breaks with no clue why. Surfacing the error saves the 2am debugging session.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A failed call either surfaces the error to a caller who can react or recovers safely, for example by rolling back the partial work and failing closed, instead of logging and then continuing (or silently continuing) with bad or missing data.
practices.holdsAs: Failures surface or recover, never get swallowed
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: added failure paths propagate or meaningfully record failures, or deliberately absorb them with an evidenced safe reason.

## The standard
When this change introduces a failure path — a call that can throw, reject or return an error — the failure should stay visible: surfaced to a caller who can react, or recorded with enough context that someone can diagnose it later. Handled: the error propagates (rethrown, wrapped with context, returned or forwarded), is recorded meaningfully (logged at a level a human would notice, a failure metric, an error state the UI reads), or is deliberately absorbed with an in-diff comment naming WHY that is safe. Swallowed: the failure is discarded — an empty or no-op catch, a caught error variable that is never used, an ignored error return, a dropped async rejection, a result discarded with a `try?`-style shortcut, and a failed lookup or parse answered by a bare early return or an `if let` with no else branch: nothing logs it, no state carries it and no comment says why silence is safe. A handler that logs the failure at a level a human would notice and leaves the caller an empty value the interface renders as an empty state has recorded it — that is handled, not swallowed; it is a swallow only when nothing records the failure and nothing can react to it. These are illustrations, not a closed list; recognise the same shape in any language or idiom as an experienced reviewer would. Judge this as a craft practice in how the ADDED code handles errors, not a line-by-line lint sweep.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop only when the hand-written change adds no failure path at all. That value says this work had no subject for the practice; saying it about a change with sound error handling tells the developer there was nothing here to see. It is valid only after the enumeration below finds no added error-handling construct. Source code is the subject: a change that adds no source-code line — a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff — has no subject here and is NOT_APPLICABLE.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers and the visible in-diff context. It establishes every failure path the change adds — a closed set you can enumerate from the added lines — and where each error goes. It never establishes that the handling is CORRECT, that the recovery works, or that paths outside the diff behave.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when where a caught error goes, or what downstream does with the missing value, sits just outside the hunk. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
Per-commit patches are not in your context; reason from what the diff shows. If the change adds a failure path but the relevant diff is truncated or unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation: unread required evidence establishes neither absence nor uncertainty in the work.

## Judge
Enumerate, then classify. First list every added error-handling construct — `catch`, `try?` or `try!`, `guard … else`, `if let`, an early `return` or `throw`, `Result` or `.failure`, a `??` fallback on a failable call — quoting each added line; then classify each as handled (surfaced, logged, propagated) or swallowed. Do not assume a clean surface from a glance. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- NOT_MET: a quotable swallowed failure. Quote the exact added hunk that shows the discard; if you cannot point to the dropped error in a quoted added line, you do not have an observation.
- MET: the change adds failure paths, you walked every one, and each propagates, records, or is deliberately absorbed with a stated why. The swallow that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with `evidence.search` over the diff and say in the boundary what you did NOT establish, so the strength stays a claim about what is visibly there and not a warranty.
- UNDETERMINED: a failure path you did find whose handling the diff and pinned source genuinely do not show you; name the path and what would settle it. It is what you say after the scan, never a shortcut around it.
One observation per review. Name the single most consequential swallowed failure, not an exhaustive list.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a formative practice to grow, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a swallow on a best-effort or clearly secondary path — cleanup, teardown, optional telemetry, or a failure merely logged a touch too quietly. MAJOR: a swallow that hides a real fault from the caller or user, on a path that persists, communicates, authenticates, parses or otherwise carries consequence. Several distinct swallows, together hiding more of the change's failures, lean MAJOR. Identical constructs yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Judge only constructs this diff adds or modifies (new-side `[L<n>]` markers); never grade pre-existing context or assume code you cannot see. For NOT_MET, cite the added hunk with the discard. For MET, cite the constructs you enumerated and state the boundary: not that the handling is correct, not that recovery works, not that code outside the diff behaves. Never claim to run, compile or test. Never invent a construct, an exoneration, or a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the observable behaviour; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether inputs and edge cases are validated belongs to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`; a deliberate fail-fast crash on an unrecoverable state belongs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`. Here only: does an added failure stay visible, or is it dropped?

practices.name: Validate inputs and edge cases at the boundary
practices.whyItMatters: Data from a user, a file, or another service will not always arrive in the shape you expected: it can be empty, null, negative, or huge. Checking it where it enters means a clear rejection instead of a confusing crash three layers deep.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Code that reads an external value first asks what happens if it is missing or out of range and handles that on purpose, so an empty list or a malformed payload meets a clean guard instead of a null-pointer surprise.
practices.holdsAs: External values meet a guard before they are used
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: added consuming sites handle the obvious bad case of values they do not control.

## The standard
Judge whether added or modified code that consumes a value it does not control handles the obvious failure case on purpose, instead of assuming a happy path. A boundary value enters from outside the local logic: a request param, body or header; text a user typed, once it is parsed or used as a number; a decoded network or file payload, including a bundled data file; a collection filled at runtime, such as a response array or a stored list the user populates; an env, config or defaults read; the result of a third-party or RPC call. Not a boundary value: a parameter of the app's own function or view, a framework callback's arguments, view state the code owns, an author literal or constant, and a value a control already bounds (a Slider or Stepper range, a Picker over an enum). A site is in scope only when the same change also USES that value — indexes or slices it, divides by it, converts it to an integer, aggregates it, or passes it into logic that assumes a shape. A value merely forwarded, stored or displayed as the type it already has is not a consuming site: an empty string saved or shown breaks nothing.
A guard is anything on the value's path that rules out the case the site itself needs, in the hunk or in code you can trace to: a count, bounds or empty check (`isEmpty` guards `[0]`, not `[1]` or `[0..<2]`); a zero check before integer division or before a ratio that is shown or converted to an integer; a clamp; do/catch, `try?`, or a `try` that propagates out of a throwing function; a default for an absent value; an early return; a button disabled on the bad case. An operation already total on the bad case needs no guard: a Swift optional the type forces the author to unwrap (`Int(text)`, `.first`, `dict[key]`, `URL(string:)`, `as?`) handled with `if let`, `guard let`, `?.` or `??`; `reduce`, `map`, `filter`, `prefix` or `ForEach` over an empty collection; `items[i]` inside `ForEach(items.indices)`. A default counts unless it is an extreme sentinel (`Int.max`, `.infinity`) that reaches output unchanged. Judge the PRACTICE — is the obvious failure handled at all — not an exhaustive lint: a finite check on a decoded Double, or a zero check on a field the source never sends as zero, is not the obvious case.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change consumes no boundary value at all: an empty diff, a diff with no consuming site, or only generated or vendored files remaining. Source code is the subject: a change that adds no source-code line — a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff — has no subject here and is NOT_APPLICABLE. So is a change whose values are all typed in-app data, view state and bounded controls, such as a view drawing a typed array it was handed. Never invent an input surface.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers and the visible in-diff context. It establishes every consuming site the change introduces — a closed set you can enumerate from the added lines — and whether each meets a guard you can see. It never establishes that the guards are sufficient for every input or that callers beyond the diff are safe.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when the guard that would decide a site could sit outside the hunk — above a truncated hunk, or in the caller or view that builds the value. It establishes whether such a guard exists. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
Per-commit patches are not in your context. If the context a deciding site needs remains unavailable after reading the pinned source, report a collection gap and record no observation, rather than asserting absence or inapplicability.

## Judge
Scan the changed lines for a boundary value that gets consumed and trace each to its guard; then assess the standard.
- NOT_MET: a boundary value is consumed with nothing on its path ruling out its obvious bad case, so a realistic input — an empty or short response array, an empty bundled list, a library the user has not filled yet — crashes the new path or shows a wrong value. For example `Array(items[0..<2])` on a decoded array behind only an `isEmpty` check, or a minimum seeded with `Int.max` and printed while the list is still empty. Quote the exact `[L<n>]` span of each unguarded site, name the realistic input that breaks it and the missing guard ("count >= 2 before [0..<2]").
- MET: the ordinary result when the change consumes boundary values: you walked every consuming site and each handles its obvious bad case. Looks like a lapse but is not: `a[3]` inside `if a.count >= 4`; `Int(text)` bound with `guard let`; `try decoder.decode` in a throwing function whose caller catches; `steps[index]` when the only way in is a button disabled while `steps` is empty; `offset / 250` in a gesture. The claim is about the coverage of your reading, nothing about correctness.
- UNDETERMINED for a consuming site you can see whose guard the diff and the pinned source do not settle; name the site and what would settle it. Having walked every site and found each guarded is MET, not UNDETERMINED. Missing required context is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, covering every unguarded site found.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a practice to grow, not a merge gate. Calibrate to the demonstrated consequence at the boundary and explain the observable risk. MINOR, the usual band: an omission on a low-impact operation. MAJOR: a missing check on a consequential operation, which one site can warrant; several harmless omissions do not escalate on their own. Identical hunks yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Judge only the added and modified lines and their visible in-diff context, plus pinned source you actually read; a site in unchanged code is never charged, even when a changed line feeds it. For NOT_MET, cite the `[L<n>]` span of each unguarded site. For MET, record `evidence.search` over the diff and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish: that the guards are sufficient, that they cover every case, that callers beyond the diff are safe. Never assert a missing guard you cannot point to; never claim to run, compile or test anything; never invent a clean bill of health. Describe the observable code behaviour, never intent or character.

## Defer
A value interpolated raw into a URL, query, command or markup belongs to `validates-and-escapes-untrusted-input`. A crash operator the author wrote — `x!`, `try!`, `as!`, `fatalError`, `unwrap()` — belongs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`: it is neither a guard nor a consuming site here. An implicit trap stays here: an unchecked subscript or slice, an integer division, a conversion to an integer of a value that can be NaN or infinite. The quality of error handling once input is guarded belongs to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; a catch that merely prevents the crash satisfies the guard here regardless of its body. Do not repeat another practice's complaint, and do not let another kind of defect stand in for this one.

practices.name: Avoid crashing on recoverable problems
practices.whyItMatters: Reaching for a force-unwrap or a panic on a condition that can actually happen turns an ordinary hiccup into a hard crash for your users. A problem the code can recover from deserves a graceful path, not a deliberate stop.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Where a value might legitimately be absent, the code unwraps it safely and falls back to a default or a clear error, instead of force-unwrapping and bringing the whole thing down.
practices.holdsAs: Missing values fall back instead of crashing
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: added crash-shaped operators are safe under their captured provenance or contract, rather than aborting on recoverable runtime failure.

## The standard
Code degrades gracefully on ordinary, recoverable runtime failure rather than deliberately aborting. A chosen crash is an ADDED crash operator the author wrote — force-unwrapping or force-casting a value that can legitimately be absent, `try!` on a call that can throw, or a deliberate abort, panic, exit or fatal error — when its value rides an ordinary runtime path: user input, network, database, disk, a decoded payload, a fallible API's result. Judge two things: can a real input reach the operator and make it fail, and did the change crash on it anyway. Bad, for example: `try! decoder.decode(T.self, from: data)` on a server response; `Int(ageText)!` on text a user typed; `results.first!` on a fetched array; `fatalError` in the catch of a network call. Not a chosen crash, though each looks like one: a genuine programmer invariant that cannot fail unless surrounding code is already broken (an unreachable enum default, a force unwrap of a value just proven non-nil); a fail-fast at a CLI or startup entry point where aborting IS the contract; data the author ships — a literal, a constant, an Info.plist key the change commits, a resource bundled with the app, `URL(string: "https://api.example.com")!`; an operation total by language or platform contract (`String.data(using: .utf8)!`). Code that runs only in an Xcode `#Preview`, a preview-only sample or in tests is not an ordinary runtime path: `try! ModelContainer(…)` or `fatalError` in a preview is scaffolding. A `!` alone is not the defect; whether the operation can ACTUALLY return nil or throw on some real input is. Reason about provenance across languages as an experienced reviewer would, not from the spelling of a construct or a precompute label.

## Occasion
This is a gate, decided by a closed list of crash operators the author writes: a force unwrap (`x!`, `.first!`, `dict[key]!`), `try!`, a force cast (`as!`), `fatalError`, `precondition`/`preconditionFailure`, `assert`/`assertionFailure`, `exit`/`abort` — or their equivalents in another language (`panic`, `unwrap()`, `expect()`, `!!`, `process.exit`, a non-null assertion, `Optional.get()`). An implicit trap — a subscript, a slice, an integer division, a trapping numeric conversion — is not on the list: it is an unguarded edge case, judged by `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop only when the added source lines contain no crash operator: a docs-, config- or data-only diff, a generated- or vendored-only diff, or code with none. An operator the change guards on the same path — behind `guard let`, `if let`, a nil check — is still observed and handled: the occasion holds and the cell is judged below, never NOT_APPLICABLE. The precompute lists lines whose spelling matches, with whether each sits in a preview block or a test file; a listed line is a place to read, not a crash, and the scan below is over the added lines themselves.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers. It establishes the closed set of crash operators the change adds and, where the hunk shows it, where each crashed-on value came from. It never establishes anything about removed lines, unchanged code or code outside the diff, and it never establishes that anything compiled or ran.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it only to trace the origin of a value the hunk crashes on but does not source, or where the operator runs. It never adds an operator to judge — only operators the diff adds are judged — and it never establishes that unchanged code cannot crash.
If the diff is truncated or unavailable for a change that adds a crash operator, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Scan first, then classify. Enumerate every crash operator in the added lines and trace where each crashed-on value came from and where the code runs; look before you leap. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- NOT_MET: a quotable added operator on an ordinary runtime path that crashes on a value with a named runtime source, and a real input you can name — a missing field, a failed request, text a user typed — makes it return nil or throw. Quote the deciding added line, name the source and the input.
- MET: the change adds crash operators from the closed list, you read every one, and each is guarded on its path, sits on a genuine programmer invariant, a total operation, author-shipped data, preview or test code, or an entry-point contract rather than an ordinary runtime path. Looks like a lapse but is not: `try! ModelContainer(for: Person.self, configurations: inMemory)` inside `#Preview`; `URL(string: "https://api.example.com")!` on a literal. Record it with `evidence.search` over the diff and say in the boundary that you judged the operators the diff adds, not whether unchanged code can still crash.
- UNDETERMINED: an operator on an ordinary runtime path whose value provenance the diff and pinned source do not settle — you see the diff, not the whole program. Name the operator and the fact that would settle it. It is earned by the trace running out of evidence, never by skipping the trace, and it is never filed under NOT_APPLICABLE, which claims no operator was here. A crash you cannot tie to a runtime-sourced value and a real input is not groundable as a negative.
One observation per review. When NOT_MET, name the single most consequential chosen crash and show the shape of the graceful alternative for that line — a guard or `if let`, try-with-fallback, return-an-error, `Result`; do not rewrite the whole change.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a defensive-programming practice to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band, and the ceiling when the input that makes the operation fail is possible but unusual. MAJOR: a clearly recoverable failure on a clearly ordinary runtime source — decoded or fetched input crashed on outright. Genuine uncertainty about recoverability lowers the band. Identical hunks yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Cite the exact added-line span and the value's origin from observable diff evidence. Judge only added or modified lines with new-side `[L<n>]` markers; never reason about removed lines or code outside the diff, and never claim to compile or run it. Never invent a file, a line, a value source or a clean bill you did not verify. For MET, cite the operators you enumerated and state the boundary you did not cross. Describe the observable behaviour of the code; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Empty or swallowed catches and logged-and-continued errors belong to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; missing input validation and implicit traps — an unchecked subscript or slice, an integer division, a trapping conversion — belong to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`. Here only: does an added crash operator deliberately crash on a recoverable runtime condition?

groups.name: Making changes secure by default
groups.description: Make each change secure by default. Validate and escape untrusted input before it reaches a dangerous sink, avoid insecure defaults and over-broad permissions, and change dependencies deliberately.

practices.name: Neutralize untrusted input before a dangerous sink
practices.whyItMatters: Gluing raw user input straight into a query, a shell command, or a page is how injection bugs are born, the kind that leak a database or run an attacker's code. Parameterizing or escaping it first is what keeps that door shut.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: User-supplied values reach the database through bound parameters and the page through proper escaping, never concatenated into a SQL string or dropped into HTML as-is.
practices.holdsAs: Untrusted input is bound or escaped before a sink
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: untrusted input is neutralized for the exact dangerous sink it reaches in added code.

## The standard
When code added in this diff carries a value from outside the trust boundary into an operation where that value can change the operation's meaning, the value must be neutralized first — parameterized, escaped for the exact sink context, or validated against an allow-list or strict type — rather than concatenated or interpolated raw. Reason as an experienced security reviewer. A source is any externally-controlled value: a request param, header or body, an uploaded filename, a CLI arg, a remote service's response. A dangerous sink is any place where raw text changes execution: a built query string, a shell command, an HTML or template render, a filesystem path, a redirect target, a deserializer or eval, or a constructed URL whose path or query interpolates the value — `"/auth/\(token)"` then `URL(string: base + path)`, where the fix is percent-encoding via the platform URL builder, not raw interpolation. These lists are illustrative; recognize the shape in any language or stack, including sinks not named here. Neutralized looks like: bound as a parameter, run through a context-correct encoder, passed as an args array to exec, confined under a canonicalized base path, rendered through auto-escaping left on. Not neutralized looks like: string-concatenated or interpolated straight into the sink with nothing in the quoted hunk neutralizing it. For the constructed URL, the most common sink in an app, the rules are these: a remote or typed String interpolated into a path or query segment is a flow, and it is neutralized only by an encoder correct for the segment — `.urlQueryAllowed` is not a safe encoder for an individual query value or path segment: reserved delimiters can remain and change structure. Use a component builder or an encoder appropriate to the exact component; a value whose type renders as digits (an integer, a coordinate) cannot change the URL's meaning and is no flow; a whole remote URL string handed to the platform parser (`URL(string: remoteUrl)`) and then to a loader is parsed, not interpolated, and is no sink here; an author constant is no source.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop only when no untrusted value reaches a dangerous sink in the added lines at all. A dangerous sink is a query, command, path, URL or markup built from the value as text. A source-to-sink flow remains an occasion when a typed or parameterized API neutralizes it — a prepared statement, a component-built URL or an auto-escaped render can establish MET. A value only displayed by a text control that does not interpret markup reaches no dangerous sink and is NOT_APPLICABLE. Scan the added lines for a source-to-sink flow before abstaining; do not skip the scan because the diff looks routine. When the diff contains a sink-shaped line — raw input concatenated into a query, command, path or markup — and you still abstain, name the single most suspicious line by file:line and state why it is safe.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified `[L<n>]` lines and their immediate in-diff context. It establishes the closed set of source-to-sink flows this change introduces and whether each is neutralized in those same lines. It never establishes that code outside the diff sanitizes — or fails to sanitize — the value; never assume either.
2. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`) and the checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): which paths are generated or vendored. They establish the hand-written remainder you assess. They never establish neutralization for a flow the added lines do not show.
Trace only what you can see. If the diff was not captured completely, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: a quotable added hunk where a source reaches a sink unneutralized. Name the source and the sink end-to-end.
- MET: the added lines do carry untrusted input toward a sink, and you traced every introduced flow and each is neutralized before its sink. The injection that could have arrived with this change did not. This is a covered reading of the diff, never a security clearance.
- UNDETERMINED for a flow you can see whose neutralization the added lines do not settle; name the flow and what would settle it. UNDETERMINED comes after the scan, never instead of it. No flow visible at all is NOT_APPLICABLE, not UNDETERMINED.
