One observation per review, covering every unneutralized flow found; show the shape of the fix for the single most consequential one.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a security practice to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a render, redirect or header-style flow; the lightest nudge when the value is partly constrained but the context-correct escape is still missing. MAJOR: raw input that changes code or data execution — injection, traversal, RCE shapes. Identical hunks land at the same level.

## Grounding
For NOT_MET quote the exact added `[L<n>]` hunk where the source reaches the sink and name both ends; if you cannot point to both on quoted added lines, it is not assertable. For MET record `evidence.search` over the diff and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish: that the escaping is correct for every input, that sinks reached from unchanged code are safe, that the application has no other exposure. Never claim the code runs, compiles, is exploitable, or that a payload triggers; assert only the visible practice. Never invent a file, a line or a clean bill. Describe the observable behaviour — raw input flowing into a sink — never intent or character.

## Defer
A generic missing bounds, null or format check with no dangerous sink belongs to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`; a committed secret belongs to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`. Defer to the sibling rather than double-flag. Here only: a taint-to-sink injection flow.

practices.name: Avoid insecure defaults and over-broad permissions
practices.whyItMatters: A default or permission that ships wider than it needs sits quietly until someone exploits it, and this kind of misconfiguration is among the most common security gaps there is. Starting locked down means you only open what you can justify.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A new endpoint or credential grants exactly the access it needs and no more, with scoped permissions and a specific allowed origin from an allowlist, not an origin reflected back from the request or a blanket wildcard, instead of a permissive default dropped in to make things work.
practices.holdsAs: New access grants exactly what it needs and no more
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: added access and exposure settings stay appropriately constrained under the captured boundaries and safeguards.

## The standard
Code should start locked down and open only what it can justify. Hunt the added lines for a change that ships an insecure default or widens an access or exposure boundary without an adequate, evidenced justification. Judge the SETTING the change adopts, not the data flowing through it, and never as a blanket vulnerability scan. A sink-hunt, not a posture rating: do not read the top-level intent, conclude "looks secure" and stop. Walk these sink classes over the added lines; they are classes to think in, not a closed value list, so recognise the same shape on any stack:
1. transport, certificate or host verification toggled off;
2. cross-origin, CORS or permission scope widened — a credentialed response that reflects the request Origin back without an allowlist, or a bare wildcard on an authenticated route;
3. a file, resource or object mode made world-readable or world-writable, or otherwise over-broad;
4. an existing auth or authz guard removed or loosened;
5. secret or credential exposure — trace dataflow here, do not pattern-match names: inspect EVERY logging, string-interpolation, persistence and URL-building call in the added lines and ask what the interpolated value can hold at runtime. A print or log of a request or response body, a header, or any value derived from an auth, login, token or credential exchange is a leak even when the variable is not named "token" (a response body that carries the issued token, for example);
6. a debug, verbose-error or permissive default shipped to a non-test surface.
Spotting one tightened setting (an ATS flag removed, say) does not discharge the hunt; finish every class. A candidate sink class establishes what to inspect, not an automatic defect. Clean: a setting correctly scoped, least-privilege or tightened; a widening whose quoted purpose and captured constraints establish an appropriate exception. A reason, or a test, sample or local filename, does not by itself make exposure safe: verify the actual boundary, the permitted audience and the applicable safeguards from the captured evidence. The absence of an insecure setting is a clean baseline, not a hardening act.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the added lines touch no setting of any sink class at all: a pure UI, layout, documentation, model or test change with no transport, origin, permission, file-mode, auth, credential, logging or debug setting in it. That value claims the work had no subject here; MET is for a change that touches such a setting and does so securely. An added logging, print or persistence call that interpolates any runtime value touches class 5 (credential exposure) and is a setting of that class: a change with one is never NOT_APPLICABLE; walk the class and record what the value can hold. Never abstain on a shallow pass. When the diff contains a config-shaped line (a keychain, permission, CORS or allow-all setting, a token in a URL or path), NOT_APPLICABLE must name the single most suspicious line by file and `[L<n>]` and state why it is safe. Assess only the hand-written remainder of a generated- or vendored-dominated diff.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added lines with their `[L<n>]` markers, and any removed or weakened guard line. It establishes every candidate sink the change introduces — a closed corpus you can walk — and any in-diff comment or profile guard that justifies a widening. It never establishes that the existing configuration is sound, that unchanged settings are safe, or that the system has no other exposure.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when the boundary, audience or safeguard that would decide a candidate line sits outside the hunk (a dev profile, a network policy, the route's auth wrapper). It establishes the constraints an exception rests on. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria, when present: leads to inspect, never evidence. An absent or empty candidate list is never grounds for NOT_APPLICABLE while a candidate line is visible.
Never infer a setting from a filename or a count you cannot quote.

## Judge
Walk every sink class first; then assess the standard.
- NOT_MET: a concrete added setting whose exposure is inappropriate under the evidenced constraints. Quote the added `[L<n>]` line, or the removed or weakened guard line, and name the file.
- MET: the added lines touch at least one setting of a sink class, you walked every class over them, and none was touched insecurely. A COVERED search over a closed corpus, not an impression: an unwalked class makes it a false claim rather than an incomplete one. Record it with `evidence.search` over the diff, name the sink classes you walked in `lookedFor`, and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish. A report on a search, never a security clearance.
- UNDETERMINED: a candidate sink line is visible but the fact that would settle it is not; name the line and what would settle it. Never file an unreadable sink under NOT_APPLICABLE.
Before either abstention, state in the rationale what you found for the credential-exposure class (5). One observation per review; with several issues, name the single most consequential and mention the rest in a clause.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a security-hygiene practice to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a lower-blast-radius misconfiguration. MAJOR: a meaningfully widened blast radius — disabled verification, credentialed origin-reflection or wildcard exposure, a removed or loosened auth guard, or exposed credential material — when the captured boundaries establish consequential exposure. A merely asserted internal or dev rationale does not reduce that consequence; an evidenced appropriate exception is not a negative to grade at all. Do not sum severities.

## Grounding
Every observation quotes the exact added `[L<n>]` line, or the removed or weakened guard line, and names the file. A claim that a setting was added, removed, hardened or mitigated must quote the changed line that does it. An appropriate exception must quote both the justification and the constraints that support it, and it does not remove an otherwise present review occasion. Never claim to run, compile or test; never invent a file, a line or a clean bill of health. Point forward to the safer default: verification on; the exact origin named instead of `*`; the toggle behind a dev profile; the least-privilege mode; the guard restored or its reason recorded. Talk about the configuration, never the contributor.

## Defer
Whether untrusted input is escaped or validated belongs to `validates-and-escapes-untrusted-input`. This practice is the terminal owner of exposed credential material — a hardcoded secret, token, API key or password on a non-test path, or in a URL or log: report it here at MAJOR, never defer it and never NOT_APPLICABLE it.

practices.name: Change dependencies deliberately
practices.whyItMatters: Every dependency you add is code you now trust and have to keep patched, and many malicious packages slip in disguised as a real name a letter or two off. A one-line note on why a package is there, plus a lockfile that moves with the manifest, lets a reviewer sanity-check the addition and keeps the build reproducible.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A new package arrives with a sentence on what it is for. The manifest and resolution stay consistent with the ecosystem and the repository policy, updating a lockfile when needed rather than requiring one for every edit.
practices.holdsAs: Dependency changes stay coherent and notable choices have a reason
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a dependency edit whose manifest and lockfile stay coherent under the ecosystem's resolution rules, with a recorded reason for a notable addition or bump.

## The standard
Judge whether this pull request edits its dependencies deliberately. Two things hold together: the manifest and any lockfile remain consistent with the ecosystem's resolution rules and the repository's documented policy, and a notable new dependency or version bump carries a one-line reason a reviewer can read — in the manifest context, the title or body, or a commit subject. This is a supply-chain workflow practice about how a dependency edit is justified and kept coherent. It is never a claim about the dependency's own correctness, its CVEs, or whether the chosen version is the "right" one. The principle — coherence plus a traceable reason for notable changes — decides, not a fixed file list: reason as an experienced reviewer about manifests, lockfiles and ecosystems not named here. A patch or minor bump and a transitive-only delta need no prose. A large generated lockfile delta is normal evidence of coherence, not a problem. A supported version range is not itself a defect: libraries may deliberately declare compatible ranges, and a manifest edit need not change an already compatible locked resolution.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change edits no external dependency: no added, removed or changed declaration, version constraint, source, resolution or pin of a third-party package, library, framework, plugin, container image or workflow action, in a manifest or lockfile of any ecosystem. The changed lines decide, not the file's name. Internal wiring alone — an internal target or module, a test target that depends on the app, a scheme or test-plan entry, build settings, sources or resources — declares no external dependency and is NOT_APPLICABLE, even inside a dependency manifest. A resolution change on its own, such as a lockfile refresh, is an occasion. A deciding hunk that failed acquisition is a collection gap, not NOT_APPLICABLE.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) and the file spread (`work/change/files.json`): the manifest hunks and the matching or missing lockfile spans. They establish what changed on the dependency surface and whether manifest and lockfile move together. They never establish the dependency's quality or the correctness of the chosen version.
2. The title (`context/metadata.json`) and the whole description (`context/description.md`): where an explaining sentence for a notable add or bump may live. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
3. The commit subjects and bodies (`context/commits.json`): a subject can carry the reason. Per-commit patches are not in your context; judge from subjects, the file spread and the quoted hunks.
4. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the repository's documented policy — a stated reproducibility requirement, a lockfile rule, a pinning convention. It establishes the policy a constraint removal is measured against. It never establishes a defect on its own.
Before calling a notable change unexplained you must have read the diff, the title, the body and the commit subjects. If one of those surfaces was not materialized for you, your search is incomplete: report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the dependency edit is coherent and, where a notable add or bump needs one, explained. A new direct runtime dependency arrives with a sentence on what it is for and any required resolution update is present; a routine transitive resolution refresh is internally consistent.
- NOT_MET: the captured manifest and lockfile contradict one another under the ecosystem's resolution rules, with the deciding entries quoted; or a resolution constraint is removed in conflict with an evidenced repository reproducibility requirement. Establish the ecosystem's semantics and the captured policy before reporting inconsistency.
- NOT_MET: a notable add or bump is coherent but lands as an unexplained pin — no quotable why in the manifest context, the title, the body or the commit subjects. Name the pin and the surfaces you read.
- UNDETERMINED when the deciding policy or resolution context remains ambiguous after reading the sources; name the question. An unchanged or absent lockfile alone proves neither coherence nor a defect. A required source that was not captured is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review. Identical hunks yield identical assessments.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on dependency deliberateness alone — a non-blocking practice to grow, not a merge gate. Scale to how much reproducibility is actually at risk. MINOR, the usual band: an unexplained but coherent notable pin — a formative nudge. MAJOR: manifest and lockfile out of step on something that ships — the most serious case here.

## Grounding
Quote the manifest line, the matching or missing lockfile span, and the explaining sentence or commit subject verbatim. For NOT_MET the citations show the pin and the boundary searched: the diff, the title, the body, the commit subjects. Never invent a file, a reason, a CVE, or a clean bill you did not verify. Never claim a build resolved or ran. Describe the observable edit; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Artifact hygiene about generated churn belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`; review size belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`. Here only: is the dependency edit coherent, and is a notable change explained?

groups.name: Recording decisions and documenting changes
groups.description: Capture the why. Record the rationale behind significant design decisions, and document changes to public APIs and shared behaviour, so the people who maintain or build on the code later can understand it.

practices.name: Record significant decisions and the rationale
practices.whyItMatters: When you pick one design over another, the rationale is the first thing to fade. A maintainer who cannot find why you chose it will either undo a good decision or be too afraid to touch it, and both cost the team later.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A meaningful design choice arrives with its rationale written down, in the description or a short architecture decision record (ADR), such as 'chose an event queue over direct calls so a slow consumer cannot block checkout', not just the code that does it.
practices.holdsAs: Significant decisions land with their reasoning
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a written rationale for the architecturally significant decision this change makes, recorded where a future maintainer can find it.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when this pull request makes an architecturally SIGNIFICANT decision, is the WHY recorded — a constraint, a trade-off, or an alternative rejected — rather than left to be reverse-engineered from the code? A recorded WHY may be one clause, but it must say something the code does not already show: the need the decision serves ("so a customer can save a draft and return to it", "a stored type because attachments must survive a restart") or the constraint that forced it ("the platform only ships the SDK as a package") records it; the lapse is silence about the decision, not brevity, and a clause quoted for the description's WHY may be the same clause. A sentence that names the dependency, the model or the mechanism and the effect it produces ("added the confetti package; a confetti effect fires on the button") restates WHAT the diff shows and is not a rationale, and a commit subject that names the addition is a label, not a why. Never demand the alternatives considered or the reason this framework over another: the need served is the rationale a maintainer needs. Significance is a closed list, so two readers find the same subject: a new third-party dependency or framework added by hand to a manifest; a change to a PERSISTED model or schema (a stored type, a migration, a field that is saved); a public-contract or wire-API change (an endpoint, a message format, an exported library API); a new cross-cutting mechanism the rest of the app plugs into (a shared aspect, interceptor or event bus, a base class many types extend); an auth or security mechanism; the removal of a feature and its stored data. Not on the list, and never significant on their own: a call to an external web service (an HTTP API consumed at runtime is a mechanism used, not a dependency added to a manifest); a view or view model and how screens navigate; an in-memory draft, cache or value type; adopting the stack the project already uses (its persistence framework, UI framework or map kit); a helper, extension or calculation; a rename. When the only candidate is one of these, stage 1 fails and the cell is NOT_APPLICABLE. Work in two stages, in order. (1) Decide whether the hand-written diff contains a significant decision. (2) Only if it does, check whether its rationale is recorded in the title, the description, a commit subject, or a linked ADR or design document. A reason given in a review comment or the conversation is not recorded where a maintainer finds it and does not count; the discussion is where a rationale was asked for, not where it lives. A rationale clause counts in prose or inside a bullet or checklist item — "chose X because Y", "an event queue so a slow consumer can't block checkout", "to avoid Z" — so scan the whole body. Restating WHAT changed, an empty or template body, or a bare "added dependency X" does not record a why.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change is routine and carries no architectural decision: tests, formatting, docs, a rename without a contract change, a version bump of an already-present dependency, a tuned constant or threshold on an internal symbol, or an empty diff. Significance comes from hand-written hunks only: a dependency echoed solely in a lockfile with no manifest edit is not an independent decision; a hand-authored migration changeset is. When the diff is unreadable, the change still made whatever decisions it made and you could not read them: report a collection gap and record no observation, never a routine or a significant verdict.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the added lines that establish significance, and any ADR or design document added in the same change. It establishes what was decided; it never supplies the why by itself.
2. The title (`context/metadata.json`) and the WHOLE description (`context/description.md`): every paragraph, bullet and checklist item. They establish a recorded rationale you can quote. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
3. The commit subjects and bodies (`context/commits.json`): a rationale stated there counts. Per-commit patches are not in your context; never claim a per-commit file mapping.
4. A linked ADR or design document materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`: read it before concluding the why is absent. Cite its file path together with the quoted or closely paraphrased rationale sentence; a bare URL is not evidence the why was recorded. When the change names a specific document that was not materialised, the rationale may be there: report a collection gap and record no observation, never a claim against prose you were not shown.
5. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): what a changed symbol or mechanism means, and an in-repository ADR the change points to. It never supplies a rationale the change did not write.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: a significant decision is present and its rationale is written down in one of the sources above, so the intent survives without re-reading the code.
- NOT_MET: a significant decision ships with no recorded why anywhere in the description, the commit subjects, or a linked ADR or materialised document. Name the decision.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. Having searched every source and found no why is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED; a document you were not shown is a collection gap.
One observation per review. When several significant decisions co-occur, judge them together in one observation.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on rationale alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a single contained unexplained decision — one new dependency, one isolated column, one app-internal class. MAJOR: the genuinely consequential — an unexplained auth or security mechanism, a persistence, public-API or wire-contract change, a real cross-cutting mechanism others build on, or several significant decisions co-occurring unexplained. When unsure, prefer the lower severity.

## Grounding
Quote the exact added `[L<n>]` line(s) that establish significance in every cell. For MET, also quote the verbatim rationale sentence, commit subject or document reference and where it lives. For NOT_MET, the citations show the search: the description, the commit subjects, and the referenced rationale sources or their absence. Never invent a rationale, never infer the why from the code itself, and never assert that the dependency, schema or endpoint is wrong — judge only whether the why is recorded. Never claim a build or test ran. Describe the observable record; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
The overall adequacy of the description — a clear title and a why for the change as a whole — belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; here judge only whether THAT significant decision's rationale is recorded, so the two never double-flag. Whether a public-surface change is documented for its consumers belongs to `documents-public-api-and-behaviour-changes`; whether a linked wiki document now contradicts the code belongs to `change-keeps-linked-docs-consistent`.

practices.name: Document public API and behaviour changes
practices.whyItMatters: People outside your code depend on what you export. Change a public function or endpoint without a note and they find out at runtime, in their own project, with no warning, and they trust your library a little less each time.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A renamed parameter or a changed response shape lands with its reference docs and a changelog line updated in the same change, so the people building on your API hear about it from you, not from a broken build.
practices.holdsAs: API and behaviour changes ship with their docs
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: consumer-facing documentation of the changed public surface — a downstream caller hears what moved from the change itself.

## The standard
Judge one practice: when the change alters a PUBLIC or SHARED surface — something a SEPARATE consumer depends on and compiles or integrates against — does the change carry, in the same diff or in the description, documentation that tells consumers what moved? Public surfaces: a library's or framework's exported symbols, a published package's API, a documented HTTP or RPC contract, a persisted or wire schema, an error or response shape callers branch on, a config default a consumer sets. Good: the renamed parameter, new endpoint, changed response field or breaking removal lands with its doc-comment, a changelog line, or a description sentence naming the consumer-facing effect. Bad: a real exported-surface change ships with nothing a consumer could read to adapt. A generated API specification or reference documents a contract when its authoritative source and meaning are captured: judge the contract and the information a consumer receives, not whether the text was handwritten. Irrelevant generated output is not documentation, and generated churn alone never establishes an authored contract decision.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Establish the separate consumer from the captured contract or usage, never from package type alone: an application can expose HTTP endpoints, configuration or wire formats to other consumers without publishing a library. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the changed symbols are internal types, private signatures, local refactors or app-only fields with no separate consumer, or when no public-surface change is observable in the diff and description at all. Decide whether a changed symbol is actually exported and consumer-facing as an experienced reviewer would, not by keyword; a plainly internal symbol is NOT_APPLICABLE.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the surface change itself, and any documentation shipped beside it — a doc-comment on or above the surface, a changelog or docs addition, an updated reference. It establishes what changed and what documentation arrived with it. It never establishes a consumer by itself.
2. The description (`context/description.md`): a sentence naming the consumer-facing effect. It establishes documentation a consumer would read on the change; it never establishes a surface change the diff does not show.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the contract and its usage — who depends on the surface, and the existing reference docs the diff leaves untouched. It establishes whether a separate consumer exists and where the documentation would live. It never supplies the note the change failed to write.
4. A linked wiki document the change references, when it was materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`: its body may hold the documentation consumers need. Cite its file path together with the quoted or closely paraphrased sentence relied on; a bare URL is not evidence that the document says it. When the change points at a specific document that was not materialised for you, the documentation may live there: report a collection gap and record no observation, never an undocumented surface.
An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the public-surface change carries documentation naming what moved — quote the surface change and the documenting text.
- NOT_MET: documentation exists for the change yet never names the specific changed parameter, field, route or default a consumer must adapt to. Quote both.
- NOT_MET: a real public-surface change and, after looking in every place a consumer would — the doc-comment on or above the surface, a changelog or docs addition, the description, and a materialised wiki document — nothing a consumer could read to adapt.
- UNDETERMINED only when the evidence genuinely cannot settle whether the one symbol this practice turns on crosses a module or service boundary; name the question. Do not resolve that doubt into an observation or into a claim that no public surface was here. Having looked everywhere and found no documentation for an established public surface is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review. When several surfaces change, grade by the least-documented one.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on documentation alone — a formative practice, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a new additive surface with no documentation, since nothing breaks but consumers cannot discover it; lighter still, documentation that exists yet never names the specific changed parameter or field. MAJOR: a breaking change — a removed or renamed symbol, route or field, a narrowed type, a changed default — shipping with no documentation anywhere, so callers break without a migration note. Equivalent situations land at equivalent severity.

## Grounding
Cite the diff lines of the observable surface change in every cell. For MET, quote the documenting text and its file. For NOT_MET, quote the documentation and the changed element it omits. For NOT_MET, cite the surface change and name the boundary searched: the surface's doc-comment, the changelog and docs in the diff, the description, and any materialised wiki document. Never invent a symbol, an export marker, a changelog or a clean bill you did not see. Never assert the compile or runtime correctness of the surface, and never impute intent or care; describe the documentation practice on the observable artifact only.

## Defer
The pull request's general what-and-why narrative belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; whether a design decision's rationale is recorded belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. A thin description or an unjustified choice is not an observation here. Here only: is the public-surface change documented for its consumers?

practices.name: Keep linked wiki docs consistent with the change
practices.whyItMatters: A wiki that contradicts the code is worse than no wiki: teammates act on documented behaviour that no longer holds, and the drift compounds silently until someone is burned by it.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When a change alters something the team's design or reference doc describes, the same PR brings the doc along, so the wiki keeps telling the truth about the system.
practices.holdsAs: The wiki moves with the change it describes
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the captured linked document and changed behavior agree on the same contract, setting or operational step.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when this pull request changes a documented behaviour — a config default, a public API or wire contract, a CLI flag, an error or return code, an operational step — AND a linked wiki document describes that same behaviour, does the document still agree with the code, or has the diff left it contradicting reality? Work in two stages, in order. (1) From the hand-written diff, identify a concrete behaviour, contract or config the change alters. (2) Only if a materialised document describes that same thing, check whether the document now asserts something the code contradicts: an old default, a removed flag, a renamed field, a changed status code, a superseded step. The signal is a genuine contradiction between a specific document passage and a specific diff hunk — never staleness in the abstract, and never "the code changed, so the document is probably old". The presence or absence of a wiki link is never itself the observation; a change with no relevant document is not a weakness.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when: the complete pull request description and all captured linked issues reference no wiki document, with no unreadable or uncaptured adopted linked issue that could carry the reference; the diff is empty; or the diff does not touch anything the materialised document describes. Before concluding that no wiki document is referenced, inspect the complete description and every adopted linked issue. If an adopted linked issue was not captured or cannot be read, report a collection gap and record no observation unless the missing issue cannot affect the proposed result. A captured contradiction may support NOT_MET; MET or a no-relevant-document NOT_APPLICABLE result requires every adopted reference that could change that result. No linked issue and no document reference in the complete description needs no Outline capture. A document is available to you only when the pull request references it and its body was materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`. When the pull request references a specific document that a reader would expect to describe the behaviour this diff changes, and that document was not materialised, you cannot tell whether it now contradicts the code: report a collection gap and record no observation. An unreadable diff is the same collection gap.

## Sources
1. The description (`context/description.md`) and each linked issue (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`): which wiki documents the change references, and any sentence saying the document was updated. They establish that a document is in scope; they never establish what the document says. A bare URL is not evidence of a document's content. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The materialised documents (`context/docs/<collection>/<document>.md`): the passages that describe the behaviour. They establish what the wiki asserts today. Read the file before concluding anything about it.
3. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the hand-written hunks that alter a behaviour, contract or config, and any documentation the same change updates. It establishes what the code now does; it never establishes what the wiki says.
4. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): context for what a changed symbol, flag or step means. It never supplies a document passage.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: the diff changes a documented behaviour and the materialised document still asserts the old behaviour, so a reader who trusts the wiki is misled. Quote both sides.
- MET: the diff changes something the document describes AND the same pull request updates that document, or the document already reflects the new behaviour, so code and document do not contradict.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A referenced document you were not shown is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED. Having read the materialised document and found no passage the diff makes false is MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, over the whole change.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR — the aim is a trustworthy wiki, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a contradiction on a minor or internal-facing detail, a nudge to update the document. MAJOR: a contradiction a consumer would act on wrongly — a wrong documented default or limit, a removed API or flag the document still offers, a changed auth, security or data-handling step. When unsure, prefer the lower severity.

## Grounding
Ground every NOT_MET in both sides: the exact added or removed `[L<n>]` diff line that changes the behaviour, and the verbatim sentence from the materialised `.md` document that still asserts the old behaviour, cited with its `context/docs/...` file path. If you cannot point to a specific document passage the diff makes false, do not raise the observation: never infer a contradiction you cannot cite, and never fabricate a document quote. For MET, cite the diff line of the changed behaviour and the document line (in the diff or in the materialised file) that now agrees with it. Never claim a build or test ran, and never impute intent or care; describe what the document says and what the code does.

## Defer
Whether a change was documented at all, in any surface, belongs to `documents-public-api-and-behaviour-changes`. Whether the WHY of a decision is recorded belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. Here only: does a specific linked wiki document now contradict the code?

practices.name: Say what else you considered
practices.whyItMatters: A decision record that names only the winner tells the next person what was done, not what it cost. When a constraint later changes — a library is deprecated, the traffic grows, the team shrinks — the first question is always "what else did we look at, and does that reason still hold?". If the alternatives were never written down, that question can only be answered by redoing the whole investigation, and usually it is not answered at all: the decision quietly becomes something nobody feels able to revisit.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A record that names the two or three options that were genuinely in play and gives each one a sentence saying what ruled it out — the constraint it failed, the cost it carried, the thing the team was not willing to trade. Written for someone who arrives a year later with a changed constraint, so they can tell in a minute whether the decision still stands.
practices.holdsAs: Decisions say what else was considered and why not
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the decision record names considered alternatives and their rejection reasons, or explains the evidenced absence of feasible alternatives.

## The standard
Judge whether a decision record says what else was seriously considered and why those options were not chosen. A record that states only the chosen option records an outcome; a later reader needs the reasons the others lost, because that is the only part that tells them whether the decision still holds once a constraint changes. The standard is met when the document names at least one alternative that was genuinely on the table and gives a reason it was not chosen — a constraint it failed, a cost it carried, a trade-off the team was unwilling to make — and that reason is about that alternative specifically. A reason that only restates the chosen option's merits says nothing about why the others were worse and does not count. No template or heading name is required: a document that gives the reasons in prose satisfies this as fully as one with a headed section.

## Occasion
This is a gate. The practice applies only when the document is recognisably a decision record: it names a single decision and takes a position on it. Signals: a title or heading naming a decision; a status line (proposed, accepted, superseded); a section headed with words like decision, context, consequences, options, alternatives, trade-offs. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the kind, and stop for a design overview, a runbook, a how-to guide, a meeting note, an index page, or a specification that decides nothing. Stay silent rather than asking such a document to be a decision record.

## Sources
1. The document body (`context/document.md`): the whole authored text. It establishes whether an alternative is named and whether a reason is given for it. It never establishes whether the decision was right, whether the rejected options deserved rejection, or whether the document is still current.
2. The document metadata (`context/document.json`): the title. It establishes only whether the title names a decision, for the occasion. It never establishes what the body says.
Judge the text in front of you and nothing else. An image you cannot open: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. Two cases are not absence: a record that defers its options discussion to another document you were not given, and a body that visibly breaks off before any options section. If either reflects incomplete capture, report a collection gap and record no observation. If the complete authored document itself ends without discussing alternatives, judge that omission; do not mistake unfinished writing for missing capture.

## Judge
Read the whole body before deciding. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: at least one alternative is named and a reason specific to it is given, or the record explains the constraint that left no genuine alternative. Quote the alternatives and their reasons, or the no-alternative constraint.
- NOT_MET: the document states a decision and its rationale but names no alternative at all; or it lists alternatives with no reason any of them lost (a bare bullet list of technology names); or the only reason given restates the chosen option's merits. A section headed "Alternatives considered" that is empty, or contains only "none", is absent unless the document explains why there was genuinely no other option.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A complete document either accounts for alternatives or does not; what Sources names as incomplete capture is a collection gap, not an open question, while a fully captured document that is itself unfinished is judged under the occasion and the standard. Having read the whole body and found no alternative with a reason is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, on the document as a whole.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; MINOR is the usual band: a bounded addition fixes it — one alternative and the sentence that ruled it out. Do not raise the band on this practice alone; the weight of the decision is not something the text lets you judge.

## Grounding
For MET, cite the exact lines naming the alternative and its reason, or establishing why no genuine alternative existed. For NOT_MET, cite the decision statement and the boundary you searched: the whole body, including any options or alternatives section quoted or stated to be empty. Never claim the decision was correct or incorrect, never claim a rejected alternative deserved its fate, and never claim the document is or is not up to date. Describe what the record says; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether a pull request records the decisions it makes belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. Whether the decision was right, whether the alternatives deserved rejection, and whether the document is current are not judged by any practice here. Here only: does the record name what else was considered and why it lost?

groups.name: Disciplined delivery and version control
groups.description: Keep your delivery clean. Make each commit one self-contained change, leave generated and build files out of the diff, and branch from the shared integration branch so your work stands on its own.

practices.name: Keep each commit to one logical change
practices.whyItMatters: Mixing unrelated changes in a commit makes selective review, reverts and backports harder. Keeping changes separable makes the history more useful; clear commit subjects help a reader understand that intended separation.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Separate commits for separate ideas, such as 'Fix off-by-one in pagination' in one and 'Rename helper for clarity' in another, so each can be reviewed, reverted, or backported on its own.
practices.holdsAs: Each commit holds one logical change and no more
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: how the pull request's commits are partitioned — each commit one cohesive logical change, as its authored subject and body describe it and its own files show.

## The standard
Judge one thing: whether the commits are SPLIT so each one captures a single logical change, rather than one commit tangling separable work into a bundle a reviewer cannot follow, revert, or cherry-pick on its own. One logical change is one piece of work with everything it needs: a feature with its model, view, view model, test, asset, the manifest entry for the package it uses and the navigation that reaches it; a fix with its test; a diagram with the README line that embeds it; one document's sections revised for one reason. That is one concern however many clauses or files name it ("parse the header and validate it"). Two concerns are two pieces of work that each make sense alone: two features or user stories, two unrelated fixes, behavioural work beside a chore (a reformat or lint sweep, a rename or move sweep, a dependency bump, tooling or editor settings), or code beside an unrelated document or course deliverable. Several cohesive commits in one pull request is fine here, and a chore or a revert in its own commit is the partition working, not a tangle. Decide what is separable as an experienced reviewer would; there is no fixed word list. This is a workflow practice about how the history is partitioned, never a code-defect claim.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name which case, and stop when there was no split to judge: no authored non-merge commit remains: every entry is an automatic merge commit (`parent_count` of 2 or more, or a "Merge ..." subject).

## Sources
1. The commits (`context/commits.json`): each subject, full body, `parents` and the `files` it touched against its first parent, with status and line counts. They establish the author's partition — what each commit says it holds and what it actually touched. A commit whose files carry a second piece of work its subject does not name — a whole source-tree rename or a new view under a README subject, a user-story rewrite under a diagram subject — is a tangle the subject hides; the supporting files of the work it does name never are. `git show <sha>` in the checkout gives its patch when the file list is not enough.
2. The per-file changed-line spread of the whole change (`work/change/files.json`, `work/change/diff.patch`): the overall breadth the commits together cover.
Read subjects, bodies and each commit's files together and judge conservatively. The precomputed leads below these criteria list every authored commit as one row — its subject's shape (bare, a repeat, joined clauses, cut off), how many files it only moved, and the files it edited with their line counts — as places to look, never verdicts: joined clauses are punctuation, not a count of concerns. If `context/commits.json` is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation; uncollected subjects are never authored silence and never UNDETERMINED.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: every commit holds one logical change, as its subject, body and files show. Looks like a lapse but is not: "Add cast fetching, and adjust movie fetching" where the adjustment returns what the new fetch reads; "Switch the problem statement to the new app idea, rewrite the user stories" revising one README for one reason; "Update class diagram: add Metric, drop method signatures" revising one diagram; a feature commit that also edits `project.yml` for its package; README commits later reverted, each on its own. Each is one concern.
- NOT_MET: at least one commit holds two concerns — its subject or body names both ("Extract row views, replace foregroundColor with foregroundStyle": a refactor and an API sweep; "add editor settings + more skeleton"), or its files carry one its subject does not name. Quote the deciding subject with its short SHA, name the two pieces of work, and name the path that shows an unnamed one.
- UNDETERMINED when a bare or vague subject ("fixes", "ccc", "Improve MR") leaves a commit's content open and neither its files nor its patch settle whether it holds one piece of work or two; name the commit and the missing distinction. A broad commit under a vague subject is not a tangle by breadth alone; a narrow one whose files show a single piece of work is cohesive.
One observation per review, over the whole series, including a single authored commit that can be cohesive or bundled.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on commit atomicity alone — a formative practice, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a single commit bundles separable work, and splitting it would isolate each concern. MAJOR: the history broadly tangles, so a reviewer cannot reason about or revert one concern at a time.

## Grounding
Every claim cites the commit record that supports it: quote the deciding subject(s) verbatim, each with its short SHA, for NOT_MET, and name any path from that commit's `files` that shows the unnamed concern; cite the subjects whose partition you accepted for MET. Never claim a per-commit file mapping you cannot observe. Cite the corresponding subject, SHA and file entries in the captured `context/commits.json` artifact. Never cite a diff line for this observation, and never record UNDETERMINED because the subjects have no line of their own to cite. Describe the observable split; never impute intent or character, and never frame a tangle as a defect in the code.

## Defer
Overall pull request size, and a pull request carrying several features in separate commits, belong to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; a large but cohesive partition can be a strength here. Subject wording belongs to `commit-subjects-explain-each-change`; a vague subject alone establishes neither cohesion nor a tangle. A generated or editor file swept into a commit (`.idea/`, `.Rhistory`, a regenerated `Info.plist`) belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`. Here only: does each commit hold one logical change?

practices.name: Track generated artifacts only when justified
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer catches the most problems in the hand-written lines they can read closely, and a committed build output or editor config buries that source under machine noise nobody reviews. Leaving generated files out keeps the diff to the change a person can actually check, and spares everyone the odd conflict in a file no human wrote.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Build outputs, logs and editor files stay out of the repository. Deliberately tracked generated artifacts follow the documented generation workflow; intentional regeneration can be appropriate even without a simultaneous source edit.
practices.holdsAs: Tracked artifacts follow the repository generation policy
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: tracked generated or build artifacts are justified by captured repository policy or the source-to-artifact workflow.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does the change include generated or build artifacts only where the repository's captured policy or its source-to-artifact workflow justifies tracking them? This is a repository-hygiene practice about what gets committed — never a code-defect claim about a file's contents, and generated output is not itself the defect. Judge from the file paths in the diff. Machine noise being reviewed as if it were source has a recognisable shape across any stack or language — a location or a banner that says "a tool wrote this": a build-output directory, an editor or OS cruft file, a coverage dump, a vendored or cached blob, a minified single-line bundle, or a tracked generated file someone hand-edited instead of regenerating. These are open examples, not a closed list. A repository may deliberately version-control some generated sources — a committed OpenAPI spec, a generated client, an ERD, a route tree. When such a tracked artifact moves in step with the hand-written change that drives its regeneration, that is intended, regeneration-consistent movement: do not flag it. An intentional regeneration may be appropriate without a simultaneous hand-written edit. Flag only output that is not meant to be tracked, or a tracked generated file left hand-edited or stale relative to its source.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop only for an empty change. A change whose files are all generated still has content whose inclusion can be reviewed; it is judged, not ruled out.

## Sources
1. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`) and the per-file headers of the diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the paths. They establish which paths changed and where they sit — the primary evidence. A path never establishes compile, build or runtime behaviour.
2. The patch body (`work/change/diff.patch`): open it only to confirm a flagged path is machine-emitted when the path alone is ambiguous — a "DO NOT EDIT", "@generated" or "auto-generated" banner, a minified single line. The evidence is the path plus that confirming line, never a line-by-line review of the file's contents.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the ignore rules, the documented generation workflow, and whether an artifact is tracked and which source drives it. It establishes whether tracking a generated file is intended. It never establishes manual editing or stale generation from an unchanged source file alone.
If the policy or source evidence a flag needs was not acquired, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: a quoted repository policy or an observable workflow establishes that an added artifact should not be tracked, or a tracked generated file was hand-edited or left stale relative to the source that drives it. Quote each offending path.
- MET: a complete bounded search over every changed path establishes that the changed artifacts are appropriately tracked — every path is something a person authored or intended: source, tests, docs, hand-written config, a lockfile moving in step with its manifest, or a tracked generated artifact whose regeneration is justified by the captured workflow, with or without a simultaneous source edit.
- UNDETERMINED when the one path this practice turns on is genuinely ambiguous — the path, any banner and the patch together cannot tell you whether it is machine-emitted, or whether tracking and regenerating that artifact is justified by the captured policy or workflow. Say so rather than let the doubt pass as a clean bill; name what would settle it. Having walked every path and found each justified is MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, covering every flagged path.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a practice to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a lone stray artifact. MAJOR: a committed build-output directory, several leaked artifacts, or a hand-edited generated file that should have been regenerated. Identical situations land identically.

## Grounding
Every NOT_MET names each offending path verbatim and, for a generated-file flag, quotes the confirming banner or names the tracked artifact and its driving source. If you cannot name an offending path there is nothing to flag; do not invent one. Cite a line of the flagged file from `work/change/diff.patch` (`scm.pull-request.diff`, the pinned `context/change.json`): `work/change/files.json` is derived here and is not citable; a flagged file the diff shows without numbered lines (binary, or renamed without edits) is cited through the `path` line of its entry in `context/commits.json`. For MET evidence.search records the boundary and the citations quote it: `changed_files` in `context/metadata.json` (`scm.pull-request.core`) and the paths you walked, listed in the rationale. Describe the observable fact ("this path is machine-emitted") and the next step (ignore it and drop it, or regenerate from source). Never assert compile, build or runtime behaviour from a path; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether a dependency change was deliberate or justified belongs to `changes-dependencies-deliberately`; a lockfile moving in step with its manifest is its concern. Do not infer that a lockfile was hand-edited merely because its manifest did not change — an intentional resolution refresh may update a lockfile alone. Here only: does the diff carry machine output that should not be tracked?

groups.name: Tracking work from issue to merge
groups.description: Plan and track the work so a maintainer can route it and watch it progress, and keep the issue and the change that answers it linked: split genuinely large issues into trackable sub-tasks, triage each one, name the issue the change implements, and confirm the issue's outcome when the change lands.

practices.name: Break large work into trackable subtasks
practices.whyItMatters: A big ask written as one wall of text is either 0% or 100% done, with no way to see progress or split the load. Breaking it into checkable steps turns a daunting job into pieces people can pick up and finish one at a time.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A genuinely large issue split into a task list or linked sub-issues, such as 'design the schema', 'add the endpoint', and 'wire up the UI', so progress is visible and pieces can be worked in parallel.
practices.holdsAs: Large work arrives split into trackable pieces
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a trackable breakdown of work that is large enough to need one — checkable sub-units a maintainer can watch reach done, rather than one monolithic ask.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: when the issue describes genuinely LARGE or multi-part work, is that work broken into explicit, trackable sub-units, rather than left as a single undivided block? Trackable means the parts are individually checkable or addressable: a task list of checkboxes that name work to do, a tracked sub-issue tree, or enumerated child or tracking issues the body frames as parts. Reason like a senior reviewer scanning a backlog: a big ask written as one block is either 0% or 100% done with no visible progress; a decomposed one lets pieces be picked up in parallel and tracked to done. What counts as LARGE is a judgment, not a word count: the signal is two or more SEPARABLE deliverables that could ship or be assigned independently, or an explicit epic, initiative, meta or tracking framing the issue itself chose. Largeness comes from what the parts are, never from how many items, clauses or characters there are: independent deliverables listed in one short sentence — a rename, a new tab, a theme, a changed default — are large work, while the sections, topics or checks of one page, screen or feature are parts of one deliverable, not separate work. Sequential steps of ONE cohesive flow described as a journey are a single deliverable, not several parts. A checklist of verification items is not a work breakdown unless it also names concrete implementation sub-steps.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the case, and stop when: the issue is a pure question, a support request or an open discussion with no concrete deliverable; the body is empty, title-only or an unmodified template, so nothing is quotable; or the work is a focused single-concern deliverable (one feature, one bug), which neither needs a breakdown nor is penalised for lacking one. Never manufacture a strength from the mere absence of largeness, and never make the single-concern scope judgment here — that belongs to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`.

## Sources
Your context is the issue only; there is no diff or code.
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist and enumerated list. It establishes whether the work is large (separable deliverables, epic framing) and whether a checklist or a set of framed child issues breaks it down. It never establishes largeness from title length or tone alone.
2. The labels and the sub-issue rollup (`context/metadata.json`): a label such as epic or tracking, and the `sub_issues_total` / `sub_issues_completed` figures. A non-zero rollup is a tracked sub-issue tree; a null or missing figure is unknown, never zero. The labels establish the framing the issue chose; they never by themselves establish that a breakdown exists.
3. The comments (`context/comments.json`): a later comment can supply the breakdown or the child issues. They establish a breakdown on that surface; they never establish one the text does not show.
An image in the body: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. Before concluding that no breakdown exists, scan ALL three surfaces. If the body or the comments were not captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the work is genuinely large AND a trackable breakdown is quotable — named sub-steps as a checklist ("design the schema", "add the endpoint", "wire up the UI"), a non-zero sub-issue rollup, or child issues the body frames as parts. Sibling issues in the project inventory that this body never names are not its breakdown, however well they match its sentences.
- NOT_MET: the work is clearly large AND no trackable breakdown exists on any of the three surfaces — an epic or tracking-framed issue with nothing tracked under it, or a body that enumerates several independent deliverables as prose with no way to track each. An element you cannot quote counts as absent.
- UNDETERMINED only when the text genuinely cannot settle whether its spans are one journey or several separable deliverables AND no breakdown exists on any surface; quote the ambiguous span and say what would settle it. Do not resolve that doubt into silence. Having scanned every surface and found no breakdown for clearly large work is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, over the whole issue. Identical evidence yields the same call.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on decomposition alone — a non-blocking workflow practice, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: only a couple of parts go untracked, and a short checklist would fix it. MAJOR: an issue the text itself frames as an epic, initiative, meta or tracking issue has nothing tracked under it at all.

## Grounding
Every "large" claim and every "no breakdown" claim quotes the exact span: a label name, a body sentence naming each separable deliverable, the rollup figure, or a comment. For MET, quote the checklist lines, the rollup figure or the framed child references. For NOT_MET, cite the spans that establish largeness and name the boundary searched: the body, the rollup, and the comments. Never invent largeness, never fabricate a breakdown you did not see. Never assert technical feasibility, hour estimates or design correctness, and never grade the reporter as a person; describe the observable artifact state only.

## Defer
Whether the work SHOULD have been one concern belongs to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`; treat a multi-part ask as legitimately large work needing a breakdown, and do not re-judge its scope. Whether acceptance criteria or a Definition of Done are present belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`; do not re-flag a verification checklist here. Here only: is large work DECOMPOSED into trackable parts?

practices.name: Classify the issue the way the project classifies issues
practices.whyItMatters: A label kind the project filters and groups by — type, priority, size — routes the issue to the board column, the person and the sprint it belongs to. An issue outside that scheme is the one nobody's filter shows, so it waits.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The issue carries the labels, native type, owner or milestone required by the documented project policy for its kind; fields that the policy does not require may remain unset.
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the issue satisfies the classification requirements of the documented project policy applicable to it.

## The standard
Judge whether this issue follows the labelling convention the project actually keeps, not whether every metadata field is filled. A convention must be established by an explicit documented project policy applicable to this kind of issue. Label frequency, a list of labels in use or another issue's assignment does not establish a requirement. Compare the captured issue with that policy: require only the label kinds, native type, ownership or milestone it actually mandates. A native issue type can satisfy a corresponding label kind. Never demand a classification the project does not use.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE when a captured project policy establishes that no classification requirement applies to this kind of issue. Missing policy is not evidence of no convention. Current automated capture does not supply project classification requirements, so this practice is unavailable for automated review. In a manual review, use the documented policy; failed acquisition of required policy or metadata is a collection gap.

## Sources
1. The documented project classification policy supplied to the manual review: applicable label kinds, native issue types, ownership and milestone requirements. It establishes what this issue is required to carry, not how often metadata happens to occur elsewhere.
2. The issue metadata (`context/metadata.json`): native type, labels, assignees and milestone. It establishes what this issue carries.
3. The title and body (`context/description.md`): the issue kind and any explicit routing request. A request alone does not establish a project-wide rule.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: every classification requirement applicable under the captured policy is satisfied. Quote the policy and corresponding metadata.
- NOT_MET: an applicable policy requirement is not satisfied. Quote the requirement and the complete metadata that lacks it.
- UNDETERMINED: complete supplied policy or metadata leaves the applicability of a deciding requirement genuinely ambiguous; name what would settle it. Missing required acquisition produces no observation.
One observation per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MINOR — non-blocking feedback about routing, not a merge gate. MINOR: no label at all in a labelled project, or the body asks to be routed and no label answers it. INFO: one kind of several missing.

## Grounding
Quote the applicable documented requirement and this issue's metadata. Never infer a normative convention from label frequency, labels in use, ownership on other issues or the number of people in a project. Never assess whether the work is worth doing.

## Defer
Problem framing belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`, scope to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`, and the definition of done to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: is the issue classified the way this project classifies its issues?

insufficiencyReason.description: Hephaestus captures the issue metadata, but not the project classification requirements that establish which labels, owners or milestones this issue should carry. Labels used elsewhere do not establish a required convention. A person with the project policy can assess this practice.

practices.name: Confirm the outcome before closing the issue

insufficiencyReason.description: Hephaestus reads an issue as it stands when the review runs, after the close. Its checklist, sub-issue progress and comments can all change after the close, and the issue can be reopened and closed again, so what Hephaestus reads cannot show what was still open when it was closed. Whether the outcome was confirmed at that close needs a person who saw it.

practices.whyItMatters: Closing an issue tells the whole team it is handled. Closing it with a checklist item still unticked or sub-issues still open drops that work quietly, and someone hits the gap later expecting it to be done.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Before closing, every acceptance item is checked and every tracked sub-issue is finished, or a comment says plainly what is being dropped and why, so 'closed' honestly means done.
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: evidence dated to the close accounts for the issue's stated outcome, through confirmed completion or an explained remainder.

## The standard
When an issue is CLOSED as done, judge whether its own stated definition of done was confirmed at that close — every checkable acceptance item ticked and every tracked sub-issue finished — or whether a remainder was named at the close. Assess this single closure decision only, never the work: an empty checkbox may simply never have been ticked while the work was genuinely done. A closing comment that says plainly what is being dropped or deferred and why accounts for the remainder. The question is about the record as it stood at the close, and only evidence dated to that close can answer it. Never assert compile, runtime or correctness behaviour; there is no diff or code here.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when evidence dated to this close shows the issue was not closed as done: closed as not-planned, wontfix, duplicate, superseded or deferred. The current `state_reason`, body and rollup describe the latest state, not this close, so they cannot settle whether this close was done or stated a checkable outcome; when nothing dated to the close does, the gate is unresolved and the Judge records UNDETERMINED. NOT_APPLICABLE belongs to scope facts dated to the close, never to evidence you could not read or could not date.

## Sources
1. The issue record (`context/metadata.json`): state, `state_reason`, `closed_at`, labels and the sub-issue rollup. `closed_at` dates the close and nothing else. The body, labels and rollup are their values when the review read them, which is after the close; they never show their values at the close.
2. The title and body (`context/description.md`): the current text. A checkbox can be ticked, unticked or added after the close, and the issue can be reopened and closed again, so a current checkbox is not a checkbox at the close.
3. Comments (`context/comments.json`): `created_at` dates when a comment was written, not its present text, which may since have been edited; a comment written after the close is never a disposition at the close.
4. The workspace inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): state the overlapping or closing artifact you found, quoted as `#number "title" (state)`, or that you scanned it and found none.
When the comments or the issue record were not captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
The undesirable behaviour is closing as done with a stated outcome unmet and unaccounted for. Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: evidence dated to this close shows a done-item still open at it — an unchecked acceptance or Definition-of-Done line, or a rollup short of complete — and nothing at the close names where that remainder went.
- MET: evidence dated to this close shows every checkable item ticked and every tracked sub-issue completed, or a remainder named at the close.
- UNDETERMINED: the issue was closed as done or with an unrecorded disposition, and the only record of its checklist, rollup or closing comments is the one read after the close. Name the undated fact. Never decide either cell from the current body, the current rollup or current comment text, whichever way they point.
One observation per review, on the single at-close question. Do not infer a longitudinal or developer-wide pattern from this one issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on outcome confirmation alone — non-blocking. MINOR: an open sub-issue rollup alone. MAJOR: an unconfirmed acceptance or Definition-of-Done condition with nothing at the close accounting for it. A remainder named at the close is not a negative. Identical inputs yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Every claim cites an exact quoted span and says what dates it: the state or `state_reason` value, the `closed_at` timestamp, and for either assessed cell the at-close evidence of each item it relies on. An UNDETERMINED observation quotes what was read and states that it is dated after the close. State the inventory result in every observation. Describe only observable state — "closed as done with '<quoted line>' still unchecked at the close" — never a charge against the closer. Never fabricate a checklist, a clean bill or a disposition.

## Defer
Whether a NEW or OPEN issue defines a checkable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: was the stated outcome confirmed at the close?

practices.name: Record the outcome of a closed issue
practices.whyItMatters: A closed issue is where the team looks to learn what was delivered. When its record says which items were done and what happened to the rest, the next person neither guesses nor repeats the digging.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Once an issue is closed, its list is ticked as far as the work went or a comment confirms what was done, and anything not done is named as dropped or deferred.
practices.holdsAs: Each closed issue records what became of its outcome
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the authored record of a closed issue — its body and discussion as captured now — accounts for the outcome the issue states.

## The standard
Judge one bookkeeping act on an issue that is CLOSED as this review reads it: do its body and discussion, as they stand now, account for the outcome the issue itself states? An outcome is stated when the issue gives something checkable: a task or acceptance list, a Definition of Done, Given-When-Then scenarios, or explicit outcome statements in prose. A stated item is accounted for when it is ticked, or when the body or a comment clearly confirms it done — a short confirmation is enough when it unambiguously covers the item — or, if it was not done, explicitly says which work was dropped or deferred. A remainder needs accounting only when there is one. Judge what the record says, never whether the work was done or done correctly: a tick or a confirmation records a claim, and an unticked item may describe finished work. The closed state or a closing pull or merge request accounts for nothing by itself, and a statement that names the feature counts only for the items it plainly covers. The person who closed the issue may not be its author; describe the record, never who failed to write it.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when: the captured issue is not closed; its current disposition is not planned, duplicate or superseded; or it states no checkable outcome you can quote. The current disposition is the current `state_reason`, or a comment that clearly speaks to the present close; a comment from before an earlier reopen does not decide it, and `completed` alone does not disprove an explicit current disposition statement: some providers synthesize it for every non-duplicate closure. If current statements genuinely conflict, use UNDETERMINED.

## Sources
1. The issue record (`context/metadata.json`): `state`, `state_reason` and `closed_at` as captured when this review ran. They establish the current state and disposition, never what any field said at the close.
2. The title and body (`context/description.md`): the stated outcome and its ticks as they stand now.
3. The discussion (`context/comments.json`): the mirrored comments with their author, `created_at` and `updated_at`, as they stand now; Hephaestus's own comments are left out. A comment can account for an item as fully as a tick. Its dates say when it was written and last edited, never that it existed at the close.
Sub-issue counts and other progress figures are not authored statements and decide nothing here; a sub-issue the body or a comment refers to counts only through what that text says. All of it is the record now; never claim what was true when the issue was closed. If the issue record or the discussion was not captured, or the discussion was captured only in part, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: every stated item is ticked or accounted for in the body or discussion. Quote the ticks or the text that accounts for them.
- NOT_MET: the issue is closed, states a checkable outcome, and part of it is neither ticked nor accounted for in the body or discussion. Quote the unaccounted items.
- UNDETERMINED: complete captured text leaves it genuinely ambiguous whether a statement covers an item, or what the current disposition is; name the deciding question.
One observation per review, on the issue's current authored record.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking bookkeeping. MINOR, the usual band: a few stated items neither ticked nor accounted for. MAJOR: most of the stated outcome neither ticked nor accounted for. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the stated items as written, their tick state, the `state` value, and any text you rely on with its author and dates, and say that this is the record as captured now. Never claim an item was or was not delivered, never claim the record looked this way at the close, and never read the closed state as a tick.

## Defer
Whether the issue stated a checkable outcome in the first place belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`; whether a merged change brought its linked issue's outcome into line belongs to `merge-confirms-the-linked-issue-outcome`; what the record showed at the moment of the close is a question for a person (`issue-closed-with-unmet-outcome`). Here only: does the closed issue's current authored record account for its stated outcome?

practices.name: Link the change to the issue it implements
practices.whyItMatters: A change that names the issue it answers can be read against what was asked, closes that issue when it lands, and leaves a trail anyone can follow later. One without it makes the reviewer guess what the work was for, and leaves the issue open or closed by hand.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The title, the description or the branch names the issue by number, with a closing keyword in the body when the change completes it, so the issue closes with the merge and the two stay linked.
practices.holdsAs: Every change names the issue it implements
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the pull request names the issue it implements, so the work can be read against what was asked and the issue can close with the merge.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does this pull request say which issue it implements, in a way the platform links?
