A link is the issue's number in the title (`#12: …`), a closing reference in the body (`Closes #12`, `Fixes #12`, `Resolves #12`, or the provider's equivalent), a branch created from the issue (`12-add-login`), or a captured linked work item. A link makes the issue readable from the review; only a provider-recognized closing relationship can close it when the change merges; a change with none of these stands alone. Judge the presence of the link, never the quality of the issue it points to or whether the change fulfils it.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the work has no issue to link: the repository tracks no issues (`context/project_inventory.json` lists none), or the change is of a kind that answers no issue by convention — a release or version bump, a dependency update from a bot, a revert, a merge of one long-lived branch into another. A change a person made to the product is expected to answer an issue; a missing issue is then the lapse, not the absence of an occasion.

## Sources
1. The title, source branch and body (`context/metadata.json`, `context/description.md`): the number references and closing keywords as written. They establish the link the author made. They never establish that the issue exists or that the change fulfils it.
2. The linked work items (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`, and `context/linked_work_items.json` with `how` per item) when captured: the items the platform resolved from those references, and for each whether the provider records it as a closing candidate for this change (`how: closesOnMerge`) or the text merely mentions it (`how: mentions`). A provider-recorded closing link is the link, whatever the text says; a mention is only a mention. Their absence establishes nothing when no reference was written.
3. The inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): whether the project tracks issues at all, and, for a change with no reference, whether an open issue plainly describes this work — quote its `#number "title"` if you find one, or say you scanned it and found none.
4. The commits (`context/commits.json`): a further place an issue number may appear. They establish a reference the author left in history, nothing more. The precomputed leads below these criteria list every number referenced, where it was written, and whether the inventory or the linked items hold an issue of that number with its title and state.
If the record or the inventory is unavailable for a change with no reference, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the title, body, branch or a captured linked item names an issue of this project by number, or a closing keyword names one. Quote the reference.
- NOT_MET: a reference is written but cannot be what it claims — it resolves to no issue, or claims to implement an issue whose captured contents clearly concern different work. A deliberate cross-project issue link can satisfy traceability; its closing behavior depends on the provider. Quote the reference and name the fact that breaks it.
- NOT_MET: the change is product work by a person and no title, body, branch, commit or linked item names an issue, after scanning all of them. Say what you scanned.
- UNDETERMINED: a reference whose target you cannot resolve because the inventory was not captured and the number could be a pull request as well as an issue; name what would settle it.
One observation per review.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: product work with no reference where an open issue for it plainly exists in the inventory, or a reference in the wrong form. MAJOR: a closing keyword that would close an issue the change does not fulfil, or product work with no issue at all in a project that tracks its work in issues. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the reference as written in the title, body, branch name or commit subject, or the linked item's `#number "title"`. NOT_MET names every source scanned. Never invent an issue number, and never claim an issue's content from its number alone.

## Defer
Whether the change fulfils the issue's acceptance criteria belongs to `honours-linked-issue-acceptance-criteria`; the description's what and why belong to `describe-what-and-why`. Here only: is the change linked to the issue it implements?

practices.name: Confirm the linked issue's outcome
practices.whyItMatters: A linked issue with its outcome unconfirmed tells the next person little about what was delivered. After a change merges, ticking what landed and naming what moves elsewhere keeps the tracker true.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: After a change merges, its linked issue accounts for what landed: delivered items are ticked or a closing sentence names them and says what moves elsewhere, and the issue's state matches.
practices.holdsAs: The linked issue accounts for merged work
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: for merged work, the captured record confirms the linked issue's stated outcome — its checkable items ticked or the remainder named — so the tracker accounts for what was delivered.

## The standard
Judge one thing about this merged pull request: does the captured record bring the linked issue's own definition of done into line with what landed? The merge establishes the occasion; this review assesses confirmation in the capture, not the issue body at merge time. An issue that stated a checkable outcome (an acceptance checklist, a Definition of Done, a Given-When-Then block, tracked sub-issues) is confirmed when the items the change delivers are ticked and any remainder is named — in the issue, in the pull request body, or in a closing comment. Assess only this bookkeeping act, never whether the work is correct: an unticked item may describe delivered work, and a ticked one may not. A closing sentence that says plainly what is done and what is deferred confirms the outcome as well as ticks do; a sentence that names the feature ("added the glossary") without naming the items confirms nothing.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when: the pull request is not merged; a complete linked-work inventory establishes no relevant item, or the linked item states no checkable outcome you can quote (a task list, an acceptance or Definition-of-Done block, a Given-When-Then, or a non-zero sub-issue rollup); or the linked item was closed as not planned, duplicate or superseded, since its outcome was deliberately abandoned. A linked item with an outcome and a merge are the occasion — every captured item this change explicitly implements, closing candidates and adopted partial work alike; a mention alone does not establish that this change must account for the item; the precomputed leads list each with its items and ticks. A user story without a task list, an outcome heading or sub-issues is no occasion, however plainly the diff delivers it.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): `state` and `merged_at`. It establishes that and when the change merged. It never establishes the issue's state.
2. Each linked item (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`: number, title, state, body; `how` in `linked_work_items.json` says whether the provider records it as a closing candidate): the checkable outcome as written, with its ticks as captured. It establishes what was stated and which items are ticked. Confirmation captured after the merge counts. A missing confirmation describes this capture; it does not establish that confirmation never happened or that it was missing at merge time. Its body is the text as mirrored at capture, and its opening and closing dates are not when any line of it was written. A closed state alone confirms nothing; the ticks or the words do.
3. The body (`context/description.md`) and the discussion (`context/general_comments.json`): a done/deferred mapping or a closing sentence. They establish what the author said was delivered. They never establish that it was.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): read only to ground a heavier severity when a named item is plainly not touched. It never establishes that an item is met.
If the linked item's body or the record's merge time is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: every item the change delivers is ticked, or a closing sentence names what was delivered and what moves elsewhere. Quote the ticked items or the sentence. A checked mapping in the merge request body can account for the item as well as prose does, but generic template checks cannot. Judge the recorded done/deferred mapping, not whether the code actually delivers the item.
- NOT_MET: the change merged, the linked item states a checkable outcome, and neither ticks nor a closing sentence account for it in the capture — items are unticked with no word, whether the issue is closed or open. Quote the unticked items and the merge time.
- UNDETERMINED: complete captured text leaves the done/deferred mapping genuinely ambiguous; name the deciding question. A truncated capture of a required checklist is a collection gap and produces no observation.
One observation per review.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one or two items unticked in the capture with the work plainly delivered, or a closing sentence that names the outcome loosely. MAJOR: most of the stated outcome is unticked and unmentioned in the captured closed issue, or the captured issue is open with nothing said. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the outcome items from the linked item as written, the tick state, the merge time from the record, and any closing sentence. Never claim an item is met or unmet from the code; never infer a tick that is not in the capture; never read a closed state as a tick. Credit a tick or a sentence in the item's body or the description as captured; say it was there before, at or after the merge only when independently dated evidence establishes that, since the creation date of a body, a description or a comment alone does not date text edited later. A later capture that confirms the outcome does not undo an earlier observation that read it unconfirmed; each stands for the capture it read.

## Defer
Whether the change fulfils the acceptance criteria belongs to `honours-linked-issue-acceptance-criteria`; the issue's own closing decision, when someone closes it by hand, belongs to `issue-closed-with-unmet-outcome`. Here only: does the captured record confirm the linked issue's outcome for the merged work?

practices.name: Track the review asks you defer
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer's ask answered with 'later' and nothing else is a promise that evaporates at the merge. Turning a deferred ask into a tracked issue, or getting the reviewer's explicit agreement to drop it, keeps the review's value after the thread is resolved.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Every review ask the author does not address in the change is either turned into an issue the thread links, or explicitly waived by the reviewer; nothing is resolved with a bare 'will do later'.
practices.holdsAs: Deferred review asks become tracked issues
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a review ask the author defers rather than addresses is turned into tracked work or explicitly waived by the reviewer, never resolved on a bare promise.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when a reviewer asked for something in a thread and the author did not do it in this change, what happened to the ask at the merge? A deferral is tracked when the thread, the body or a comment names an issue for it (`#number`, a link, "tracked in …") or the reviewer explicitly agrees to drop it ("fine to skip", "not needed", a reviewer statement accepting the author's stated reason). An approval given on the condition that the ask be done later ("I'll approve it, with the condition that you add it in your next MR") keeps the ask alive: it is a deferral that needs a tracked item, never a waiver. A deferral is bare when the ask is resolved or the change merged with only "later", "next PR", "will do" or silence. Judge only asks the author deferred; an ask the author addressed in the diff, or answered with a reason the reviewer accepted, is not a deferral.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when: the pull request is not merged; the complete captured inline and general review record contains no ask the author left unaddressed in the change — every ask was addressed in the diff or answered with a reason the reviewer accepted. A question that requests no change ("what is this for?") is not an ask, whether or not it was answered, and neither is a remark aimed at later work ("something to keep in mind next time"): it asks nothing of this change. The author is the `author` login of `context/metadata.json`; a comment by any other login is a reviewer's, and a reviewer's own "ignore" or "fine" on an ask — theirs or a bot's — is a waiver. A merged change with at least one deferred ask is the occasion.

## Sources
1. The inline review comments (`context/comments.json`: `path`, `line`, `body`, `author`, `created_at`) and the conversation (`context/general_comments.json`): every ask and every reply, with authors and dates. They establish which asks were made, which were answered, and with what words. The threads (`context/review_threads.json`) carry each thread's path, line and resolution and no words; a resolution by the author establishes nothing about the substance, and a resolution by the reviewer after the author's stated reason is the reviewer accepting it. The precomputed leads below these criteria list every comment by someone other than the author, one row each, with whether the change touches its file, whether the author replied, whether the reviewer had a later word on the thread or approved after it: decide every row that asks something.
2. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): whether an ask was addressed in the change — the file and line the thread anchors to, read as changed or not. It establishes addressed versus not; it never establishes a waiver.
3. The body and the discussion (`context/description.md`, `context/general_comments.json`): a follow-up list, an issue reference for the deferral, or the reviewer's agreement. They establish tracking or a waiver when quotable.
4. The linked work items (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`) when captured: an issue that names the deferred ask. It establishes the tracking; its absence establishes nothing when a comment names an issue by number.
If the change merged but the threads are absent or truncated, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate every ask by someone other than the author first and decide each against the diff — a two-part ask half-addressed leaves one part deferred, and a thread marked RESOLVED decides nothing. An ask is addressed only by a changed line that does what was asked; an unchanged anchor alone does not establish that the ask was unaddressed: a guard or other relevant change elsewhere can satisfy it. Inspect the request's substance and the complete changed code before deciding. An ask the author answered with a reason is deferred bare unless the reviewer explicitly accepts the reason; a later approval without such evidence is not a waiver. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: at least one ask is deferred, and every deferred ask is tracked by a named issue or explicitly waived by the reviewer. Quote the ask and the tracking reference or the waiver.
- NOT_MET: at least one ask was deferred on a bare promise or in silence — resolved or merged past with no issue and no reviewer waiver. Quote the ask and the author's last word on it, or note the silence.
- UNDETERMINED: the thread's last word could be a waiver or a deferral and the reviewer's approval carries no comment; name the fact that would settle it.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential bare deferral when there are several.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a small ask (a rename, a comment, a nit) deferred bare. MAJOR: a correctness, safety or test ask deferred on a bare promise and the change merged. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the reviewer's ask and the author's reply verbatim with their authors and dates, and the issue reference or waiver when there is one. Never infer a waiver from an approval alone, and never claim an ask was addressed without the changed line that addresses it.

## Defer
Whether the author replied to comments at all belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; a thread left unresolved at the merge belongs to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`. Here only: where did the deferred asks go?

practices.name: Merge only after someone else approved
practices.subject: MERGER
practices.whyItMatters: A change merged before anyone approved it skips the one check the team agreed on: a second pair of eyes before the code is everyone's. It is also how a reviewer's outstanding request for changes gets buried. Waiting for the approval, and re-requesting it after a rework, is what keeps the review real.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The person who merges does so after an approval from someone other than the author that is still current — no later request for changes, no dismissal — and after a rework asks for the approval again before merging.
practices.holdsAs: Nothing merges without a current approval from someone else
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the merge happens after a current approval from someone other than the author, and never over an outstanding request for changes.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the moment this pull request merged: was there, at that moment, an approval from another person — an account other than the author's whose decision is not marked `bot` — that still stood? An approval stands when it was submitted before the merge and nothing later withdrew it — no dismissal, no revocation (`UNAPPROVED`) and no request for changes by the same reviewer after it. A request for changes stands when it was submitted before the merge and no later approval by the same reviewer replaced it. A decision marked `bot` is an automated account's recorded act, never another person's review: its approval is not an approval here, and its request for changes does not stand against another person's approval. A complete bounded event record with no dismissal, revocation or later request for changes establishes no recorded withdrawal within that boundary. A latest-state snapshot alone does not establish complete historical event coverage. Merging with a standing approval and no standing request for changes is the practice; merging with none, or over a standing request for changes, is the lapse. Judge the decisions as recorded, never whether the review was thorough — that belongs to the review practices. That the author presses the merge button on their own pull request is the ordinary course in most teams and is never the lapse here; the only lapse is merging without another person's standing approval. The subject is the person who merged, whether or not that person authored the change.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when: the pull request is not merged; or the repository plainly works without review — no reviewer was requested, no review decision or review thread exists on this pull request, and the inventory shows a single-person project. A pull request with a reviewer requested, a review decision or a review comment is the occasion; a decision marked `bot` is still a review decision for this gate.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): `merged_at`, `merged_by`, `author`. It establishes who merged and when. When `merged_by` is absent, record no observation: the review cannot name the merger. A different recorded merger is still the subject.
2. The review decisions (`context/review_threads.json`, `reviewDecisions` oldest first: `state`, `author`, `submittedAt`, `body` when one was written, `dismissed`) and the threads: each decision with its author and time. Dated events establish which approvals and requests stood at the merge. A current `DISMISSED` state or `dismissed` flag with no withdrawal time establishes only the state at capture, not whether dismissal preceded merge. A `truncated` record is a collection gap for this practice. The precomputed leads below these criteria list the merge and one row per decision with `beforeMerge`, `isAuthor`, `dismissed` and `bot` computed, and each reviewer's last decision apart: decide from the rows, and quote the decision and the merge from the record.
3. The inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): whether other people work in this project, for the occasion only.
If `merged_at` or the decisions are unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: at least one APPROVED decision by another person — a login other than the author's, not marked `bot` — submitted before `merged_at`, with no later dismissal, revocation or request for changes by that reviewer, and no other person's request for changes still standing. An approval marked `bot` never makes this cell. Who pressed merge does not enter into it. Quote the approval and the merge time.
- NOT_MET: merged with no standing approval from another person — a complete record whose only approvals are marked `bot` is this case — or over another person's standing request for changes. Quote the merge time and the decisions that stood, or the absence of any.
- UNDETERMINED: the complete captured decision record carries no usable time for a deciding event, so its order relative to merge cannot be settled. This includes a current dismissal or revocation with no independently dated withdrawal event; an original review submission timestamp does not date a later withdrawal. A truncated required record is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: merged with no approval where a reviewer was requested and had not answered. MAJOR: merged over a standing request for changes, or after an approval was dismissed and not renewed. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote `merged_at`, `merged_by` and each decision as recorded with its `author`, `state` and `submittedAt`. Identity is the login as recorded, compared as text: the same login is the same account. Whether an account is automated is the captured `bot` marker, never the login's shape or a display name; a decision without the marker counts as its reviewer's own. Never infer that a reviewer is the author from a display name, a repository path or a namespace; never infer an approval from a comment or a thumbs-up; never treat the author's own approval as one.

## Defer
Whether review threads were resolved belongs to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`. Here only: did another person approve before the merge?

practices.name: Record the plan before the first commit
practices.whyItMatters: A tracked issue written before the first recorded commit gives reviewers a prior statement of the work. Commit timestamps provide a recorded ordering, not proof of when someone actually started thinking or coding.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The tracked issue this change implements has an opening timestamp no later than the earliest captured commit author timestamp. The record names both times without inferring intent or unrecorded work.
practices.holdsAs: The issue exists before the first recorded commit
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the tracked issue this change implements exists no later than the earliest captured authored commit, without inferring actual work-start or motive.

## The standard
Judge one thing: did the issue this pull request implements exist no later than the first recorded commit? The earliest captured commit author date (`context/commits.json`, `authoredAt`) is the recorded timing proxy. It does not establish when actual work began, and the pull request creation time is a handoff time, not a substitute for it. The issue's opening is its `createdAt` in the linked work item. An issue opened before the first captured commit precedes that recorded step; an issue opened after it follows that step. Neither timing establishes the author's intent or the order of unrecorded work. Judge only the recorded order of the two dates, never the quality of the issue or of the change.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when: no named issue is one this pull request implements — a captured item or one among the `unresolvedReferences` — because the description names none, or rules each out (`Not related to #N`, an aside about other work); or the change is of a kind that answers no issue by convention — a release, a bot dependency update, a revert. Only a candidate issue the precomputed leads list can be that issue: one captured as this repository's closing candidate (`how: closesOnMerge`, including a link made in the provider's UI), or named by a closing keyword, the title, the branch or the author's own `Related to #N`. One named only by `Related to` counts when the description or the issue shows this change delivers part of that issue's work, not when the sentence is about other work. A number the leads do not list is no occasion — a bare `#N`, a `Related to` in a quotation, code or HTML comment, another project's issue. A related issue is captured as a mention, not a closing candidate: never say it closed or will close with this merge. Whether an issue is linked at all belongs to `links-the-change-to-its-issue`; here the linked issue is the occasion.

## Sources
1. The linked work item (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`, its opening line `Opened <time>`, and `linked_work_items.json`, `createdAt`): when the issue was opened. It establishes the plan's date.
2. The commits (`context/commits.json`, `authoredAt`): author dates of recorded commits. Require a usable author date for every captured commit and compare the earliest; neither a commit date nor a handoff timestamp substitutes for missing author dates. These dates do not establish actual work-start.
3. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): the identity of the reviewed work, never a substitute start time.
4. The precomputed leads below these criteria: each candidate issue, how it was named, its opening time, the earliest commit's author date and the hours between them, computed; read the two dates from it and check them against the sources above.
Failed or missing required linked-work-item or commit capture is a collection gap and produces no observation. Successfully captured records with missing native dates leave the timing UNDETERMINED.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the issue's `createdAt` is no later than the earliest captured commit's usable `authoredAt`, and every captured commit has a usable author date. Quote both times.
- NOT_MET: the issue's `createdAt` is later than the earliest captured commit's usable `authoredAt`, and every captured commit has a usable author date. Quote both times.
- UNDETERMINED: the complete captured commit record is empty or any captured commit has no usable author date, so the timing proxy cannot be established; or the issue this change implements has no opening time here — its number is among the `unresolvedReferences`, so this repository holds no synchronized issue under it, or its linked item carries no `createdAt`. Record as the open question which issue that is and when it was opened, and as what would settle it that issue's opening time in this repository; never claim it exists, predates the work or closes. Or several named issues remain plausible as the one this change implements, their dates fall in different outcomes, and the description and issues do not settle which. Name them; never choose the favourable one.
One observation per review, on the issue the change implements; when several plausible issues fall in the same cell, on the one a closing candidate names, else the title, else the branch, else the `Related to`.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MINOR on this alone — non-blocking. Calibrate the nudge to the recorded planning gap and its coordination cost; elapsed time alone does not establish an intention or raise severity.

## Grounding
Cite the linked item's `Opened <time>` line and the reviewed pull request record; cite the earliest usable author date and SHA from the captured `context/commits.json` artifact. Never infer an order from issue and pull request numbers; never read a commit date where an author date exists.

## Defer
Whether the change names its issue belongs to `links-the-change-to-its-issue`; whether the issue states a checkable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: did the issue exist before the first recorded commit?

groups.name: Building iOS apps well
groups.description: Write SwiftUI the way it is designed to be written: views that describe the screen from state they are handed, state owned where it belongs, concurrency that is structured, an interface everyone can use, a preview for every screen, and permissions declared truthfully. These practices run only on changes that touch Swift code.

practices.name: Keep networking and persistence out of views

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: A SwiftUI view that fetches, decodes or saves is a view nobody can preview, test or reuse, and its logic is invisible to the next screen that needs the same data. Keeping that work in a model or store is what lets the view stay a description of the screen.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Views describe the screen from state they are handed; requests, decoding and file or preference access live in a model, store or service the view talks to through a method or a binding, and SwiftData is used through its own view-side idiom.
practices.holdsAs: Views render the state they are handed and never fetch or persist
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: added SwiftUI view code delegates I/O appropriately or uses the framework's supported view-side persistence idiom.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the SwiftUI code this change adds: does a `View` type perform I/O itself? I/O in a view is a `URLSession` or `URLRequest` call, `JSONDecoder`/`JSONEncoder` use, `UserDefaults` or `FileManager` access, `Data(contentsOf:)`, a Core Data fetch request, or a `fetch`/`load`/`save` implemented inside a `struct … : View` — in `body`, a modifier closure (`.task`, `.onAppear`, a button action) or a method of the view. A view that calls a model's method (`store.load()`, `viewModel.save(item)`) or passes a `Binding` is not performing I/O, and SwiftData's own idiom — `@Query`, and `modelContext.insert`/`delete` through `@Environment(\.modelContext)` — is the framework's designed use of a view, not I/O the view took on. The judgement is about where the work lives, never about the architecture's name.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change adds no code inside a SwiftUI view type: no added line lies within a `struct … : View` (or a `some View` computed property) — a model-only, service-only, test-only or non-Swift change carries no surface. Added lines inside a view type are the occasion, whether or not they perform I/O.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added lines and the type each hunk lies in, read from the hunk header and the surrounding declaration. It establishes which added lines are inside a view type and which call I/O. It never establishes what unchanged code does.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the enclosing type of a hunk when the diff context does not show it, and whether a called method belongs to a model or store. Read it only to place a line; it never adds an I/O call the diff does not show.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the I/O calls it found inside view types, as leads to inspect, never as conclusions.
If the diff of a Swift file is truncated where a view type is edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Scan the added lines inside view types first, then assess the standard.
The undesirable behaviour is I/O inside a view. Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: an added line inside a view type performs I/O itself — a `URLSession`/`URLRequest` call, `JSONDecoder`, `UserDefaults`, `FileManager`, `Data(contentsOf:)`, a Core Data fetch or an inline fetch-and-parse. Quote the line and name the view type.
- MET: a complete bounded review of the added view code shows no direct I/O. The view may need no I/O at all, or it delegates required I/O to a model, store or service. Cite the added view code and its enclosing declaration; quote a delegating call only when one exists.
- UNDETERMINED: the hunk shows the call but neither the context nor the checkout shows whether the enclosing type is a view; name the declaration that would settle it.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential I/O line when there are several.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one read (`UserDefaults`, a decode) inside a view, or I/O in a small preview-only or prototype view. MAJOR: a network request or a persistence write implemented inside a shipped view, or the same I/O repeated in several views. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` added line that performs the I/O and the `struct … : View` declaration it lies in, For MET, cite the added view code and its enclosing declaration, and record the diff as the source searched: every added line inside a view type was read. Include a delegating call when relevant. Never claim I/O from a method name alone (`load()` may be a model call); never claim a type is a view without its declaration; never count a SwiftData `modelContext` call as I/O.

## Defer
Duplicated logic across views belongs to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; oversized view bodies to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`. Here only: does the view do I/O itself?

practices.name: Own SwiftUI state at the right level

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: State declared in the wrong place is the root of the bugs that make SwiftUI feel unpredictable: a model recreated on every render, a value copied into two views that drift apart, a derived value stored and forgotten. Declaring each piece of state where it is owned keeps the screen a function of its data.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Value state a single view owns is `@State`; a shared model is `@Observable` and injected through the environment or passed down, never recreated in a child; a child that edits a parent's value takes a `Binding`; a derived value is computed, not stored.
practices.holdsAs: Each piece of state lives at the level that owns it
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: each piece of SwiftUI state declared where it is owned — view-local values as `@State`, shared models observed and injected, edits through `Binding`, derived values computed rather than stored.

## The standard
Judge the state declarations this change adds to SwiftUI views against four rules. (1) A value one view owns and mutates is `@State` (or `@AppStorage` for a persisted setting); a `let` or plain `var` that the view mutates is a lapse. (2) A model shared by more than one view is one object: `@Observable` (or `ObservableObject`) created once by its owner and reached through `@Environment`, `@Bindable` or a passed reference — a child view that creates its own instance of a shared model (`@State private var store = Store()` in a child, `StateObject` for a model the parent already holds) is a lapse. (3) A child that edits a parent's value takes a `Binding` (`@Binding`, `$value`), not a copy it mutates. (4) A value derivable from other state (a count, a filtered list, a formatted string) is a computed property, not a second stored variable kept in sync by hand. Judge declarations and how they are wired, never naming or file layout.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change adds no state declaration or state wiring to a SwiftUI view: no added `@State`, `@Binding`, `@Environment`, `@Bindable`, `@AppStorage`, `@Observable`, `ObservableObject`, `StateObject`, `ObservedObject`, or a mutable stored property inside a view type. A change to a view's layout alone carries no surface.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added declarations and the wiring that hands state between views (`init` arguments, `.environment(…)`, `$` bindings). It establishes what was declared where. It never establishes what unchanged views hold.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether a model type is `@Observable`, whether a parent already owns an instance a child recreates, and whether a stored value is derivable from other declared state. Read it to place a declaration; it never adds a declaration the diff does not show.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the declarations it found inside view types, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a view's declarations are edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added state declarations first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added declaration follows the four rules — local values `@State`, shared models observed once and injected, edits through bindings, derived values computed. Quote the declaration you accepted as the representative.
- NOT_MET: a declaration breaks a rule — a mutable stored property in a view without `@State`; a child creating a second instance of a model the parent owns; a copied value the child mutates where a `Binding` was needed; a stored value kept in sync by hand with the state it derives from. Quote the declaration and name the rule.
- UNDETERMINED: whether a model is shared or owned by this view alone cannot be told from the diff and the checkout; name the type and the fact that would settle it.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential declaration when several break a rule.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a derived value stored, or a mutable `var` that should be `@State` in a leaf view. MAJOR: a shared model recreated in a child (state that silently resets or diverges), or a copied value edited where the parent's value was meant to change. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` declaration and, for a shared-model lapse, the parent's declaration of the same model. Never claim a model is shared without a second view that holds it; never claim a value is derivable without naming the state it derives from.

## Defer
I/O inside views belongs to `keeps-views-free-of-networking-and-persistence`; concurrency belongs to `uses-structured-concurrency-safely`. Here only: is the state declared where it is owned?

practices.name: Make the UI accessible by default

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: A control a screen reader cannot name, a label that cannot grow with the user's text size, an image that says nothing — each locks a group of people out of the screen, and each is a line the author could have written when the view was made. Accessibility added later is the expensive kind.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Every icon-only control and meaningful image has a label; text uses semantic fonts so Dynamic Type works; nothing is fixed to a size that clips at larger text; colour is never the only signal.
practices.holdsAs: Every control carries a label and text scales with the user
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the added SwiftUI interface is usable with a screen reader and at large text sizes — icon-only controls and meaningful images labelled, text sized semantically, layout free of size caps that clip.

## The standard
Judge the interface code this change adds against a closed list of accessibility facts. (1) An icon-only control — a `Button`, `Toggle`, `Link` or tappable `Image` whose visible content is an `Image(systemName:)` or an asset image with no text — carries an `accessibilityLabel` (or a `Label` with a text title). (2) A meaningful image (an asset that carries information) carries a label or is marked `.accessibilityHidden(true)` when decorative. (3) Text, and an SF Symbol shown with it, use a semantic font (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, `.title2`, …) or a scaled custom font, not `.font(.system(size: 14))` or a fixed-size custom font — a symbol sized in points stays small when the text around it grows. (4) No text container is capped in height (`.frame(height:)`, `.lineLimit(1)` on body copy) in a way that clips at larger text. (5) A state shown by colour alone (red for error, green for done) is also shown by text, an icon or a trait. Judge added lines only; an existing lapse the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change adds no interface code: no added `Image`, `Button`, `Toggle`, `Text`, `Label`, `.font(`, `.frame(` or colour-state line inside a SwiftUI view. Added interface lines are the occasion, whether or not they carry a lapse.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added interface lines and the modifiers attached to them in the same expression. It establishes what each control and text carries. A modifier on the same view chain counts; one on a distant ancestor does not establish a label for an inner icon.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether an asset image is decorative or informative, and which font overload a custom font uses: `.custom(_:size:)` scales with the body style, `.custom(_:size:relativeTo:)` scales with the style it names, and only `.custom(_:fixedSize:)` stays fixed. Read it to classify; it never adds a control the diff does not show.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the icon-only controls, fixed-size fonts and height caps it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a view body is edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added controls, images and text first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added icon-only control and meaningful image is labelled, added text uses a semantic or scaling font, no added cap clips text, and no added state relies on colour alone. Quote a representative labelled control or scaling font.
- NOT_MET: at least one added item breaks the list — an unlabelled icon-only control or informative image, a fixed-size font, a clipping cap, a colour-only state. Quote the line and name the rule.
- UNDETERMINED: an image whose informative or decorative role the checkout does not settle; name the asset.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential lapse when there are several; count the rest in the summary.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one unlabelled icon or one fixed-size font. MAJOR: a primary action of the screen unreachable by screen reader, or a screen whose main text cannot scale. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` line of the control, image, font or cap. Never claim a label is missing without reading the whole view chain the control sits in; never claim clipping from a `.frame` on a non-text container.

## Defer
Localisation of the strings belongs to no practice here; magic numbers in layout to none. Here only: can everyone use what was added?

practices.name: Use structured concurrency safely

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: An unstructured task that outlives its view, UI state mutated off the main actor, a fire-and-forget request that cannot be cancelled — these are the crashes and stale screens that appear only on a slow network. Swift's structured concurrency prevents them when it is used the way it is designed.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: View-lifecycle work runs in `.task` or another effective cancellation lifecycle. A synchronous user action can start a Task whose lifetime fits the operation; UI state stays correctly isolated and needed results or failures are handled.
practices.holdsAs: Async work is scoped to its view and cancelled with it
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: async work tied to the lifetime that owns it, UI state mutated on the main actor, and no fire-and-forget task where structure was available.

## The standard
Judge the concurrency code this change adds against a closed list. (1) View-lifecycle work belongs in `.task { }` or an equivalent observed cancellation lifecycle. A `Task { }` in a synchronous button action is a native bridge to asynchronous work, not a defect by itself. Judge whether its lifetime and cancellation fit the operation: work that must stop with the view has an effective cancellation path, while a user-initiated operation can legitimately complete after the view disappears. A stored handle or a written reason can establish intent but is not mandatory when the captured code already establishes the lifecycle. (2) State the UI reads is mutated on the main actor: a type that holds view state is isolated to the main actor — by `@MainActor`, by the module's default actor isolation or by what it inherits — or the mutation is `await MainActor.run`; a mutation of `@Published`/`@Observable` UI state from a background context is a lapse. (3) Detached work and dispatch queues have an evidenced need for their independent execution or scheduling; the captured code may establish that need without a redundant comment. (4) A result needed by the operation is consumed or its failure meaningfully handled; a task can perform a side effect without its handle being stored. Judge added lines; existing concurrency the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change adds no concurrency: no added `async`, `await`, `Task`, `.task`, `@MainActor`, `MainActor.run`, `Task.detached`, `DispatchQueue` or actor declaration. Added concurrency is the occasion, whether or not it carries a lapse.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added concurrency constructs and where they sit (a view modifier, a model method, a service). It establishes what was written. It never establishes the actor a type is isolated to when that declaration is outside the diff.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the declaration of the type a mutation lands in (`@MainActor` or not), and whether a `Task` handle is stored. Read it to place a construct; it never adds one.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the `Task {` blocks, `.onAppear` with async work, detached tasks and dispatch queues it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where async code is added, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added constructs first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added construct follows the list — view-lifecycle work cancelled appropriately, user-triggered async work with an appropriate lifetime, UI state isolated correctly, and needed results consumed. Quote a representative construct.
- NOT_MET: an added construct breaks the list — view-lifecycle work that can outlive its owner without appropriate cancellation, UI state mutated off the main actor, detached work or a dispatch queue with no evidenced need, an unconsumed result needed by the operation. Quote the line and name the rule.
- UNDETERMINED: an added line mutates UI state from an async context and the isolation of its type is in neither the diff nor the checkout; name the type. An added call into an unchanged method is judged as a call, never by what that method does inside.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential lapse when there are several.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a lifecycle mismatch on a short local operation. MAJOR: a network request in an uncancelled task that writes view state, or UI state mutated from a background context. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` construct and, for an actor lapse, the declaration of the type mutated. Never claim a mutation is off the main actor without the type's isolation; never claim a task is fire-and-forget when a handle is stored in the same hunk.

## Defer
Swallowed errors in async code belong to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; crash-shaped constructs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`. Here only: is the concurrency structured?

practices.name: Ship a preview with each new view

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: A SwiftUI view without a preview is a screen nobody can see without running the whole app to it, and the first thing the next person deletes when it breaks. A preview with representative data is the cheapest verification a view can have, and the way a reviewer sees what changed.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The new screens and presentation a change adds can be seen in a `#Preview` with representative sample data — including an empty, loading or error state when they have one — so they can be checked without launching the app.
practices.holdsAs: New views ship with previews that show what they present
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the new SwiftUI presentation a change adds arriving with a `#Preview` (or `PreviewProvider`) that renders it with representative data and its important states.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when this change adds new SwiftUI view types, can the presentation they add be seen in a preview from the same change? A preview is a `#Preview` block or a `PreviewProvider`. It covers a view it constructs, and a view that a host it constructs demonstrably renders: a new row, badge or section shown through a previewed host's body is covered by that preview. It is representative when it hands the presentation sample data of the shape it renders (a filled model, a non-empty list) rather than defaults only, and it is complete when presentation that has an empty, loading or error state is previewed in that state too. A view that only owns lifecycle or effects — starting and cancelling work, holding the model — and passes everything it shows to a content view adds no presentation of its own: representative previews of that content view cover it, and it needs no new initializer, injection or architecture just so a preview can construct it. What such a wrapper renders itself — a navigation title, a toolbar, an overlay, other chrome, or a state the content view never receives — is its own presentation, and a preview must show it. A preview that constructs the view with a fresh or live view model and no sample shows only the view's first state — a spinner, an empty list, a prompt — and a live fetch inside a preview is not sample data; such a preview exists but is not representative. A preview for an existing view the change edits is welcome but not required. Judge coverage and representativeness, never layout, naming, or which type a `#Preview` names.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change adds no new view type: no added `struct … : View` declaration in a non-test file. An edit to an existing view, a model-only change or a preview-only change carries no surface.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): the added `struct … : View` declarations and the `#Preview`/`PreviewProvider` blocks in the same change. It establishes which new views a preview constructs and what data it passes. It never establishes that a preview renders.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): a preview that lives in another file of the same change, sample-data helpers it uses, the body of a host it constructs, and the body of a new owner view. Read it to find the preview, to establish that a host renders a new view with the data the preview supplies, and to establish that an owner passes everything it shows to a previewed content view; it never supplies a preview the change did not add.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the new view types and the previews it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a new view is declared, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the new view types first — every added `struct … : View`, `private` and file-scoped ones included — and for each name the presentation it adds and the preview that covers it. A view is covered by a preview that constructs it; a nested view, by a preview that constructs a host whose body you read renders it with that preview's data; an effect-only owner, by tracing its body to the content view it passes everything to and naming that content's previews, while any chrome or state the owner renders itself still needs a preview that shows it. Never assume a host renders a view you did not trace; a helper's smallness goes to the severity, not to the outcome. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: every new view's presentation is covered by a preview in the same change that hands it representative data and shows its important states. Quote the declaration and its covering preview; for a nested view also the host line that renders it, and for an effect-only owner the line in its body that delegates to the content view.
- NOT_MET: every new view is covered, but a preview renders the presentation with nothing representative — an empty list for a list screen, a placeholder model with default values — or omits a state the view plainly has. Quote the preview and name what it lacks.
- NOT_MET: at least one new view's presentation is covered by no preview in the change — presentation no preview covers, or a wrapper's own chrome or state that no preview shows — after scanning every Swift file in the diff. Quote the declaration and say what you scanned.
- UNDETERMINED: a preview exists in the checkout but the diff does not show whether this change added it, or whether a host renders the new view, or an owner only delegates, cannot be read; name the file.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential view when there are several.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MINOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR: a new view with no preview or with an unrepresentative one. INFO: a small part of covered presentation left out — a row's alternate state, a wrapper's toolbar button — while the main presentation is previewed. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` `struct … : View` declaration and the covering `#Preview` line — with the host line that renders a nested view, or the owner's line that delegates to its previewed content view — or for absent the declaration and the scan. Never claim a preview renders or compiles; never claim a host covers a view, or an owner only delegates, without quoting the line in its body that shows it.

## Defer
How to verify the change as a whole belongs to `states-how-to-verify-the-change`; tests for logic to `ships-tests-with-the-change`. Here only: can the new screen be seen?

practices.name: Declare permissions truthfully and ask at the point of use

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: A capability the app requests without a usage description crashes on the device; one with a boilerplate description fails App Review and the user's trust; one requested at launch instead of at the moment it is needed is denied and never asked again. The declaration and the ask are part of the feature.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When a change adds a capability that needs the user's permission, the `Info.plist` usage description arrives in the same change, says truthfully what the app does with the access, and the permission is requested where the feature needs it, not at launch.
practices.holdsAs: Permissions say truthfully why and are asked for in use
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a capability that needs the user's permission arriving with a truthful usage description and a request made where the feature needs it.

## The standard
Judge the permission-bearing capabilities this change adds against three facts. (1) Declaration: when the platform requires usage-description keys for the access actually requested, the matching keys are present in `Info.plist`, `project.yml` or the target's build settings. Determine the keys from the actual authorization API and deployment target, not an import or one fixed key per framework. For example, modern EventKit full or write-only calendar access uses the corresponding `NSCalendarsFullAccessUsageDescription` or `NSCalendarsWriteOnlyAccessUsageDescription`; legacy calendar APIs differ. Notification authorization needs no usage-description key, and the system photo picker needs no full-library authorization. (2) Truth: the description names what the app does with the access, not a placeholder ("needed", "for the app", an empty string). (3) Point of use: the authorization request (`requestWhenInUseAuthorization`, `requestAuthorization`, `PHPhotoLibrary.requestAuthorization`, …) is made from the feature that needs it, not from app launch or a root view's `onAppear`. Judge added capabilities; an existing one the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change adds no permission-bearing capability: no added permission-requiring access through `CoreLocation`, direct photo-library APIs, `AVFoundation` capture, `UserNotifications`, `EventKit`, `Contacts`, `HealthKit`, `AppTrackingTransparency` or an authorization request. `SwiftUI`'s `PhotosPicker` or `PHPickerViewController` alone needs no full-library permission and is not the occasion; an import alone does not establish restricted access.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): the added capability code, authorization requests, and usage-description keys in `Info.plist`, `project.yml` or `*.pbxproj`. It establishes what was added where. It never establishes what the app already declared.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the existing `Info.plist`/`project.yml` for a key the change relies on but did not add, and the call site of the request. Read it to complete the picture; a key present there satisfies the declaration.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the capabilities, requests and usage keys it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where the capability is added, or the project's plist is unreadable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added capabilities first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added permission-requiring capability has a truthful usage key when required (in the change or checkout), and authorization is requested at the point of use. Quote the required key and request, or name the platform exemption.
- NOT_MET: the key is present but the description is a placeholder, or the request is made at launch or from a root view rather than the feature. Quote the description or the request site.
- NOT_MET: an added capability requires a usage key but has none anywhere in the change or the checkout. Quote the capability line and say where you looked.
- UNDETERMINED: the usage keys live in a build setting or generated file the checkout does not carry; name it.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential capability when there are several.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a placeholder description, or a request made one screen early. MAJOR: a capability with no usage key at all (a crash on device), or a request made at launch for a feature the user has not reached. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` capability or request line and the plist/project key as written. Never claim a key is missing without stating the files scanned; never claim a request site is launch without the call chain that reaches it.

## Defer
Over-broad permissions and insecure defaults belong to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`. Here only: is the permission declared truthfully and asked for at the point of use?

practices.name: Use adaptive colors so every appearance works

precondition.skipReason: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: A screen built from literal colors is right in one appearance and wrong in the other: white text vanishes on a light background, a hard-coded card stays white in Dark Mode, and every screen has to be revisited when the palette changes. Semantic and asset colors adapt on their own, and the whole app follows one palette.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Text, backgrounds and fills use semantic colors (`.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`), materials, the accent color or named asset colors with light and dark variants; a literal is used only where the color is part of the content, such as text over a fill the same view sets.
practices.holdsAs: Colors adapt to light and dark appearance alike
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the added interface takes its colors from the system's semantic set, materials, the accent color or asset colors with both appearances, not from literals that hold one appearance.

## The standard
Judge the color choices the change adds to SwiftUI views against a closed list. A literal is `Color.white`, `Color.black`, `.white` or `.black` as a foreground, background or fill, `Color(red:green:blue:)`, `Color(hex:)` or a hex-parsing initializer, `UIColor(red:)`, `Color(uiColor: .white/.black)`, and a color from `.gray`/`.systemGray` when it stands for text on a background. An adaptive color is a semantic one (`.primary`, `.secondary`, `.tertiary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.secondarySystemBackground`, `.label`), a material (`.ultraThinMaterial`, `.regularMaterial`), the accent (`.accentColor`, `.tint`) or a named asset color (`Color("Card")`, `Color(.card)`) — an asset color is adaptive when its colorset carries a dark appearance. A literal is not a lapse where the color is the content: text or a symbol over a fill or image the same view sets, a brand color deliberately constant, a shadow. Judge the added lines only.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change sets no color in a SwiftUI view: no added `.foregroundStyle`, `.foregroundColor`, `.background`, `.fill`, `.tint`, `.shadow(color:` or `Color`/`UIColor` expression inside a view type. Added color lines are the occasion, whether or not they carry a lapse.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: each added color expression and the modifier chain it sits in — what it colors (text, background, fill) and what fill the same view sets around it. It establishes the literal and its role. It never establishes an unchanged view's colors.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the asset catalog (`*.xcassets/<name>.colorset/Contents.json`) for a named color's appearances, and a color extension (`Color+App.swift`) a name may resolve to. Read it to classify a name; a `Color("x")` whose colorset has only one appearance is a literal in disguise.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the literal and adaptive color lines it found and, for each named asset color, whether its colorset has a dark appearance, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a view body is edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added color expressions first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added color is adaptive, or a literal only where the color is the content. Quote a representative adaptive color.
- NOT_MET: an added literal colors text on a system background, a screen or card background, or a fill the rest of the interface adapts around — one appearance baked in. Quote the line and name what it colors.
- UNDETERMINED: a named color whose colorset the checkout does not carry and whose appearance the diff does not show; name the asset.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential literal when there are several; count the rest in the summary.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one literal text or fill color on a secondary element. MAJOR: a screen or card background, or the primary text of a screen, hard-coded to one appearance. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` color line and, when the role matters, the fill or background line of the same view; for an asset color, the colorset's appearances. Never call a color a literal without its line; never call a named color adaptive without its colorset or its definition.

## Defer
Labels, fonts and colour-only state belong to `makes-ui-accessible-by-default`. Here only: does the color hold in both appearances?

groups.name: Communicating in the open
groups.description: How you talk to teammates in shared channels: ask questions someone can actually answer, give answers people can act on, and keep others informed about where the work stands and what is blocking it. This is about the clarity of the exchange, not the correctness of the code being discussed.

practices.name: Ask questions a teammate can answer
practices.whyItMatters: A vague question forces the person helping you to stop and ask what you actually mean before they can even start, turning a one-message answer into a slow exchange. A question that carries its own context gets answered on the first reply.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A question that says what you are trying to do, what you already tried, and exactly where it broke, so a teammate can answer it in a single reply without asking you anything first.
practices.holdsAs: Questions carry the goal, the attempt and the error
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a question posed in the captured exchange carries enough context — the goal, what was tried, what happened — for a teammate to answer it in one reply.

## The standard
Judge whether a question raised in this conversation gives a teammate enough to answer it in a single reply, rather than forcing a round of clarifying questions first. A well-formed ask names the concrete goal, what was already tried, and what actually happened or is blocking. A bare "it doesn't work" or "how do I do this?" with no context makes the responder guess. Judge only the observable way the question is posed; never whether the underlying problem is real, hard or worth solving. Use judgment about how much context the question genuinely needs: a quick clarification among people who plainly share the context is not a defect.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the turn is not actually a question (a statement, an acknowledgement, social chat), or when there is no settled conversation to read. A real question whose needed context is supplied by the surrounding turns is not NOT_APPLICABLE; it is MET.

## Sources
1. The turn that poses the question (`context/conversation_thread.json`): its stated objective, what was tried, the exact behaviour seen or the specific point of confusion. It establishes how the question is posed. It never establishes whether the problem is real or worth solving.
2. The surrounding turns of the same thread (`context/conversation_thread.json`): earlier turns may supply the context the question leans on; a later reply that has to ask what was meant shows what the responder had to extract first. They establish what context was shared inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether what the question leans on was supplied in a turn you never saw, report a collection gap and record no observation; that is neither absent nor UNDETERMINED.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: a knowledgeable teammate could answer the question from the message alone, or from the message plus the surrounding turns, because it states the objective and the specific point of confusion or the exact behaviour seen. A quick clarification between people who share obvious context belongs here.
- NOT_MET: the question is so thin on context that answering it requires asking the author what they mean, what they tried, or what they expected — and no surrounding turn supplies it. Name the missing element.
- UNDETERMINED only when every declared turn was captured and the meaning still genuinely admits incompatible readings; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. Having read the whole thread and found the context missing is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED. A thread that begins mid-conversation is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, on the question turn you assessed.

## Severity
NOT_MET only. Scale to how much a responder must extract before they can help. MINOR, the usual band: a little more detail would sharpen the ask. MAJOR: the question as written cannot be answered without a full exchange of clarifications first. Never above MAJOR on question phrasing alone; this is a formative practice, never a gate.

## Grounding
Quote the exact turn you assessed. For MET where the surrounding turns supply the context, quote those turns too. For NOT_MET, the citations show the question and the boundary you searched: the whole captured thread, with no turn supplying the goal, the attempt or the observed behaviour. Describe the observable gap — "the question names no goal and no attempt" — never laziness or intent. Never invent missing context, grade an exchange you cannot quote, or claim the problem is or is not real.

## Defer
Whether the reply moves the asker forward belongs to `gives-actionable-answers`. Here only: does the question, as posed, let a teammate answer it in one reply?

practices.name: Give answers people can act on
practices.whyItMatters: When someone asks for help, a reply that only gestures at the problem leaves them exactly as stuck as before and burns another round of messages. An answer with a concrete next step lets them get moving right away.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A reply that either solves the question outright or points to the exact next step or place to look, so the person who asked can act on it immediately instead of asking again.
practices.holdsAs: Answers give the next step, not another question
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a reply to a question in the captured exchange gives the asker something to act on now — the answer, the exact place to look, or the next step.

## The standard
Judge whether a reply to someone's question actually moves them forward, rather than leaving them where they started. A useful answer either resolves the question directly or names a concrete next step the asker can take. A reply that only restates the problem, points vaguely at "the docs", or answers a different question does not. A short answer can be fully actionable; length is not the signal. Judge only the observable helpfulness of the reply as written, never whether its technical content is ultimately correct. Use judgment about what the asker needed.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the turn is not answering a question; when no question was actually asked; when the reply is a reasonable partial step in an ongoing exchange; or when there is no settled conversation to read.

## Sources
1. The question turn (`context/conversation_thread.json`): what was asked and what the asker needed. It establishes the question the reply is measured against. It never establishes whether the problem is real or hard.
2. The reply turn (`context/conversation_thread.json`): the answer given, the place named, the step proposed. It establishes what the asker can do next. It never establishes that the answer is technically right.
3. The surrounding turns (`context/conversation_thread.json`): whether the exchange is still in progress, and whether the answer had already been given elsewhere in the thread. They establish the state of the exchange inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing; judge the reply by its own words. When a real question and its reply are both in front of you but the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether the answer had already been given elsewhere in it, report a collection gap and record no observation; that is neither absent nor UNDETERMINED.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the asker could act on the reply immediately because it gives the answer, the specific place to look, or the exact next step.
- NOT_MET: a genuine question was met with a reply that leaves the asker still stuck — too vague to act on, or it sidesteps what was asked. Name what the asker still lacks.
- UNDETERMINED only when every declared turn was captured and the meaning still genuinely admits incompatible readings; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. Having read the reply and the surrounding turns and found no actionable content is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED. A thread that begins mid-conversation is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, on the question-and-reply pair you assessed.

## Severity
NOT_MET only. Scale to how stuck the asker remains after the reply. MINOR, the usual band: the answer is nearly there and one pointer would land it. MAJOR: a real question is met with a reply that cannot be acted on at all. Never above MAJOR on reply clarity alone; this is a formative practice, never a gate.

## Grounding
Quote the question and the reply you assessed. For NOT_MET, the citations show the question, the reply, and the boundary you searched: the surrounding captured turns, with no other turn supplying the answer. Describe the observable gap — "the reply names no place to look and no step" — never dismissiveness. Never fabricate an answer the reply did not give, and never claim the reply's content is correct or incorrect.

## Defer
Whether the question itself carried enough context to be answerable belongs to `asks-answerable-questions`. Here only: does the reply, as written, let the asker move forward?

practices.name: Post clear status and blocker updates
practices.whyItMatters: When work stalls quietly, the people depending on it keep waiting without knowing anything is wrong, and a blocker someone else could have cleared in minutes sits for days. A plain update on where things stand and what you need keeps the team moving.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: An update that says where the work stands and, when you are stuck, names the blocker and what would unblock it, so teammates can plan around it or step in to help.
practices.holdsAs: Updates say where the work stands and what blocks it
practices.criteria:
Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: an update about ongoing work says where things stand and, when stuck, names the blocker and what would clear it.

## The standard
Judge whether an update about ongoing work tells the team where things stand and, when the author is stuck, names the blocker plainly along with what is needed to clear it. A clear update lets teammates plan around the work or step in to unblock it; an update so vague no one can tell whether help is needed leaves the team guessing. Judge only the observable clarity of the update, never whether the work itself is on track. Use judgment about how much an update needs to say: a brief "still on it, no blockers" among teammates already in sync is fine, and a real update made clear by its surrounding context is a good update, not a missing one.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the turn is not a status update, when there is no in-flight work or blocker to report, or when there is no settled conversation to read. A real update whose standing or blocker is established by the surrounding turns is not NOT_APPLICABLE; it is MET.

## Sources
1. The update turn (`context/conversation_thread.json`): what it says about the current standing, whether it reports being blocked, what it names as the blocker and what it asks for. It establishes the clarity of the update as posted. It never establishes whether the work is actually on track or whether the blocker is real.
2. The surrounding turns of the same thread (`context/conversation_thread.json`): earlier turns may already establish the standing an update omits, or show that the teammates are in sync; a later turn that has to ask what is needed shows what the update left unsaid. They establish what was shared inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When an update IS posted but the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether the standing it omits was already established, report a collection gap and record no observation; that is neither absent nor UNDETERMINED.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the update states the current standing and, if blocked, says what is blocking and what would unblock it — from the turn alone or from the turn plus the surrounding thread.
- NOT_MET: an update on stalled or in-flight work that hides a blocker behind a vague line, or reports being stuck without naming what is actually needed, so no one can plan or help. Quote the vague line and name what the team cannot tell from it.
- UNDETERMINED only when every declared turn was captured and the update's meaning still genuinely admits incompatible readings; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. A thread that begins mid-conversation is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, on the update turn you assessed.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on update clarity alone — a formative practice, never a gate. Scale to how much the update leaves the team unable to plan or help. MINOR, the usual band: the standing is clear but the ask is fuzzy. MAJOR: a real blocker is present yet the update gives the team nothing to act on.

## Grounding
Quote the update you assessed. For MET where the surrounding turns supply the standing or the ask, quote those turns too. For NOT_MET, quote the vague line and the turns you read around it. Describe the observable gap — "the update says it is blocked and names no blocker" — never avoidance or intent. Never invent a blocker the author did not mention, and never claim the work is or is not on track.

## Defer
Whether a question posed in the thread carries enough context to answer belongs to `asks-answerable-questions`; whether a reply moves the asker forward belongs to `gives-actionable-answers`. Here only: does the update tell the team where things stand and what would unblock them?
